subtopic: LIVESTOCK, MEAT AND HAY    LIFTING OF UNITED STATES EMBARGO

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: LIVESTOCK, MEAT AND HAY    LIFTING OF UNITED STATES EMBARGO
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief statement with respect to the lifting of the United States embargo against our livestock, meat and hay. Most hon. members will have read in the press or heard on the radio yesterday's news report from Washington indicating the early lifting of the embargo in so far as hay from eastern provinces is concerned. It will be remembered that on November 28 a news report came from Washington which was interpreted to mean that the embargo against livestock, meat and other products affected, would be lifted on March 1, 1953.
The announcement said: "If present favourable conditions continue Canada will be declared free of foot-and-mouth disease on March 1, 1953".
Since the statement did not actually say that the embargo would be lifted on March 1, and because we had maintained frequent contact with the United States authorities and had reason to expect that the embargo against some products at least might be lifted at an earlier date than March 1, we refrained from making any public comment pending further discussion with the United States authorities.
Shortly afterward I arranged to meet Secretary Brannan in Washington and actually did meet him on December 5. I can tell the house that the meeting was most favourable, that I was assured that the United States authorities regarded our measures for the eradication of foot-and-mouth disease as being wholly effective, and further that they are anxious to see normal trade in livestock, meat and other products affected, resumed as soon as possible.
After my visit to Washington, the acting secretary of agriculture published a notice in the federal register expressing the intention of the department to lift the embargo against Canadian livestock and meat and stating that representations on the proposal would be received from the public until January 16.
As I mentioned a moment ago, yesterday's news from Washington has been taken by some to mean that the embargo had actually been lifted in so far as hay originating in eastern Canadian provinces was concerned. According to information we have from Washington, that is not exactly the case. Yesterday the department of agriculture in Washington posted a public notice to the effect that hay for use as feed would be allowed to enter the United States from eastern Canada after the publication of the official notice in the federal register. We understand that the official notice may be published within a matter of a few days.
While no assurance whatever can be given as to what, if any, further action the United States authorities may take to advance the date of the lifting of the embargo, I think the house will agree that the steps already taken by the United States government are most welcome and support the view that further steps may be taken before March 1.

The hours suggested from 11 o'clock to
II	o'clock are the old hours pertaining to morning sittings. I think it could be understood that if we had had a good day up until ten o'clock and if a speaker finishes on or after that time, a motion to adjourn would then be supported by the house. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEBATE IN REPLY TO SPEECH FROM THE THRONE -CHANGE IN HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Acting Prime Minister for meeting in part the point about which I was getting to my feet a moment ago. I am happy to support the motion in so far as it provides for morning sittings during the remainder of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I offer that support because I was a member of Your Honour's committee on procedure which

wrestled with this question of hours and which made the recommendation that if the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne lasted more than a week we should establish morning sittings.
However, I am disturbed-although my concern has been lessened somewhat by what the Acting Prime Minister has said just now-by the fact that this motion calls for the house to sit until eleven o'clock in the evening. I think it should be put on the record that the recommendation made by the committee in this regard, to be found on page 602 of Votes and Proceedings for June 27, 1952, reads as follows:
Your committee also recommends that, without amending the standing orders, consideration should be given by the house at the beginning of next session to holding morning sittings during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, starting approximately a week after the opening of parliament, subject to the suspension of said morning sittings if the debate on the address is interrupted for other business.
I point out that when we made that recommendation there was no suggestion that the sitting hours should be extended beyond ten o'clock at night. I think it is fair to say that not only the committee but the house as a whole wrestled with this question of the proper hours of sitting for two full sessions and we are all quite satisfied with the hours that have been arrived at, namely, 2.30 to 10 o'clock with the usual intermission.
I think all of us, particularly those of us who have had years of experience with the eleven o'clock closing, find that the ten o'clock closing hour is much better all round. Accordingly it seems to me we should not try to carry this house past ten o'clock at night. I welcome the suggestion which the Acting Prime Minister has made that it might be that we will adjourn at ten o'clock every evening despite the terms of this motion. I hope that in future even the possibility of going on to eleven o'clock will not be included in the motion because it seems to me that it would meet with the spirit of the committee's recommendation and with the will of the house generally if it were established that ten o'clock at night is late enough, bearing in mind that for most of us our day starts at nine o'clock in the morning.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Blanchette (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PAYMENT OF SERVICEMEN'S TRAVELLING EXPENSES
speechtext:
The
hon. gentleman was good enough to send me notice of his question. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has also inquired in respect to the same matter.
The present position regarding transportation costs for men in the armed forces going on leave is, briefly, as follows: Personnel proceeding to, or returning from, service in the Far East or Europe are provided at public expense with free transportation, berth and

meals to their stated home address; in other words, when they are on special embarkation, or disembarkation leave.
Personnel serving in Canada are entitled to one annual leave and are granted an allowance calculated at the rate of 1J cents per mile for each mile of the complete journey in excess of 500 miles. The question of an increase in the mileage rate, and a reduction in the distance beyond which the mileage allowance is payable, are both at present under consideration. On leaves other than those referred to above, a member of the services bears his own expenses.
I might mention that in many cases where military transportation is following the route of a man who is going on leave, and room is available, he is given free transportation.

The house resumed, from Thursday, December 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. L. Deslieres for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Blackmore.
(Translation):
Mr J. H. Rousseau (Rimouski): Mr. Speaker, I would like to sum up in a few sentences the remarks I made before the adjournment of the house last night. I gave, first of all, the reasons why I am speaking in French again this year. I then offered you my congratulations for the way in which you have improved your pronunciation, especially when you read the opening prayers in French. I then added my tribute to the congratulations already offered the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I then congratulated the members of the press gallery, whom I called the photographers of our ideas, of our feelings and of our speeches, which they have the art of condensing in such a way as to please their readers. I then mentioned extraordinary happenings and even heavenly interventions which contributed to the allied victory during the wars of 1914-1918 and 1939-45, wars for which the allies were not prepared. I also stated that those two wars were very costly in money and human lives, and had it not been for the courage and the indomitable energy of the Right Hon. Winston Churchill, after the disaster at Dunkirk, the whole world would be today under the intolerable yoke of nazism. I have expressed my sincere thanks to the hon. ministers, to their parliamentary assistants and their subordinates for their liberality in meeting all just and reasonable requests from my electors. I stated that the Liberal government was managing the business of Canada in the interest of Canadians, in much the same way as directors of large corporations do, in the interest and for the benefit of their shareholders.
I now pursue my remarks. In my humble opinion, three factors may help us to prevent another war, which would be more terrible, more devastating than the wars of 1914-18 and 1939-45, because of the new weapons now in use. These three factors are:
First, the rosary crusades spreading the recitation of the rosary all over Canada.
The Address-Mr. Rousseau This is the answer of the faithful to the request they received from our Lady of Fatima.
Moral rearmament, that admirable movement which has produced such good results in the countries where it is known, which puts order into every class of society, from the point of view of spirituality and morality as well as from that of human endeavour, has made of all those men and women who have taken part in it citizens respectful of moral, religious and civil laws. I might add that it is this movement which communism fears above everything else.
And finally, this expensive but necessary preparation. Dollars, once lost, can be recovered, but not human lives.
I therefore believe that we must not criticize the government on account of the expenditure involved in this defence effort, especially since all the moneys spent have been honestly spent.
In spite of this enormous expenditure, the government have found a way to legislate for the Canadian people in a wise, farseeing fashion, to carry out those works necessary to a healthy national economy, from one ocean to the other, such as the Halifax-Dartmouth bridge or the Canso bridge in the east, the St. Lawrence seaway project in central Canada, the irrigation of 500,000 acres of land in Saskatchewan.
Among those wise legislative measures I shall mention but two: those concerning old age pensions and family allowances.
During my 50 years' experience as a country notary, I have been the confidant of many families who found themselves in sorrowful situations. Very often an old man or an old woman, after having given away all their earthly goods to their son, would come crying for an explanation of certain clauses of their act of donation, wondering whether they could be deprived of their annuity. This meant that the son wished to get rid of his aged parents to cease paying them an annuity. Today, thanks to that wise and provident piece of legislation, the children would like to see their aged parents, who are the protectors of our families, live as long as possible, because they will continue to receive monthly cheques of $40 as long as they live and share them with their children and grandchildren.
We are all Christians and we all know the great commandment, "honour thy father and mother". This act, therefore, helps children to put this commandment into practice; these young people thus ensure for themselves happy old age, because, as you well know,

The Address-Mr. Rousseau Mr. Speaker, we reap as we sow. Therefore, honour is due to the Liberal government for having initiated this wonderful policy of old age pensions at 70. An old man has no longer the strength and courage to beg for himself; he now finds joy and happiness in his generosity to others.
Honour is also due to the Liberal government for their family allowances, which in the case of each child, from the day of his birth to the age of 16, amount to a total of $1,188. Since that act has been in operation, one can see convents and colleges full of pupils who would not be, without the allowances, in a position to attend these courses. Mr. Speaker, I have received hundreds of letters from mothers in my constituency, asking that the allowances be doubled, instead of spending money for war purposes.
To this I will give a frank and clear answer. Defence expenditures, as T have attempted to demonstrate, are absolutely necessary to the security of Canada and of its people. In fact, if the communists should ever take control of this country, liberty in all its forms would disappear; religious, civil and individual freedom. Everything would become the property of the state. That would, of course, be the knell of family allowances such as we know them now.
I am therefore convinced that everyone will readily admit that it is preferable to continue our defence effort so as to prevent this and keep family allowances at their present level.
I hasten to add though that, as soon as the danger of war has passed, as soon as defence expenditures cease, I will ask the government to increase, to double even, the family allowances which are such a boon to our large families.
I will also ask the government to assist those incapacitated persons who, while they are not old enough to receive the old age pension, and are not entitled either to the pension for the blind, are yet unable to earn their living and weigh heavily upon their families.
Mr. Speaker, should we set aside our present government which is a good government made up of honest, competent, conscientious and devoted ministers, for the sole reason that a change is in order? Do the shareholders of a company ever cast aside directors whose management has been wise and who show yearly surpluses? Of course the answer is no.
That is why we Liberals believe that the population of Canada will keep its trust in the Liberal party which gave the nation such good laws, which administers public affairs so honestly that bank deposits are larger than

ever, and which allows all social classes more comfort and more pleasures than they have ever enjoyed since Canada came into existence.
The ship "Canada" is manned by a first-class crew. Her captain is prudent, enlightened, conscientious and thoroughly honest. Indeed our very distinguished Prime Minister has succeeded in surrounding himself with officers who are both qualified and hardworking in their own sphere. Then why should we change, since the consequences of such a move cannot be foreseen. In that respect, I beg leave to retell one of the witty stories which that great Canadian, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, told in 1908 at Murray Bay, in Charlevoix county, during a speech he made before a large gathering of people.
"My good friends," he said, "our opponents ask you to elect a new government. Would you be any better off if you did? I claim that you wouldn't. Let me tell you a story as old as the world but very true: The Lord had finished His wonderful creative work, the universe He had made so beautiful because He wanted the happiness of Adam and Eve to be as perfect as possible. These two human beings were perfectly happy in the garden of Eden, as they had been for a long time, when Satan, jealous at the sight of their happiness, came to Eve and asked her if she was happy. Eve answered that they were.
"And Satan said to her: 'You cannot be
perfectly happy since you cannot eat those beautiful apples on that tree. I know that you have been forbidden to eat of that fruit but that is because the Lord does not want you to become His equals. Eat of that fruit and you shall be as gods.' And Eve went to Adam and was so successful in her pleading that both of them ate of the fruit. You know what happened afterwards to the human race, what we have had to pay for that grave error committed by our first parents."
To bring my speech to an end, I say: We have a good government, let us keep it.

Let us refer, for a moment, to what took place recently. On Tuesday, December 9, before the orders of the day were called, I asked a plain and wholesome question of the Minister of Transport.
This was my question:
Has the Canadian maritime commission reported to the minister with reference to federal aid for improvements to the ferry service between Wood Island and Caribou, the connecting line between Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia? If not, why not?
The answer I received to that was one big, plain, No. It would seem the answer to the first question was that there has been no report. They go to the Canadian maritime commission, and according to the terms of confederation of 1873 between the province of Prince Edward Island and the Dominion of Canada that commission has no authority whatsoever to deal with the question of transportation. The maritime commission is simply a buffer commission. I notice that my secretary put it as "bluffer" commission. It is only a buffer commission for the Minister of Transport and the government.
As I said a year ago, when the representatives of the Northumberland ferry company come here they should never have anything to do with this buffer commission. They should make their demands on the Minister of Transport and the government. They should place their arguments and claims before them and file their brief with them. Then they would not have to wait for days for the buffer commission to make up excuses for the government so that they can turn around and say, "According to the maritime commission we cannot do this" or "we cannot do that".
I said a moment ago that I was not going to say anything about this matter but now that I have entered upon it I will say a bit more. In the last two or three years the situation has become such that the ferry company cannot handle more than two-thirds of the freight, passengers, automobiles and trucks requiring transportation from Caribou on one side of the strait and Wood Island on the other. If you wish to cross the strait in the busy season you have to make application forty-eight hours before the boat sails for space for your car or truck unless you have a priority.
What we want there and what the Northumberland Ferries Limited is seeking is assistance. The company is not coming to the government asking for something for nothing. In
rising to take part in this debate this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I am aware and fully appreciate that this order of business has been before the house for at least three weeks, and that any remarks or suggestions that I might make will be largely repetitious. It seems to me that I have been in this house for quite a number of sessions, probably too long, but I would say that in my opinion I have never made a partisan speech.
I feel that there are enough politicians in the house without me. I was elected and chosen as a member whose duty it is to represent all the people and all the factions in the riding, to give consideration to suggestions that are made and, to the best of my ability, to keep the record straight while at the same time being true to myself.
I would crave the indulgence of this house this afternoon to divert from that record for a few moments. I wish to refer to some statements, and what I believe are unfair references, that have been made by members in neighbouring constituencies. I refer to the member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) who, in his remarks on November 25, 1952, as found at page 89 of Hansard, said:
One thing I should like to mention particularly is the reference to mail courier contracts. The Conservative party has long pointed out that changes were due in our rural mail service. Last fall many of the Liberal members from western Ontario took part in the debate on the postal estimates,


and all mentioned the rural mail service. It was quite obvious that they had been tipped off that changes were going to be made and therefore they had better get in on the ground floor.
To me that was an interesting statement for him to make. I should like to remind the hon. member for Middlesex East that rural mail delivery was established in this country over 45 years ago, and that the same method of awarding mail courier contracts -by calling for public tenders-as then initiated still prevails. According to the Post Office Act the contracts must be awarded to the lowest tenderer, if the party is reliable and provides good bondsmen.
I am sure that if he will look up Hansard of former years he will find that many hon. members spoke in this house on the evils of this system at least ten years before he came to this house, and not just on the eve of an election, as he states. I am sure that the party to which the hon. member adheres sat on the government benches for some time during that long period, and they did not change those regulations or even improve them. I am sure that some of the members in this house recall the period of 1930 to 1935. I believe the postmaster general at that time was Hon. Mr. Sauve. What did he do in 1933? For at least the greater part of that year all rural mail couriers whose contracts expired during that period were not given the privilege of renewing their contracts even at the previous tender price, but were ruthlessly told that they could only get a contract by slicing the cost. Some were offered a four-year contract with a ten per cent reduction, some even more1 than that. They could take it or leave it or it would go for public tender. Those were the so-called hungry thirties, and the couriers had no choice; they had to take what was offered and sign up for a four-year contract.
When I came to this house in 1935 I went to the post office officials and endeavoured to have those mail contracts restored to their former level but I was told by the officials that they could do nothing about it, that they had signed up for a four-year contract and there was no provision to raise their pay without the calling of public tenders. These mail couriers never obtained any relief until this government brought in an act called the Mail Contracts Supplemental Payments Act in 1947. It was then extended to 1948 when all mail couriers received an adjustment in salaries at least to some standard of equal pay for their services. I am sure that the rural mail couriers throughout Canada-and I am speaking particularly of those in Ontario-will not be fooled by that story of the hon. member

for Middlesex East, for they know what treatment they received during that regime.
There is an old adage to this effect; if you want to know what a man's future is, look into his past. I would say that adage applies to political parties as well; and to the hon. member for Middlesex East I would suggest that, before he makes any statement like the one to which I have referred, he had better review some of the past records of the Post Office Department *and their operations during the last forty years.
At this time I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) the fact that the house has now been in session since November 20, that we are looking for that committee of the house to be set up to study and to make recommendations with regard to this problem and would like to have it set up as soon as possible after the Christmas recess.
I wish now to discuss a question that has had a great deal of publicity on the radio and in the press as well as in this house during the past two weeks. I refer to the sugar beet industry of Canada, particularly as it applies to Ontario and to my own riding of Lambton-Kent.
My colleague the hon. member for Kent, Ontario (Mr. Huffman) a few days ago gave an interesting resume of the sugar beet industry in Ontario, especially as it applies to Chatham; and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) also gave us some interesting data on the sugar beet industry in Alberta. I wish to point out to this house that Wallaceburg this year is celebrating its 51st anniversary, with the distinctive record of having the oldest and the second largest sugar beet factory in Canada.
The operation of this plant alone is of vital importance to the livelihood of some 2,000 farmers, 500 factory workers and a countless number of field workers, merchants, truckers and many others of the community who are viewing with a great deal of concern the importation of Cuban refined sugar into our market here in western Ontario. Already the movement of Cuban refined sugar into Canada approaches in volume the annual production of our local plant in Wallaceburg. Some 12,000 acres of sugar beets have been grown in this vicinity to supply the Wallaceburg plant. The beets have recently been harvested. Last year the farmers, for a similar acreage, received approximately $2,200,000. Losing this important industry would undoubtedly depress the farm and urban economy of this whole community. So I will endeavour to put on the record some information with regard to the actual situation that
The Address-Mr. MacKenzie has brought about this condition; and again I want to be fair in this analysis. If my figures are not correct, I am sorry. I may say that I obtained them from what I felt were quite authoritative sources.
As has been stated by previous speakers, we have in Canada seven sugar beet refineries situated in four provinces, and they have just concluded a season during which they have operated to almost full capacity. This year the beet sugar in Canada will meet about one-quarter of all our requirements here in Canada. We must remember that the actual refining operations last only about three months in the year or a little bit better, but it is a most important industry in our whole farming operations.
The hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), when speaking in this house on this question a few days ago, said that early in October a delegation had come to Ottawa to interview some government officials and that no newspaper reporter was present but that a statement was made to the press afterwards, perhaps as an alibi. I can readily understand why the hon. member for Lamb-ton West would think this to be strange, because I feel sure that if he had been on that delegation everybody would have known about it.
This conference and the delegation were organized by the refineries and the growers from all four provinces and they were well represented. I was with them for two days and assisted them in every way I possibly could. Believe it or not, I have been closely associated with the beet growing industry and with the beet growers for the past 25 years, and I know something about their problems and about what the industry means to this country. Many a time I have come to Ottawa with various delegations. I see no useful purpose to be gained in calling in the press, for occasionally one can accomplish more without too much publicity. But on this occasion I am confident that no effort was made by anyone to exclude the press. I have never read an account of it anywhere in the press, and in any case I can see no importance or no significance attached to that statement.
The facts are that we cannot increase to any marked degree our sugar beet production in Canada unless we have more refineries. That being true, we must import from other countries 75 per cent or more of the sugar that we consume in Canada. It is difficult to obtain the actual per capita consumption of sugar but it is high, and will probably average between 95 and 100 pounds per capita per year, so that our actual requirements would be something over thirteen million

I hold in my hand an editorial from the Ottawa Citizen of December 2. I am not going to read it, but I will give the gist of it. The editorial in the Citizen claims that the current sugar difficulties spring from a three-year trade agreement made with Cuba, whereby Canada accepts 75,000 tons of raw sugar a year for three years, 1951, 1952 and 1953, and concessions were obtained by Canada for wheat, fish and potatoes in return, and also some flour.

COMMONS	-
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the present difficulties we are in have no bearing on this trade treaty at all; that we had to import raw sugar from some place, and it made little difference where it came from. It might even have helped the situation to bring in this raw sugar from Cuba; otherwise if we had obtained all our raw sugar from empire or other sources, Cuba might easily have unloaded greater quantities of surplus refined sugar here.
This refined sugar from Cuba comes in under the general tariff or the most-favourednation treaty, which, in this case, is just the same. The duty on Cuban refined sugar is $1.89 a hundredweight, plus a maximum of 75 cents a hundredweight, if the antidumping regulations can be applied. Whether this concession is of a great deal of value I am not in a position to say. I will say this, however, I am not an economist but it has increased the trade with Cuba, and as a matter of fact it costs nothing from the consolidated revenue fund, as it is a bookkeeping account. faced serious handicaps in the past and survived, and it will continue to survive. I am sure the government officials are well aware of the present situation and I would suggest two or three courses that might be adopted in order to protect-and I do not like the word "protect"-to safeguard our sugar beet industry from any unfair competition:
1.	The government might review the Canadian tariff to see if it provides reasonable, but not too great, protection to Canadian refineries.
2.	It may be that the Cuban refineries are able to buy raw sugar more cheaply than it is being sold on world markets, and thus are in a position to compete unfairly with our refineries. Not only have we emphasized the necessity of importing from the United Kingdom those things which we have to import, and said that we should concentrate on getting them from there, if possible; but in this regard we have made specific suggestions which have been, unfortunately, disregarded by the government to the detriment of this country and of our trade.
I will give just one example, Mr. Speaker. Two years ago we made a positive recommendation that Canada should buy or attempt to buy the British Centurion tank, rather than United States tanks; but the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce both stated positively at that time that Canada would buy United States tanks. The Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), as reported at page 912 of Hansard for 1951, said:
We will procure our tanks from the United States.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) said on May 9, 1951, as reported at page 2872 of Hansard:
We have now the opportunity of buying from the United States the latest tanks, and they will be coming with the equipment for the two divisions we transferred to Europe.
We said that they should place orders for Centurion tanks. The ministers said they were going to buy in the United States. It has recently been announced that the decision has been made to buy Centurion tanks. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, just how much money has been wasted in the meantime on United States tanks. I do not want to be offensive, but it is safe to say the United States tanks are not the best tanks, and not as good as Centurions. How much money was wasted, and how much time was lost before they decided to make the change-a change which should have been made earlier both from a tactical point of view and from a trade and economic point of view-so that the dollars which would go to Britain for her tanks might have been used by her in return to buy from Canada?
I conclude by saying it is absolute nonsense for the government to suggest that we have not made concrete proposals. There are others which could be made, but I am not going to extend my remarks now to make them. I shall do so at a later date along with other suggestions along the same line. But I say that two of the reasons our agricultural producers find themselves without their traditional market in the United Kingdom for their products at the present time are, first, that the government has been so dilatory and shown such a lack of interest in the

question of commonwealth economic conferences and trade; and, second, that they have overlooked opportunities of making purchases from Britain either directly or by taking out licences to manufacture British equipment in Canada, for both of which dollars would go overseas, thus directly increasing the flow of dollars which the United Kingdom would have had with which to buy from us, while at the same time serving our own defence purposes.

Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for giving me a couple of minutes so I can answer points which have been raised by the hon. member for Kamloops with regard to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who of course is still in London.
This quite extraordinary statement of the hon. member for Kamloops apparently is an attempt to anticipate, by reading newspaper headlines, what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself will report to this house when he returns here tomorrow. However, I want to make it quite clear now to all hon. members-I am sure it is already clear to all except the hon. member for Kamloops-that there is no roadblock to commonwealth trade as far as Canada is concerned. What are the roadblocks to commonwealth trade today? Import and export restrictions on goods; bans on goods; currency controls; bans on export of currency from the sterling bloc. Canada today has no export or import controls on any of her goods, other than the export of strategic materials to behind the iron curtain. Our currency is one of the two or three currencies in the world which is completely convertible to any other currency on open money markets. We have done the right thing. It was difficult in the post-war period to get to this free trading position, but we did it because of the courageous financial and economic measures of this government, and in particular those sponsored by the Minister of Finance.
We have heard this cry for convertibility of sterling from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) on the hustings. Never has he got down to brass tacks on how it is to be done. The hon. member for Kamloops suggested that was not the job of the opposition. I place Colonel Drew's solution of convertibility of sterling on the same plane as General MacArthur's solution to end the war in Korea, which he apparently has kept for some time from the government.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
The Address-Mr. Sinclair

I sat through your speech, so you can at least take these two minutes in reply.
But actually the press clippings to which he referred do indicate that the conference has realized that the only way to increase commonwealth trade and world trade is to take the course which Canada took: Not more restrictions; not more currency restrictions; not more import and export restrictions, but the other direction of getting away from both these quantitative and qualitative trade restrictions, and getting away from currency restrictions. The same press clippings, which I read, have also indicated that the majority of the commonwealth members agree that the way to expand trade is not by confining our trade to any one bloc of nations but to seek to expand trade to every country in the world as we and 34 other nations have done in the general agreements on tariffs and trade, which we signed at Geneva, Annecy and Torquay.
The hon. member mentioned, too, the difference in the Tory and Liberal attitudes toward trade. Every year since 1945 in this house we have heard the same calamity chorus from the Tories, about how our trade was falling off and we were facing ruin. Well, let me give you not the calamity chorus, but just the rough group of hard facts. In 1930, when R. B. Bennett came to power with the Tory policy that he was going to blast his way into the markets of the world, he had a commonwealth conference.
Will the hon. member permit a question now?

The hon. gentleman of course does not afford me the courtesy that I have shown him, of listening to him. I am now speaking of facts from the record. He did call a commonwealth conference, yes. His solution at that conference to world stagnation of trade was to advocate raising the barriers higher against all countries outside the commonwealth, and a British minister at that time rightly called that Tory policy "humbug". It was humbug then and it is humbug today.
A Liberal government took over in 1935. Canada's total export and import trade that year was $1-3 billion. This year it is over $8 billion. That is the difference between Liberal policy and Tory policy as far as trade is concerned. And here in this house, despite-
If there ever was humbug, that is humbug.

Here in this house this year, despite what we hear from the hon. member for Kamloops, we have heard Tory members

Let me read the whole editorial in the leading financial paper of Canada, the Financial Post, of this week. If my hon. friend reads beyond the headlines, he may have read this;
Gloomsters wrong again

And we admit it; trade in the world today is always difficult.

Mr. Speaker, my re-entry into this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne arises from my concern over a ghost-a ghost of something that most of us had hoped was dead but which, for a great many people in my province at any rate, is very much alive. The agony being caused to

these people is such that, with Christmas just around the corner, I feel the government should take action to end its existence for all time.
A good idea.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I gather that my hon. friend wants that observation to apply to the government. I do not mind that, but I was referring to the ghost of the means test under the former Old Age Pensions Act.
Hon. members in the house generally, even those who voted against the removal of the means test not many months ago, rejoice in the fact that it no longer applies to the old age pension so far as Canadians of 70 years of age and over are concerned. As one who for many years urged that the means test should be abolished I, too, was most happy to be here and to take part in enacting the legislation in which provision was made for a universal old age pension to all 70 years of age and over. But the fact is that in my province-it may be happening in others, but I shall confine my remarks to my own province, because I have evidence of what is happening there-Canadians 70 years of age and over, who are now drawing the new federal pension free of any means test, are in many cases being hounded for repayments arising from alleged overpayments during the years they were under the former old age pension legislation, to which was attached a means test.
Someone may say to me immediately that if this is happening primarily in Manitoba, then it must be something for the government of that province to deal with. Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is true that the letters, a number of which I have here and to which I shall later refer, which are being sent to old age pensioners in Manitoba making demand for repayment, are from officials of the old age pensions board in that province. I must point out, however, that in a number of these letters-and I shall offer quotations in support of what I say-it is being said to the people in Manitoba that the province is obligated to seek these recoveries by virtue of the terms of the federal legislation. Not only are Manitoba old age pensioners being told in these letters that the villain of the piece is the federal government, but it is also a matter of record that this question has been tossed back and forth for several months between Ottawa and the provinces. I have been in the midst of that tossing about, myself, as will be evident from some of the matters of record which 1 shall recall at this time.
On March 12 of last session, as reported at pages 356 and 357 of Hansard. I asked the
The Address-Mr. Knowles Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) if it was not time to advise the provinces that they did not need to continue any longer the practice of making recoveries from the estates of deceased pensioners, or the practice of making recoveries in cases of alleged overpayment. The minister told me on that occasion there was nothing he could do about it because it was a matter governed by the existing law.
Well, one could not do much through questions asked on the orders of the day, so at the first opportunity after that date I took part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, which was then in progress, and drew the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the fact that on February 12, 1952, a statement concerning this matter had been made in the Manitoba legislature by the minister of health and public welfare in that province.
Despite the fact that in the Manitoba legislature they have no record equivalent to our Hansard, this statement was regarded as of sufficient importance to merit its being reported in the votes and proceedings of the legislative assembly for February 12, 1952.
I quote from page 2 the words of Hon. Mr. Schultz:
In regard to the collection of claims against the estates of deceased pensioners in this group the legislation of the federal government and the obligations under the agreement submitted for signature by the federal government compels this province in accordance with similar agreements with every other province, to collect from the estates of deceased pensioners where the estate is over $2,000 net. Neither Manitoba nor any other province has any option in this matter at the present time.
When I drew this to the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare during the course of my speech in that debate of the last session he chose to interrupt me at that point, as is recorded at page 545 of Hansard for March 18, 1952, by making this interesting interjection:

Of course Mr. Schultz knows that is not a correct statement, as does my hon. friend.
Well, I made a reply to that at greater length than I would wish to quote in full at this time, the main point of which was that I hoped what the Minister of National Health and Welfare was then saying would set the matter right, and that the provinces would realize that they did not have to continue the policy of making recoveries, as was the case when we were under the former Old Age Pensions Act.
As a matter of fact the exchanges continued during the course of that speech until, I thought, the minister changed his ground
