But at the end he said:
This is a matter determined by existing law and on the basis of agreements between the federal and provincial governments; and until we know the attitude of all governments in respect to this matter we cannot take any action with regard to the existing law. Surely that is the situation, and I should think my hon. friend would be the first to agree that I have correctly stated it.
It seems to me that what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) made clear by his interjections in my speech was that in the first place Mr. Schultz had no right to put the blame entirely on the federal government, which would seem to suggest that from the standpoint of the Minister of National Health and Welfare the blame goes back to Manitoba. But then he also suggested there is something the federal government can do about it, because he says it is covered by the existing law. The existing law is the Old Age Pensions Act of 1926 passed by the parliament of Canada which is still on the statute books, and under which the policy of recoveries is still being pursued.
I have asked repeatedly that this former act be rescinded or repealed, whichever is the correct term, so that the recovery policies required under it could be discontinued. There is a provision in the Old Age Security Act, chapter 18 of the statutes of 1951, second session, section 13, subsection 2, which reads as follows:
The Old Age Pensions Act is repealed on a day to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council.
It was on the basis of the authority vested in the governor in council to do away with the former Old Age Pensions Act that I asked again just a few days ago for the end of that act to be effected. Before I refer to the question I asked a few days ago, may I say that after getting from the Minister of National Health and Welfare last spring the view that Mr. Schultz was wrong, that Manitoba was not being compelled by federal legislation to continue this policy of making these recoveries I drew that information to the attention of the officials of the provincial old age pensions board in Manitoba. I found them quite interested. They referred to Hansard themselves and noted with interest, as I say, what the minister had said.
I expressed the hope to these officials that as the result of what the Minister of National Health and Welfare had said they would feel free to discontinue seeking to make recoveries out of estates of deceased pensioners, and to discontinue seeking to make recoveries from elderly people still alive for little overpayments that they are supposed to have had
(Mr. Knowles.]

in 1951, 1950 or in earlier years. My discussion with these officials was for the most part verbal, but on one occasion we had an exchange of letters about a particular case. At that time I asked how things were going with regard to the policy of recovery and I had this reply from Mr. Locksley D. McNeill, chairman of what is now the old age assistance and blind persons allowances board of Manitoba. It is dated September 23, 1952. This is what he said in the last paragraph of his letter:
The recovery policy appears to stand pretty much as it was earlier in the spring, that is, the dominion government has not specifically agreed that the provinces may feel free to discontinue their efforts to make recoveries against those estates which are in excess of $2,000.
So it goes, Mr. Speaker, back and forth. Manitoba says: We do this because we are compelled to do so by Ottawa, by the federal legislation, by the fact that the federal government has not released us from the necessity of doing it. The Minister of National Health and Welfare says that under federal legislation the provinces are not compelled to do it. The province comes back and says there has been no change, that they are still being forced to do it under the terms of federal legislation.
I pick up for a moment one of the many letters I have that have been written to old age pensioners in Manitoba seeking recoveries of overpayments. This one is dated August 1, 1952, and is likewise over the signature of Mr. McNeill, chairman of the board of that province. It was addressed to Mr. and Mrs. B, former residents of Winnipeg who are now residing in a town outside the city of Winnipeg. After having pressed the case for repayment-and I will come back to this case later-he says:
You can see from this that the matter is one which is in a sense out of our hands. We carry out the procedure laid down by the dominion legislation.
The latest chapter in this story, so far as this parliament is concerned, took place this session on November 24 when I put a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
I put it to him in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and it will be found at page 18 of Hansard for that date. My question reads as follows:
Can the Prime Minister say when the former Old Age Pensions Act will be repealed so that provinces like Manitoba, which are pressing needy pensioners to make repayment and which are still making recoveries out of the estates of deceased pensioners, can discontinue this practice?

The Prime Minister referred the question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and this was his reply:
I want to thank the member for Winnipeg North Centre for giving notice of this question. A similar question was answered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on June 24, page 3610 of Hansard, and on June 27 last, page 3833 of Hansard. It is the intention of the government to proclaim the repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act as soon as there is agreement from the provinces which cosponsored this act that this should be done. Not all of the provinces have yet agreed on the desirability of repeal at this time, but it is hoped that agreement will be reached shortly so that the necessary proclamation can be made.
I recall very well, of course, the statements the Minister of National Health and Welfare made on this matter during the last session, and I confess I am disturbed at the suggestion that this federal law cannot be repealed, despite the fact that parliament has given the governor in council power to do so, until there is consent of all the provinces with respect to the matter. In the answer of the parliamentary assistant which I have just quoted he used the phrase, "the provinces which co-sponsored this act." May I remind him and the government of a bit of ancient history with respect to this matter which nevertheless is important because it bears upon this act. On April 15, 1926, when the Old Age Pensions Act was under discussion and was being put through the house for the first time-I should not say the first time because it was the second time; the first time it was put through it was killed in the other place-there was a request from the Conservative opposition of that day to have the old age pensions bill delayed. But Mr. King, who was then Prime Minister, replied in these terms, as recorded at pages 2501 and 2502 of Hansard for April 15, 1926:
The bill has been prepared with a view to avoiding delays and in order to enable any provincial government that may care to enact at once, with respect to old age pensions, legislation in conformity with the requirements of this measure to take advantage of the proposed scheme. If some provinces do not desire to pass such legislation, that determination will in no way affect the situation except in so far as they are concerned. But as a federal government we want to show our readiness at the earliest possible moment to assist any province as soon as it is prepared to enact legislation along the lines here laid down.
I read that quotation to remind hon. members of what they all know, namely that when the Old Age Pensions Act was first put upon the statute books it was made law in precisely those terms. It was enabling legislation which came into effect in the various provinces over a long period of time. I believe it was eight or nine years before all of the then nine provinces took advantage of the law, but the provinces that were ready to 68108-40A
The Address-Mr. Knowles enter into such meagre generosity as that measure involved were not held back because some of the other provinces were not ready. In other words the original law was not a co-sponsored piece of legislation at all. It was an act of the federal parliament which was put upon the statute books in such a manner that the provinces could participate in it as they wished.
I think it is perfectly reasonable for me to ask that the same practice, the same spirit be followed now so far as ending the means test Old Age Pensions Act is concerned. If there are some provinces that insist on being permitted to continue to make these recoveries, perchance the federal government might feel that it has to yield to their desire, but if there are provinces which infer, as Mr. Schultz I take it has inferred-he is no longer the minister, but he was at that time-that but for the federal government standing in their way they would like to discontinue these recoveries, then I suggest that the federal government should indicate to these provinces that so far as it is concerned it will be all right for them to discontinue these recoveries.
I know of cases where attempts are being made to collect from the estates of deceased pensioners. It seems to me that is a most abhorrent practice which is completely in violation of the whole idea that this parliament finally arrived at, that the means test should be done away with. If the means test is dead, let it stay dead. What I suggest is even more abhorrent and more repugnant to our thinking today is the way in which old people who are still alive are being pressed for the repayment of amounts that they got in 1951 or 1950. It is coming close to Christmas. Cannot the government take action on this matter right away? It could be done under the section I read in the Old Age Security Act repealing the Old Age Pensions Act whenever the government so decides, and that would be the end of it.
If it cannot do it that way then it could write to a province like Manitoba, who say they are doing this because the federal government wants them to, and say that so far as Ottawa is concerned Manitoba does not need to press these old people any more. When the amounts are collected they are pitifully small, not to mention the administrative and collection costs. Those costs must represent a large percentage of the amount recovered. After an amount is recovered by a province like Manitoba it is permitted to retain only 25 per cent because that was the portion put in by the province to the former pension. The 75 per cent remitted to Ottawa is so small in terms of federal revenues and

The Address-Mr. Knowles budgets that I am sure it is not for the purpose of getting in dollars that this policy of pressing for these repayments is still being pursued.
I said I would indicate to the house the nature of some of these cases and refer to some of the letters I have on my desk. So that hon. members may know that I am not just talking about something I have just heard about or one single case, may I say that this matter has been the subject of more correspondence than any other one subject since I came to this session in the middle of November.
The letters I have received from some of these old people who have only $40 per month and who think that money is theirs without any attachment are heart-rending indeed. They wonder how they are going to find the $5, the $10, the $100 or whatever it may be to meet the demand of the Manitoba government, which Manitoba says it is making because Ottawa requires it to do so.
Here is the case of Mr. and Mrs. D who live on Agnes street in my constituency of Winnipeg North Centre. I have here a letter over the signature of an official of the old age pensions board in Winnipeg telling them that the return from a little bit of property they had before they ever went on pension would have to be computed as so much income per year so long as that pension lasted. It so happened that these people, like a good many others in my city, made a little money during the flood year of 1950 when people were called upon to take all sorts of jobs. At any rate it added up that these people obtained $34.09 in 1950-mind you it was the two of them-more than the means test in that year allowed them to have. In 1951 the means test was still in effect but the authorities in Manitoba did not get around to deducting that alleged overpayment of $34.09 from these people. Instead they have now found by their own methods of computation that in 1951 the two of them had obtained $48.09 more than they were permitted to obtain in that year. Well along in 1952 these two old people who receive the present pension of $40 a month, which everyone from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) down receives, who think it is theirs because there is no means test, get these demanding letters requiring them to pay back the sum of those two amounts or $82.18.
That may not seem a large sum to certain people, but it is an awful lot of money to two old people who have only $40 a month each, or a total of $80 a month between them. In connection with this particular case I happen to know that while this correspondence has been going on the husband has passed away. What will happen by way of further pressure


on the widow to pay both her husband's share and her own share of the back debt, coupled with the fact that her income is now reduced to $40 per month, is something for hon. members to contemplate.
I suggest that it is a reprehensible practice the Manitoba authorities are pursuing. If I could put the blame wholly on Manitoba I would not be making this speech today in the House of Commons. But they say they are doing it because of the federal legislation. They go further and say that even if the legislation has not been wiped out they are quite willing to discontinue this practice if Ottawa would release them from the necessity of collecting these overpayments, but that release has not yet been given.
Here is the case of Mr. and Mrs. S who live on Langside street in my constituency. Due to illness, one of them is living with one son and daughter-in-law and the other with another. In November of 1952 the board reviewed the files of these people and considered Mrs. S as receiving free board from the son and daughter-in-law with whom she is living on a farm just outside Winnipeg. They add it all up and they bill this old couple for overpayment in the amount of $5, and they ask each of them to please remit $2.50.
A Liberal government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That amount may not seem great to many of us, but it is a tough amount for people to get together when their income is only $40 a month. What a disgrace for governments to put into operation all this administrative machinery and undergo this administrative cost in order to get $2.50 each out of these old people. I say to the federal government: Come on, it is Christmas. If you cannot do it for any other reason, because it is Christmas time repeal this old- law and put an end to this policy of recovery.
Here is another case of Mr. S, who lives on Preston avenue in the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). The details of that case are rather involved. It dates back a number of years, and I would not be surprised to get word that this -man has died since the last time I heard from him. Yet he is being pressed for a rather large sum dating back over -a number of years, a sum which there is simply no possible way on earth for him to repay.
Here is the case of Mr. G, who lives on Cathedral avenue in Winnipeg. His case, like that of Mr. D, who lives on Craig street, arises from the fact that he went out and did a little work during the time of the flood we had in Manitoba in 1950. The

The Address-Mr. Knowles
result was that they had a little bit more money. It is not a great amount, something in the neighbourhood of $40 or $50 in each case, more than they should have had that year in view of the ceiling that then applied. Now they are being pressed for the repayment of those amounts. Bear in mind that again the board failed to make the adjustment in 1951 when the means test was still in effect. They are a year and a half late in doing it, but still this pressure is being applied. These Manitoba officials are saying: we have to do this; we are compelled to do it by the terms of the federal legislation.
I am not really sure that is the case, because I am told that in some of the province's it is not being done. If some of the other provinces are not required by the federal legislation to do it, I am not sure that Manitoba can make that case stick. They are, however, taking that stand. So long as they do, I suggest it is the responsibility of this government at Ottawa to put an end to it by repealing that act.
Here is the case of Mrs. B, who lives on Ingersoll street. Again there are overpayments for two years, one of $60.04 in 1950 and another of $72.01 in 1951. No attempt was made to make an adjustment in 1951 for the alleged overpayment in 1950. Again, well along in 1952 after these people think the means test is dead, its ugly ghost rises up in the form of these letters saying the old age pensions authorities want them somehow, out of their $40 a month, to make repayment.
I refer also -to the case of Mr. and Mrs. B, who were former residents of Winnipeg and who are now living in a town not far from the city. I find some very interesting language in the letters that have been written to this couple. By the way, this claim arises from receipt of unemployment insurance by one of the parties back in 1949. There was never any secret about it. It was reported to the old age pensions board. I believe these people had every right to feel that, with the abolition of the means test and the beginning of the new federal pension at the rate of $40 per month, they had nothing more to worry about. Lo and behold, when they have nothing else but their $40 a month they are called upon to make this repayment.
This particular couple wrote some letters of protest, and did their best to argue that they should not be required to -make the required repayment. The chairman of the board in Manitoba, Mr. L. D. McNeill, wrote them on August 1, 1952, and said this, amongst other things:
The situation appears to be that we have no alternative other than to ask for repayment of any
overpayment of pension. If these payments are not refunded or arrangements are not made for the repayment of same, we are required to send this information to the director of old age assistance (formerly the director of old age pensions) in Ottawa. He passes it on to the treasury branch of the dominion government. It is then up to the officials of the treasury department to decide whether or not to hold back old age security payments.
Now, Mr. Speaker, imagine that threat being handed to senior citizens today, the threat that unless you somehow find it possible out of this $40 a month to pay back these moneys you are alleged to have received two or three years ago, this glorious, free federal pension of $40 per month will be interfered with. As a matter of fact, if you examine that language closely, it is quite significant. Even the chairman of the board in Manitoba does not assert that Ottawa will hold back the old age security payments. He merely says that it will be up to the federal treasury to decide whether or not they will do that.
I have had some correspondence with the deputy minister of welfare concerning that very point. From the correspondence I have had it is quite clear to me that, up to the present time at any rate, no decision has been made by the federal government to hold back any old age security cheque, even though it may be argued they have the right to do so-not under the terms of the Old Age Security Act but under the terms of the Financial Administration Act. I am quite satisfied that this government at Ottawa is not going to hold back any of those old age security cheques. I can think of one good reason why they will not do it, if there are not others. But the fear that it might be done is being held over some of these people in Manitoba by the board there, and it is being done by that board on the basis that they are required to do it by Ottawa. This letter from which I have just quoted goes on to say:
You can see from this that the matter is one which is in a sense out of our hands. We carryout the procedure laid down by the dominion legislation.
I could cite other cases of these attempts that are being made to recover these alleged overpayments from the older people of Manitoba. I draw your attention to the fact that all of them are people who, by virtue of the fact they were on the old age pension when the means test was in existence, are people who needed it. They are people who now, whatever they may have had in the past, have nothing else but their $40 a month. For them to be hounded in this way by the provincial government with the apparent authority of the federal government is, I suggest, completely out of keeping with what

The Address-Mr. Knowles this country has accepted, namely the idea and principle that so far as our older citizens 70 years of age and over are concerned the means test should be considered as completely dead.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will give more active consideration to this matter, and will And it possible within the next few days to take advantage of the provision of the Old Age Security Act which I read, and call a halt to this procedure by proclaiming as dead the former Old Age Pensions Act, with its means test and its recovery provisions. Let us call a halt to these practices right away. I have just a bit more to say, Mr. Speaker, but since I believe I have another five minutes perhaps I should reserve it for eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe there are about five minutes left of the time allotted to me. Hon. members will recall that during the 35 minutes in which I had the floor just prior to six o'clock, I devoted my time to the making of an appeal to the government to proclaim, within the next few days, the repeal of the former means-test Old Age Pensions Act so that the recoveries still being made under that act might cease. I will not take further time to speak on that phase of the matter now.
However, I do not want to conclude a speech on the subject of old age pensions without repeating my view, which I hold strongly, that there should now be an increase in the amount we are paying to our old age pensioners. Many figures are being suggested in editorials in many responsible newspapers and magazines in this country, and the surveys that are made by various bodies all make it clear that there simply is no sound reason at all for leaving the pension at the figure of $40 a month. I have said before that it should be a much higher figure, certainly not less than $60 a month. I hope we shall get action on this urgent matter without having to wait too long. I repeat likewise that, in my view, the means test should be removed at the age of 65.
Along with these improvements in our social welfare legislation I feel, as all of us in this group have stated, that the time has come for further improvements in the War Veterans Allowance Act, particularly as suggested by the Canadian Legion in their brief recently presented to the government.


There are other groups about which I have had something to say from time to time- indeed I have mentioned them at this session-such as the superannuated civil servants, our blind pensioners, and others, to whom we should be giving a much better break than is the case at the present time.
One of the reasons that I return to the attack, so far as the need for a wider measure of social security is concerned, including our program of health insurance, is because of some of the things the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) has said in the last two or three days. I believe it was in a speech on Wednesday of this week that he sought to pare down the federal government's budget to a mere $675 million. You see, Mr. Speaker, this is the way the government talks. Whenever we are asking for increased social security provisions, we are told by 'this government: "That costs money. It is a good idea but you cannot have it because it costs too much money." But when the government is under attack as to the size of its budget, spokesmen like the Minister of Fisheries stand up and say: "Look here, our budget really is not $4J billion a year at all. Half of it is for defence. That is abnormal. Then $1 billion is for social welfare payments. Those are just transfer payments; they are not expenditures." Then the Minister of Fisheries goes on and takes out the interest paid on the national debt. So he boils it all down to a federal budget, so far as normal expenditui'es, as he defined them, are concerned, of merely $675 million.
I am not now quarrelling with that method of arguing first one way and then the other, but I emphasize the truth of what the Minister of Fisheries said the other day and what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) says when he speaks on this matter, namely that social security provisions, whether they be for old age security or for health or other items, are really just transfer payments, are really just a case of transferring or re-channelling a portion of the wealth produced by this country into the effort to provide health and security for our people. Far from anyone standing up in this house or anywhere else and saying that we cannot afford to have these things, I submit that Canada, with the huge wealth we are producing and with our claim to being a civilized nation, cannot afford not to have reasonable and adequate measures of social security.
This afternoon the Minister of Fisheries got into the debate again. He read with pride an editorial in the current issue of the Financial Post which pointed out that the

gross national product for 1952 was likely to exceed $23 billion as compared with $21-2 billion for the year 1951. That represents an increase, of which he boasted, of more than $1,800 million in this one year. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when we are able to achieve an increase of that magnitude in the wealth we are producing, or an increase to that extent in our gross national product, there is no place for the fallacious argument that we cannot afford reasonable measures of health and social security for our people.
I thrill, as do all hon. members, to the reports we receive these days about the tremendous growth and expansion that is taking place in this country. It is good to learn of the great advances in production we may anticipate in the years that lie ahead. I join with other hon. members in hoping that the realization will be even greater than the anticipation. However, I plead for the common-sense, civilized approach that will take the stand that, with all this wealth we are creating, we are not going to leave some of our deserving Canadians out in the cold but rather that we are going to accept the principle of transfer payments and rechannel or redistribute some of that wealth in such a way as to make provision for adequate welfare and adequate social security for all our Canadian people.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Gladly.
From his research has he available an estimate of the number of additional persons who would become eligible for the old age pension under a reduction of the age limit to 65?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have the figures as has the hon. member, because we were both members of the old age security committee of 1950.
Not up to date.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not have them on my desk, but the point I have been making-
Answer the question. Do not mislead the public.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is the hon. member's approach that misleads the public when he tries to argue that adequate social security cannot be afforded. The fact is that we can pay for the entire social security program that we in this party are arguing for out of one source, namely the increase in this one year in our gross national product.

Mr. Speaker, a Scotsman was once asked to make a speech and the first thing he said was: "I would
The Address-Mr. A. C. Murray like to say a few things before I begin". So tonight I should like to say a few words before I begin. First of all I am sure I express the warmest greetings to a distinguished guest to the capital city today, one who I understand is being entertained this evening by the Speaker of the house. This is a distinguished man from the land of Scotland, James Miller, Lord Provost of Edinburgh, and Mrs. Ella J. Miller, Lady Provost of Edinburgh. I am sure that as one in whom Scottish blood runs strong I express the sentiments of all hon. members in extending the warmest greetings to this distinguished couple on this occasion. I am sure we are all mindful of the Scot today and of the part he is playing in the affairs of the world. With a shrewd, prudent -and peaceful conscience in the discharge of duty to a degree above all others, being imbued with tremendous powers of concentration, the Scottish race has made an impression upon the world to which no other race can yet lay claim. So I repeat how proud we are to welcome to this parliament of Canada our distinguished guests on this great occasion.
Likewise I say to you tonight that I am sure that by whatever waters of Babylon our tents may be pitched, we are all proud to serve in this parliament of Canada and in particular to have a part in the building of this great nation. I say likewise how proud we are as Canadians and as members of the government today to have as the Prime Minister of this country and as the leader of our party one so distinguished in the past, one so notable in the present, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. I repeat what I have said elsewhere, that it is not wealth or riches that bring greatness to a country or to a party; it is the men who travel in its service treading like the stars to their selected place.
As we think of the part the Prime Minister is playing in the world of international affairs and in affairs that directly affect our country I am sure all government members will join me in saying that we yield to few in our admiration for one so devoted to his people and to the welfare of all mankind. As 1 think of the part the Prime Minister and members of this government are playing I am reminded of the lines:
Give me men, to match my mountains,
Give me men, to match my plains,
Men of courage, men of action,
Men with Canada in their brains.
So I say tonight, give me the men of this government of today, men imbued with the spirit of unity, with a common allegiance to democratic ideals and the welfare of all our people, and I will give you men who are

The Address-Mr. A. C. Murray making for Canada today its rightful place in the sun among the nations of the world.
It is a great land in which you and I are privileged to live, and it is playing its part among the nations of the world. To couch it in the language of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), there is one contribution which I feel in the long run may well be the most important contribution that our country can make to the world today. Our country is a unique example of international good will and co-operation which could be extended to all nations. Our country is a dominion which extends from sea to sea, an association of provinces which are bound together, not by any military strength, not by any charter, not by any covenant or by any legal instrument. That which binds Canada together today are the great and mighty intangibles of life. The basis of our relationship is friendship and a spirit of co-operation, an attitude of progress with a common allegiance to democratic ideals and fundamental moral principles. Those qualities which have shown themselves so capable of transcending and bridging great disparities of race and religion within our own country can, I feel, achieve a like purpose in the world.
As our own Prime Minister once said at a London conference of prime ministers, while it may be necessary for some considerable time for peace-loving countries to maintain military strength in order to resist or deter aggression, there can never be real peace or real security in the world until we can achieve something of that mutual co-operation and understanding among all nations which today we are striving to maintain within our own commonwealth. That I feel is the ultimate objective of the whole world, the ultimate goal at which peace and brotherhood will be the ideals of men and nations everywhere.
I say that this is a great country. I ask any member of this house: Do you know of any other country in the world, perhaps barring the United States of America, that enjoys a higher standard of living than we do here in Canada? Do you know of any other country whose currency is at a premium in the market places of the world? Do you know of any other country in the world where opportunity still knocks and where by simple fundamentals you can find it to the extent that you can in this land of Canada?
I am sure there must be thousands and thousands of people throughout the world tonight who would give everything they have if they could only come to this land of Canada to enjoy our privileges, to enjoy the prosperity that has been made possible


through the policies promulgated by the Liberal government of today, policies that transcend the bickerings and lamentations that go out from this house, policies that have built and strengthened the pillars of unity, of security and of freedom for all our people.
Yet with all our policy, with all our prosperity, with all our technological progress, with all our material acquisitions, with all our natural resources, are we removing today some of the barnacles that still cling to the life of this country? I am reminded that hon. members who come from the sea may know something of the barnacle, that tiny animal that lives within the sea and clings to the passing hulls of vessels. It propagates with great rapidity and spreads a concrete-like substance across the hull of a ship which if neglected cuts down steerageway and the efficiency and effectiveness of the ship.
I appreciate that we have eliminated two of the barnacles that previously clung to this chamber, and which had been here long before I came to the house in 1949. One of the barnacles that has been removed is the lack of acoustics. Now with a man sitting at the console a member's voice is amplified through this new sound reinforcing system so his speech is brought to all parts of the Commons most distinctly, and likewise to the galleries. I say that a bouquet should go to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) for his perseverance, his industry and his initiative in seeing that this barnacle of inefficient acoustics has been removed.
Then I should also like to present a bouquet to the Speaker of the House for seeing to it that the evening hours of sitting are regulated so we can now adjourn at ten o'clock. I am sure all members will agree that the former closing hour was a barnacle upon the life of this chamber. In these days of national crisis, these days of worry, stress and strain, we need to keep fit, we need desperately to keep our manhood and our womanhood of this and other democracies physically fit and mentally alert. I think some of us make a ghastly mistake when we do not see to it that we keep fit; for a man who may do one hour's less work per day, but save himself for the task that needs to be done for the national welfare, is far better alive with one hour less activity than dead, with his genius, his brains, his talents and his powers lost to his fellow man.
Oh, Mr. Speaker, there are barnacles elsewhere, everywhere. I was amazed the other day to read of the betting odds on successful marriages. I am amazed each year at the number of divorce cases that come before parliament, about which every member knows. It is unbelievable. Why? Barnacles,

that is all; tiny, nonsensical things that somehow get a grip on married life, that cling with all the tenacity of a barnacle to the hull of a ship, and cause that glorious ship of matrimony to lose its course and go on the rocks; things that could be so easily forgotten, things that become pitched battles when, with a little understanding and a little smile, they could be avoided.
That is what happens. Oh, I appreciate that the barnacles of government are not centred here at Ottawa alone. They are centred in the minds of men and women who will not vote when an election comes. When a war is on they will fight, they will buy bonds, they will do this, that, and everything else to bring about peace; but when peace comes they will not bother to go to the polls to choose the best man or the best woman to represent them at the councils or in the parliament of our nation. They slip back into that luxurious and splendid slumber of the democratic citizen, who thinks only of his nation's safety when it is in danger.
There are barnacles everywhere. I suppose members of the opposition will say that taxation is a barnacle in the life of Canada today. But let me remind them that their demands for lower taxation are incompatible with demands for increased government services necessitating heavy expenditures. Here we have hon. members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition proposing savings that amount to $116 million a year, whereas new services requested by the Progressive Conservative party would add $600 million a year to the federal budget.
I say to hon. members of the opposition, as I have said elsewhere, that you cannot have your cake and eat it too. If we want to build our defences strong and maintain the attributes of decency throughout the world, and if we want social security for all our people, then let us do first things first. Let us build so those who follow after us may enjoy the shade. Let us realize that if we want all these things, then we must be prepared to pay for them.
I presume there are a few barnacles in every trade and in every profession. It seems to me that no man who does not understand the principles of a particular trade or profession has any right to criticize it. My purpose in rising at this time is not to criticize; rather, it is to suggest to myself, as well as to the members of the government and to all hon. members in the house, that sometimes it is best to take the hull of the ship of state onto a set of ways, clean off the barnacles and set it sailing again, shipshape and clean, and on a voyage toward a happy harbour.
The Address-Mr. A. C. Murray
I think, sir, of the Department of National Health and Welfare and its wonderful record of achievement. Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is a barnacle on the record of that department.
I wonder, sir, if we realize that as a result of the research that has been conducted by that department and by men of science, and as a result of the growth of medicine and pharmacy, all of us are living longer than was expected at our births. I recognize, of course, that today a woman lives possibly four and a half to five years longer than a man. We have heard the reason suggested: that we take such good care of them. Nevertheless we have added almost a score of years to our life expectancy in the last half century. This poses a terrific problem for those engaged in life insurance, and those concerned with annuity and pension schemes.
I suggest the growth of science has been an important factor. Believe me when I tell you that in New York state in 1928 nearly 2,000 people out of every 100,000 died as a result of appendicitis; by 1948 the number was brought down to 440 for every 100,000 of the population. In 1928 the figures show that 16,000 people out of every 100,000 of the population died of the pneumonias, while in 1948 only 5,132 died. In 1928 1,950 out of every 100,000 died of influenza, while in 1948 there were only 114. There is the answer. Here in Canada also, as a result of the new drugs, the new antibiotics, every one of us is living longer than was expected for us at our births.
I think of insulin, which was discovered by that great Canadian, Sir Frederick Banting. Formerly, when sugar was discovered in a child's urine it was a foregone conclusion that it would never reach the age of 21 years. As a result of that great discovery, thousands upon thousands of people can now live to a ripe and useful age. I think of penicillin, discovered by Sir Alexander Fleming, and what a great benefactor to mankind he has been. I think in the same way about streptomycin, aureomycin, terramycin. Mr. Speaker, I can vouch for the fact that there are hundreds of promising new drugs on the horizon, and the horizon is equally challenging and tremendous.
Every one of us has more years of life expectancy than was anticipated at our births. What are we going to do with them? All of us are working fewer hours than we used to, but what are we going to do with our added leisure? It lays a terrific obligation and responsibility upon the family and the school to teach people the joy of living well the leisure time, and giving them guidance in how to spend the coin of leisure wisely.

The Address-Mr. A. C. Murray
The Department of National Health and Welfare has played, and is playing, a significant role in the health and welfare of our citizens. It has carefully re-examined the way to human welfare and, as a result of its endeavours, we have gone forward steadily and in freedom toward a decent level of life. There is a strong tide flowing in the affairs of men; social injustices are being swept aside and human progress is at the flood. Yet, with this great record, there is a barnacle on the life of this department. The hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) referred to it in his speech in seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Other hon. members have referred to it again and again, and I refer to it today. I mean, of course, that the government should do something to remove the means test on pensions for the blind. Tonight I am mindful of the biblical injunction:
And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known:	I will make darkness light before
them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them.
Surely we in this chamber cannot do less. It seems to me that the idea of the blindness allowance being a payment for their handicap has been lost sight of by the legislators. The means test and its regulations are so restrictive that they discourage blind persons from trying to better themselves. I am informed that since blind persons over 70 years of age have been transferred to the Old Age Security Act, under which they now benefit by the elimination of the means test, there are only about 4,000 of the 19,000 blind adults who do not receive the allowance. These are the ones whose income is above the allowable income in order to qualify for the allowance. These persons are blind, and need and would be encouraged by the allowance in coping with their handicap. Surely it would not place too great a burden on the various governments to agree to the elimination of this restrictive legislation.
Eighty per cent of all blindness occurs in adult life, and I need not say that the loss of sight in adult life has the effect of wrecking hopes and plans as well as the sense of security. Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is not a member of this house who would not like to see this barnacle, this restrictive means test on the blind, removed. I know, sir, that today our troops are fighting in Korea, and none of us is unmindful of the terrific sacrifice that is being made. There is the sacrifice being made by those who cannot see. There is more to a fight than is seen in the game. There is the fight that enters not the limelight of publicity. There is the fight that some day we hope will bring about peace. But today it is the fight of every one of us in


this chamber to give what we can to life, to serve not for ourselves but so that those in darkness can share and know the joy of living too.
So, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the blind in my home county of Oxford, who have appealed to me to speak for them and likewise for all Canadian blind persons, I want to say that although I may have been halting in my words I have been struck by the sincerity with which hon. gentlemen preceding me have spoken on this subject, and I earnestly hope and pray that the government will do its part to remove this barnacle that is upon it at the present time.
Then I should like to briefly commend the government and the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) in particular for the legislation envisaged in the speech from the throne whereby in all likelihood some compensation is to be given to the rural mail carriers for the extra cost entailed today in fulfilling their duties. These men and women travel in all kinds of weather to see that the mail goes through. I am sure all hon. members appreciate their reasonable request for further compensation and hope the government, having taken cognizance of this pressing problem, will see to it that equitable compensation is made feasible. May I say frankly that as the member for Oxford I look forward to that day when mail service will be made available directly to all rural mail patrons where roads are passable and kept open. To me, Mr. Speaker, it is a barnacle on this fine department that on account of regulations a great number of people living in our rural parts are penalized by reason of distance and other qualifying factors. I feel that some revision could be made in these outmoded laws whereby our rural people, who pay their taxes just the same as the rest of us, might enjoy the privilege of direct mail service to their gates which their neighbour may now be receiving.
I presume that taxation is in the minds of many of our citizens. It is one of the greatest barnacles in the road of progress today. I recall that when I spoke in last year's budget debate I credited our Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) with being the architect of a fiscal policy that has made Canada the envy of the world. I said that as a result Canada's credit abroad was being strengthened, inflation was being controlled, capital for investment was being attracted and the Canadian dollar was at a premium in the market places of the world. At that time I made the suggestion that the weight on corporations was too heavy. Likewise today I reiterate that, national defence permitting, every effort should be made to reduce corporation and personal income taxes. I do not know that

I can interpret with greater propriety what I should like to say than to quote the words of Mr. B. C. Gardner, president of the Bank of Montreal, when at a recent shareholders' annual meeting he said:
On the domestic side, development of Canada's resources and the expansion of industrial capacity should not be stifled by heavy taxes on business. With capital requirements running ahead of the amount new savings can provide, development is dependent on what industry itself can plow back in the way of undistributed profits and depreciation reserves. While a corporate tax rate which takes more than half of every dollar of profit may be a convenient fiscal devise, such a burden of taxation directly upon enterprise has very dubious connotations from the standpoint of enhanced national well-being.
Expanding on the president's remarks, Gordon R. Ball, general manager of the Bank of Montreal, said:
It is essential in a country like ours, requiring as it does large sums of risk and investment money, that the tax climate provide an inducement to this type of capital.
So I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that, national defence costs permitting, the Minister of Finance should give his profound attention to this matter of easing the tax structure on all our citizens. Oh, I suppose, sir, there are barnacles in everyone's constituency. I know that for a long time there has been a barnacle existing in the town of Ingersoll in my constituency, a barnacle represented by the hazardous traffic tie-up that prevails where the C.N.R. tracks in that town cross highway No. 2. Since becoming a member of the house I have earnestly endeavoured to have it eliminated, and I am grateful to Mr. A. J. Lomas, vice-president of the C.N.R., for his co-operation in this direction. In his last letter to me under date of November 27, 1952, the vice-president informs me that he has included this item in their 1953 capital budget and is hopeful that the necessary approval will be obtained to carry out this work. While I realize that this is a matter of internal management, I can but emphasize again on behalf of the citizens of that fine community of Ingersoll the urgency and importance of seeing that the capital amount needed for this work be approved and that remedial action be facilitated as quickly as possible.
Then, Mr. Speaker, while I am thinking of the C.N.R. I think also of the fine C.N.R. station that the Speaker of this house has in his own city of Brantford. I mention it by way of contrast with the dingy and ancient C.N.R. station at Woodstock, Ontario, with its poor lighting, its dismal, unkempt, internal appearance which is not a credit to the C.N.R. or to the lovely city of Woodstock from which I come-Woodstock, Ontario, sir, which is
The Address-Mr. A. C. Murray noted for its beauty, for its key of freedom to visiting tourists, for its surrounding fertile fields and for its friendly people. I say, sir, that station is a barnacle in the life of my community, and likewise a barnacle on the main line of the Canadian National Railways. This, too, may be a matter for internal management, but in passing I make mention of it in order to emphasize that something should be done about it.
Well, sir, I am honest enough to say that I do not know all the problems of government, but I do know that my business as a pharmacist depends upon the good will of the public who patronize me; and any of us who carry on a business or a profession where we are dependent upon the good will of our customers or clients must make sure there are no barnacles on the mind, or on the institution of which we are a part. They get there, just as easily as barnacles get on the hull of a ship, for it is easy to say "That's a good idea, but let someone else try it." It is easy to persuade oneself that things that literally cry out for the doing do not need to be done. These become barnacles; and just as ships on historic voyages have met disaster upon the rocks, when the absence of barnacles might have meant the difference between life and death, success and failure, so too with a business; so too with government.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat that I do not know all the problems of government, but here are fundamentals about mankind that I have learned and that we all can learn if we read the pages of history. One of those fundamentals is that no matter how much there may be of animosity and difference of opinion, that which is best for the greatest number eventually must come to be. That which is fairest and most straightforward and truly honest, that which benefits most largely, must inevitably one day come to be.

In the field of material production the government has given active encouragement for full use of all who are able and willing to work. Employers and employees alike have been asked to work longer and harder. The government has gone further and urged upon industry the advantages of employing older workers. Employers have also been asked not to make retirement automatic at 65 but to employ and retire workers not on the basis of chronological age and to consider each individual case on its merits. Yet at the same time the age limit as set out by the civil service commission for employment in the government service is from 21 to 40. If this is to be the considered policy of the government, can one expect industry to take seriously the exhortations to employ older workers end to think twice before retiring employees automatically at 65?
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) deserves our thanks for the broad view he takes of this question. We all know that there are myriads of men and women in this country able and eager to keep on working after 65. The work of this agency has been lauded on many sides and the standard of our public service is a credit to Canada, but I am bound to say that certain weaknesses are apparent.
Presumably a policy is laid down and regulations are made for its application. The Address-Mr. Balcom examines it that in all fairness it merits careful review and revision before any permanent scheme is adopted. The people of Nova Scotia and their friends are especially concerned since the method adopted for the distribution of the 1951-52 grants resulted in Nova Scotia universities receiving the lowest amount per student of any province in Canada; and the discrepancy, as I shall submit, is by no means trifling. Members of the house will recall that the money voted by parliament was distributed according to provincial populations at the rate of 50 cents a head, without regard to the proportion of eligible students in each province. Speaking of 50 cents a head, it reminds me that it is said that away back in 1867 Nova Scotia was sold for the price of a sheepskin, 80 cents. That has no relation to these remarks on universities.	'
The method of distributing the grants, based on provincial populations, seems to be at variance with the accepted view that universities are of national importance. Nova Scotia universities, without question, are performing a national service inasmuch as many of their graduates enter business, the professions or public life in other parts of Canada. I need not endeavour to prove such a statement as that. I should like to put before the house the picture of how federal aid per student by provinces works out on the basis of the 1951-52 figures. I will mention Nova Scotia first, and I should like hon. members to keep the figure for that province in their minds. Here is the result:

Yet surely it is unfair to penalize Nova Scotia, for that is the effect, simply because we have a high proportion of eligible students. It should not be too difficult to set up standards for all Canada and define exactly what is meant by "university" and what is meant by "eligible student", so that a system can be devised which will be fair to all, giving a uniform rate per student irrespective of location. Surely it is fair to say that one of the objectives of these federal grants to universities is to encourage these universities to educate students for the benefit of the nation. But a system which penalizes the province that has the greatest proportion of eligible students hinders rather than helps the pursuit of that objective. The case, I believe, is sound. Our universities ask for no more than a system which will be fair to all. Speaking in the debate a few days ago the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) gave us something to think about. His constituency is contiguous to the United States, and the facts and figures he quoted must be particularly galling to Canadian citizens in the border areas. There was, said the hon. member for Charlotte, a great deal of criticism with regard to the subsidization of farm and fishery products, but he submitted the most glaring example of subsidization was that represented by the difference in prices of many manufactured products here and in the United States.
Differences in cost between certain specified items in the United States and Canada were quoted. The accuracy of these comparisons may be challenged, but there can be no challenging the fact that prices in Canada are much higher in many lines than in the United States. Of course, the hon. member blames the tariff and the tendency to take advantage of the tariff as the cause of the difference.
I am sure that with these instances before us more and more Canadians are wondering if the price of Canadian economic independence is not coming too high. Canada, as everyone knows, has a very great stake in the removal of trade restrictions and in broadening the market for our exports. Yet we must recognize that protection of one kind or another is part and parcel of the commercial policy of all countries including our biggest markets, the United States and the United Kingdom. In our own country, many industries have grown up behind protective tariffs, industries which have added greatly to our


wealth and development. We are reminded from time to time that this has been done at a price, which is paid by the general public in the consumption of goods.
I believe that it would be foolish to suggest the removal of all such restrictions. We are forced to restrain to some extent the purely economic factors. The efforts to encourage the further fabrication of pulp and lumber products within our own country are well justified. The processing of industrial materials, such as iron, steel and aluminum, rather than exporting them raw, is desirable. Our very strong position with respect to certain of these very important commodities should determine our public policy. But that does not mean the same degree of protection should be accorded to each and every manufacturing project which seeks it.
It is a truism that the less well-organized groups in our society tend to be neglected. 1 dm an aiu that John Q. BubllC, US the COB- sumer who does the purchasing, is in this category. Why, for example, should the purchaser of a television set pay a certain price in Canada when the identical set can be purchased across the border for not much more than half? Is there any major part of the public interest advanced by the artificial development of this particular industry in Canada? Certainly, due to our concentration of industry in Quebec and Ontario, the mari-times are suffering in paying a high price for everything they buy.
We have today a very special interest in television. When the field of television is broadened and extended to the areas of Vancouver, Winnipeg and Halifax, I believe everyone within the range of these stations should be entitled to buy a television set at the lowest cost possible. There should be a television set in every home, not just the wealthy homes, so the people as a whole may receive the benefit of the instructive and educational features so broadcast.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, may I respectfully suggest that the government take under consideration for this item, television sets, a lowering of the protective tariffs and excise taxes so the service rendered by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in this field may be enjoyed by the largest number of people possible. As it is at present, the whole of Canada is paying for the protection of the few.
Before leaving this question of protection, may I draw the attention of the house to a very serious matter that reflects on the income of our national harbours, our railroads, and the stevedores connected with

any ports of exit, such as Halifax and Saint John. It is the matter of the export of Canadian automobiles and parts through United States ports. Automobile companies receive practically all the protection they require, but they in turn are not playing the game with the people of Canada as a whole, nor with the seaports of Canada which are equipped and capable of handling our export trade. We deplore the fact that these companies are not playing their full part as they should in shipping through Canadian ports. I think it is poor gratitude, and certainly not patriotic, for these companies to export their products through United States ports after receiving concessions from the people of Canada, including the stevedores and the railway workers who are dependent upon the movement of export traffic for their livelihood.
I would like to quote a few statistics concerning these exports. In 1948 Canadian automobile manufacturers exported through United States ports 26,082 automobiles while through Canadian ports went 22,087. At the same time automobile parts to the value of $4,454,050 were exported through United States ports, and $9,091,853 through Canadian ports. Now we come to 1951 and we find almost a complete reversal. Exports through United States ports were 50,465 cars as against 10,011 through Canadian ports. In 1951 parts went through United States ports to the value of $8,435,467; through Canadian ports just about one-half that amount, $4,534,140.
I submit, sir, the manufacturers have a poor sense of gratitude, but I wish to go further. The Matheson submission last September to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) on the non-absorption by the railways of the national harbours board top wharfage surcharges contains a statement showing country of destination, dollar value and shipping weight in tons of export traffic originating in Canada and routed via the port of New York during the month of February, 1952. The figures I am giving you now are based on the United States department of census returns. The dollar value of these February exports through New York was $31,287,998, which -means 68,126 shipping weight tons, all lost to our Canadian ports and our national revenue. Automobiles, trucks, buses, trailers and parts shipped amounted in value to $15,835,869 and in tonnage to over 53 million pounds. The automobile people are not the only offenders, because Canadian goods generally have been flowing out of United States ports instead of Canadian ports. During 1951 the value of these goods
The Address-Mr. Balcom amounted to $257 million, which was about 16 per cent of Canada's total exports to overseas countries.
These figures are disturbing, and should be to every member of this house, because the tendency to ship through United States ports is increasing. In 1949 less than 11 per cent of Canada's overseas exports went out of United States ports. In dollars this meant about $155 million, and as I have told you this amount has grown to over $257 million.
I listened with considerable interest to the several speeches on behalf of the sugar beet industry, which has been affected by the importation of Cuban cane sugar. While I have every sympathy with the speakers, I cannot go along with them in their suggested remedy, namely more protection. It seems natural, I suppose, for an industry to seek government aid when that industry appears threatened. But if my information is correct, sugar is already receiving protection to the extent of $1.89 per hundred pound bag.
In considering the suggestion for increased protection, we must remember that other commodities in addition to sugar enter into the picture. In 1951, when the Cuban agreement was made, concessions were obtained for several other items of food, one of which was an important maritime product, salt codfish. Last year Canada exported salt codfish amounting in value to $2,412,000. Then, in addition to our salt codfish, potatoes were exported from the maritimes in huge quantities. Let us not do anything to protect one product that would jeopardize the trade the maritimes are enjoying with Cuba. In other words, why rob Peter to pay Paul? Personally I think Paul is doing very well now.
Later on in the session, Mr. Speaker, I intend to have something to say about health insurance. Since this is a project so extensive and involving so many services that we have not now available, I think I can well wait until a later time to speak on it. There is a subject, however, very much alive today on which I should like to touch, namely increases in the pensions of worthy indigent parents of deceased soldiers. We all know of numbers of parents who gave everything they had in order to educate their sons only to have them, on the completion of their education, enlist in the armed services. Some of these boys were killed. Many of them were married and left families, but automatically the wife and family are provided for while the indigent mothers and fathers are left without support.

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Transport, of which I have given notice, and have sent him newspaper clippings in connection therewith. My question is prompted by a level crossing accident at the intersection of Lawrence avenue and the Canadian National Railways line in Weston last Friday night, in which two Brampton residents lost their lives.
My question is contained in a long sentence, but I believe it is as concise as I can make it and, at the same time, have it in proper form. In a case where there is a double railway track and a train is standing on one of such tracks near an unprotected level crossing or sufficiently close to a protected level crossing to make the wigwag or flashing lights operate, is there any railway regulation which calls for one of the crew of that standing train to proceed to the intersection and to warn the highway traffic of trains approaching on the other track which may be hidden from view because of the standing train?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY PRECAUTIONS
speechtext:
The answer to my hon. friend's
question is as follows:
At a protected crossing such as the one in Weston, which the hon. member has in mind, the operating rules as approved by the board of transport commissioners do not call for flag protection by a member of the crew of the standing train, since the operation of the wigwag or flashing lights is considered as sufficient protection.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY PRECAUTIONS
speechtext: In view of the number of accidents of this kind that have occurred in the past, would the minister review the situation?

I am sure that, because of this terrible tragedy, they will take the matter under consideration. Well, I do not know actually where the Secretary of State is. He is supposed to be in Newfoundland but the city clerk of the municipality of St. John's today sent a telegram to him here in Ottawa. He is not here and he is not in Newfoundland so I do not really know where he is actually. I do not know whether any of the other ministers know either.
As I said, I intend dealing chiefly with Newfoundland matters because they are noncontroversial. I won't deal with anything controversial since the rum in Ontario is of very poor quality indeed. What brings that up? Well, a column by the Junior Chamber of Commerce in the St. John's Telegram of December 6 contains this paragraph:
Plain speech is a lost art in these parts. The modern Newfoundlander needs three tots of strong rum before he clears his throat, and a good look under the sofa and behind the door before he ventures an opinion on any controversial subject:
As I say, Ontario rum is not very good and, consequently, I am not going to deal with any controversial matters. My statement is no reflection on hon. members from Newfoundland, because I do not know any one of them who partakes of such a libation- other than myself.
The first matter I wish to deal with, Mr. Speaker, is Bell island and the petition presented the other day. It is not a new subject by any means, because I note in sessional paper 149J of June 29, 1951, that I first brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) on November 19, 1949, and I did so continuously from that time until March 19, 1952. That has been a long period of time and during it I have stressed to the minister the importance of the terminal facilities between Bell island and Portugal Cove being attended to. Let me tell you that Bell island at present has the largest iron ore mine in the British empire. It has been producing constantly for some fifty-eight years and from a question answered, as it appears in Hansard of December 10, 1952, more than half of the iron ore produced in Canada in 1951 came from Bell island. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the community of Bell island has a population of more than 10,000 persons. It is a major industrial area in the province, 2,000 workmen being engaged in the mining industry. It has annual earnings of more than $6 million and the money spent, including earnings from secondary industries in the island, is very great indeed. A considerable portion of the tax on these sales, naturally, is paid to the federal government in the form of income and corporation taxes, sales tax, licence fees and royalties. The community of Bell island


is a very important factor in providing the United Nations with raw materials on which the defence of the western world lies.
We all agree that the mining industry is a hazardous one and the extension of a proper ferry service to the mainland of Newfoundland is most important, especially in view of the fact that the island is without proper hospital facilities. Last year the ferry service transported at least 100,000 passengers and 15,000 motor vehicles, together with goods and supplies of all kinds which are used by this thriving and prosperous community. Bell island required speedy dispatch of mails and freight but such service is not presently being provided. The residents of Bell island ask for a proper terminal dock to be provided at Bell island and at Portugal Cove.
The position, as the minister has told me from time to time, is that they are ferry wharves and, consequently, are not maintained by the federal government. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have to take issue with the minister there because I notice that in an advertisement in the Canada Gazette of October 4, 1952, at page 2726, there is an advertisement for the construction of ferry landings, Howe island-Pickett's ferry- Ontario. That advertisement is signed by the acting secretary of the Department of Public Works, Mr. Robert Fortier. That is a provincial ferry and the wharves are being maintained by the federal government. Moreover, term of union No. 33 provides that all Newfoundland public wharves shall be the property of the federal government. No notice was ever given to the province, nor was it ever discussed at any time until this application was made, suggesting that this ferry wharf would not be maintained by the federal government. Therefore, I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is fair and reasonable to say that, as we were not given proper notice, this wharf should be considered as a public wharf and maintained accordingly. The terminals were constructed and are maintained, I am told, by the federal government for the ferry running from Amherst island to Milhaven in Prince Edward, a distance of two miles, a ferry which carries twelve cars.
Now, Bell island has been the scene of very great activity. The Portugal Cove wharf has had the honour of being the point of embarkation of the late King George VI during his tour in 1939, and of our present Queen Elizabeth when she left Canada to return to the United Kingdom after her tour last year. I must say that it was a great disgrace to see the type of wharf from which our Princess, and now our Queen, had to embark on the little ferry in order to board her ship. It reflected no credit on the minister to say that

this was a ferry wharf and he could not put it in shape.
The other day when I commented on the fact that on Thursday last we were celebrating the fourth anniversary of the signing of the terms of union, hon. members were good enough to indicate that they approved and hoped the union would be a happy one. Now, Mr. Speaker, one of the offspring, if I may use the term, of this union is this wharf, and I am quite certain in my own mind that it is the obligation of the Minister of Public Works. I want to know what he is going to do about our Bell, meaning Bell island. So far as I am concerned the matter will not be permitted to drift any longer.
I refer you to Hansard, page 4475, of June 21, 1951. At that time, I drew attention to the great difference in the moneys being allotted for public works between the districts in Newfoundland represented by hon. members on the other side of the house and hon. members on this side of the house. On page 4474 of Hansard for that day, I said this to the minister:
From April 1, 1949, the district of St. John's East had spent in it $38,108.56 . . .
In the district of Bonavista-Twillingate represented by the Secretary of State, the amount was $267,095.21.

I am sorry if he was dissatisfied, but there was no other answer I could give to the question as it was put. Well, I disagree most heartily with him on that state-

ment, because I do not think it is factual. On the contrary I suggest that, since it has been in office, this government has considered all legitimate claims of the Islanders, and has dealt with them accordingly and granted many of them.

Well, with respect, may I remind him that Conservative administrations have been in office three, if not four, times since 1873. They came to see me about the very matter with which I am concerned at the moment, namely the application by Northumberland Ferries Limited for a new vessel.
