Well, let me say to him that that buffer commission has been very generous, or at least very fair, to Northumberland Ferries Limited. The company began its operations in 1941, at which time it received a subsidy of $34,000. That subsidy was increased from $34,000 to $158,000, thanks to the consideration given to the problem by the maritime commission. While it is true that the commission did not consider the inauguration of the service,
The Address-Mr. Chevrier it must be kept in mind that the service began in 1941, and that when the subsidy of $34,000 was paid there was only one ship in operation. Today there are two, and that has meant an increase in the subsidy.
All in all, since the service has been in existence-that is, between 1941 and 1952-a subsidy somewhat in excess of $1,030,000 has been paid to Northumberland Ferries Limited -and much of it on the recommendation of the Canadian maritime commission, which my hon. friend calls a buffer commission.
The hon. member seemed to feel that very little attention was paid to the just and rightful claims of the Islanders. Well, I can assure my hon. friend that I do not cast aside any of their claims; I give them the best possible consideration of which I am capable, as indeed the commission is doing with the present application.
The application was made to the maritime commission. In effect, it seeks a new ship. In other words, Northumberland Ferries Limited seeks the approval of the commission for the construction of a new ship. That is a pretty serious matter, and for that reason the commission must study it carefully. It has asked the company for additional information, and that information is not yet forthcoming. When it is received the commission will deal with it carefully and will report to me, at which time I will be in a position to tell my hon. friend, and all other hon. members, what the recommendation of the commission is.
Then, if I may pass from that matter to a second one, I would turn to a complaint made by the new member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) in which he expressed criticism concerning the construction of the ferry vessel between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor. This criticism came somewhat as a surprise to me, because when the announcement was made by the government that there would be a new ferry in that part of the country it was well received by the house. My recollection is that all hon. members, even those from New Brunswick, were clearly of the opinion that it was a good thing to add a new ship to this very vital service between a state in the United States and the province of Nova Scotia.
This is why I should like to take a moment to review the position, in so far as the decision concerning this ferry is concerned.
The house will recall that in 1949 Eastern Steamship Lines, a United States firm which was operating a passenger service between Boston and Yarmouth, served notice of its intention to discontinue that service entirely. The first step which the government took
654	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Chevrier was to seek out some other contractor who might be willing to give consideration to carrying on the service. The government got in touch with a number of operators, but only one offer was received. That offer could not be accepted for two reasons. First, it called for the payment of a subsidy of $300,000 per annum for ten years and over and above that a guaranteeing of a $500,000 bond issue on behalf of the applicant. The second reason why we could not accept the application was that the applicant proposed to purchase and operate the S.S. Yarmouth, the ship then being used by Eastern Steamship Lines on the service. Our investigations indicated that that ship, which was 21 years old, was definitely unsuitable for the modern type of traffic.
This inability to find a contractor who would operate the service led us to establish a committee composed of representatives of the province of Nova Scotia, of the Department of nanspoi l. cinu uj. the Canadian National Railways. The committee made an exhaustive study of the economic and operative features associated with a service between Yarmouth and Boston and after giving the whole matter careful consideration came to these conclusions. First, there should be constructed a vessel suitable for a daily round trip service and designed especially to transport a large number of refrigerated trucks and tourist automobiles. Second, Bar Harbor should be selected as the New England terminus because that point was sufficiently close to permit a daily round trip.
The hon. member made two criticisms. First, he suggested that the new vessel should operate on a triangular run and take in Saint John, New Brunswick. I should like to point out that a vessel operating on such a run would require accommodation for overnight traffic. The vessel we are building for the Bar Harbor-Yarmouth service is to provide a daily round trip service. If we were to include Saint John we certainly could not operate on the basis on which we are operating now. It would not be profitable to operate on that basis and we simply could not do it. The report of the committee to which I referred a moment ago shows conclusively that we could not economically justify the construction of a vessel of that type, namely, one with cabin accommodation, dining room lounges and necessarily a larger crew.
The other suggestion was that the former Saint John-Boston service be resumed. If we could not find an operator to run the service between Yarmouth and Boston I am extremely doubtful whether we could find one who could operate profitably between

Saint John and Boston. It is most doubtful that such a venture would be profitable under any circumstances in view of the increased cost of operation and present-day trend toward travel by motor car. I think that that suggestion answers itself.
Based upon studies which the committee to which I have referred made and based on a study which we made ourselves, it is our opinion that there will be no detrimental effect upon the tourist traffic to New Brunswick because of the operation of this new ferry between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor. On the contrary, it is our view and our anticipation that this service will encourage larger traffic inasmuch as United States tourists will find it possible to make a circular trip, either entering through New Brunswick and departing from Nova Scotia or vice versa.

National Defence-Currie Report

I find, Mr. Speaker, having thus far been able to read thirty-eight pages-I have not been able to go through the whole report-that there are some seven pages on which changes appear to have been made. Some of those changes, I must say, are purely editorial, but there are at least three pages-page 7, page 13 and page 17-where the changes seem to be quite substantial.

But, if this spirit permeated the lower echelons of the army, it is more difficult to condone the same attitudes at or near the top.
-the phrasing of the latter part of that sentence has been changed to read:

My point in raising this at the present time is to press the question I put this morning; and I hope that the Prime Minister will find out all there is to be found out about the two printings of the report-in particular that he will get a full explanation why these, and any other changes there may be, were made. Who made the changes? Did Mr. Currie make them? Did he make them on the orders of the chief of the general staff? Did he make them on the orders of someone else or on the suggestion of any of these people?

My reason lor rising this afternoon is to focus attention on the particular subject of that strike at Louiseville and the attitude of the provincial government with regard to labour relations in that province. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), if he were in his place, or his parliamentary assistant might say: "Yes, but labour relations in the province of Quebec are a matter of provincial responsibility." That is quite true, but in this strike there are federal implications. In addition to the police entering and taking over that town, because of the reading of the Riot Act that town is placed in the hands of the police exclusively. While the provinces enforce the Criminal Code-and the Riot Act is read under the Criminal Code-nevertheless we here enact these laws and are responsible for the implications in connection with their enforcement in the provinces.
For the benefit of the parliamentary assistant to the minister I should like to stress the fact that once that Riot Act is read and that town is placed under the jurisdiction of the provincial police-as this town in Quebec is at this time-there are certain penalties which apply in a situation of that kind. For example, once the Riot Act is read and the town is taken over by the police, as a result of a small gathering or of any infraction of the law or of the curfew that is imposed under the Riot Act, a man can be placed in jail, with a maximum sentence of life for any violation of that particular law. As we make those laws, I say that we should give some consideration to them when these amendments to the Criminal Code are being brought about.
There are two parties to this dispute as there are to any dispute. On the one hand, you have approximately 1,000 textile workers at that plant which is that of Associated Textiles of Canada, Limited. These textile workers are citizens of Quebec and of Canada; they are taxpayers. In the great majority of cases the wages of workers in that industry, in that province particularly, are not too high.
This strike took place last March. The interval between then and now is a long time for a dispute like that to drag along. It is reminiscent of what happened a short time ago in the asbestos industry in the same province when the police used tear gas and batons. That asbestos strike at the Johns-Manville Company should have taught the government of Quebec, and maybe the union also, that the way to settle wage negotiations today is not on the street with batons and with the use of police. But apparently nothing was learned from the strike in the asbestos industry, and now we have this
The Address-Mr. Gillis mess in Louiseville. As I stated a moment ago, on the one hand you have 1,000 workers in the textile industry-and they are Canadians with families-who are low paid and who have legitimate grievances. The union involved is the Catholic syndicates. Then on the other hand, you have the industry itself.
Let us have a look at it for a minute. I have here just a brief synopsis of it. It is the Associated Textiles of Canada, Limited. This is a wholly-owned subsidiary of United Merchants and Manufacturers, Incorporated, an American firm with head offices in Delaware, U.S.A. The parent company is a holding company owning a number of textile plants-mills, finishing plants, converters, factory facilities and merchandising outlets- in the U.S.A., Argentina, Canada and several other countries. No separate figures for the profits of the Canadian subsidiary, Associated Textiles of Canada, Limited, are available. Its net assets, as at June 30, 1951, however, were $4,610,688. Net profits of the consolidated companies, however- including Canadian and other subsidiaries- were as follows: Total net profit, 1950, $10,805,290; in 1951,	$16,158,186; or an
increase of 49 per cent over 1950. The source of this information is Moody's Industrials, 1952, so it is right up to date. As I pointed out a moment ago, you have that large group of workers and you have this huge corporation. The dispute is over wages. From the figures that I have set out here, it can be seen that in the years 1950 and 1951 the company was not in a bad position. They have substantial profits. They had an increase in their profits of 49 per cent in 1951 over 1950. The workers at that plant, in their wage demands, are not looking for a 49 per cent increase, although they would be justified if they were doing so.
In reference to the dispute itself, and in the matter of money, all of the arguments are on the side of the wage earners who are attempting to settle their grievance in the only way that befits this day and age, namely, around the conference table. The action taken in that province with respect to this dispute indicates very clearly that labour laws and conciliation in the province of Quebec must be at least thirty years outdated, because that kind of thing did happen in my own province thirty years ago. Both government and industry have discovered in that province that there is no solution in that kind of action, because nothing like that has happened in the last thirty years. Conciliation machinery prevents it.
In the last year the steel workers' union in my own province went through negotiations lasting for five months. They extended

The Address-Mr. Gillis their contract. They had conciliation board after conciliation board. Nevertheless they finished up with a good agreement, which indicates that patience and some understanding are necessary on both sides in order to work out the problems that confront the workers.
The time is past, Mr. Speaker, when the federal government should give consideration to the enacting of a basic labour relations act in order at least to fix the basic legislation so that the provinces could pass the necessary enabling legislation to prevent this kind of thing. No one can justify what is going on today in that strike in that textile plant in Quebec. I am suggesting that the labour department should at least conduct an investigation into what is taking place there, in the interest of peace, order and good government. I am sure the parliamentary assistant to the minister will agree with me that what is happening in Quebec today is certainly giving a lot of aid and comfort to the elements within the organized labour movement whose job it is to foment trouble. Mr. Duplessis and his policies are certainly doing a first-class job for them, and I think it is the responsibility of the federal Department of Labour to check up on the matter on the grounds of peace, order and good government.
In addition to that, during the consolidation of the Criminal Code that will take place within the next year, consideration should be given to some modification or changes in the section of the code that permits of police action, the reading of the Riot Act, curfew, and the taking over of a town, with the drastic penalties that are involved once that action is taken. Today that town is in this position. If a small group of men gather they can be arrested; they can be charged with violations under that section of the code, and the maximum penalty is life imprisonment. Judging by the lack of understanding that is shown in that particular field at the present time, it would not surprise me if some judge in Quebec would hand out that maximum sentence.
I rose in my place this afternoon because I think that the headlines we are getting in relation to that strike in Quebec indicate that some action on the part of the federal government is necessary to straighten out the matter, and that some over-all labour relations act should be enacted, which would lay down the basic legislation that would at least prevent this kind of thing taking place.

May I note also the visit of our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to the conference recently held in Great Britain. Their wonderful participation, their most helpful suggestions, and the way in which they dealt with difficult problems commend them to our very great admiration.
The brilliant expose delivered in this house a few days ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), and his election as president of the United Nations assembly; his capable way of dealing with most delicate questions; his outstanding attitude of gentleman at the council table have undoubtedly put him to the fore and wholly justified the esteem we all hold for him.
In a world already torn by false ideologies, already deprived of peace of mind and soul, where harmony, good will and understanding are lacking, where cold wars are in fashion, let us hope that the unceasing good will of representatives from democratic countries will find a solution to the war in Korea. The battle is still raging with as much intensity as before the cease-fire negotiations which are now in their second year, a fact which likely has no precedent in history; and yet it seems that it is still impossible to get a glimpse of peace or bonne entente on the horizon. Valiant men are called upon to make great sacrifices, and a good many of them have already given their lives so others may continue to live in order to uphold the principles of freedom in the world; purges are going on

behind the iron curtain and many democracies have been brutally silenced at the crack of the Russian knout.
Once again, those of our generation are facing the invader. True, he does not bear the same name but is always in search of domination, instilled by tendencies of imperialism, and most eager to impose his will on other nations who fall under his heel; to have them adopt his mode of living, his ideologies and his firm belief in materialism; communism bred in the twisted brain of an unbalanced professor, Karl Marx, applied by Lenin, and imposed on a good many countries of the world by ruthless methods, is accompanied by a repetition of violations of the frontiers of once free countries.
Yesterday we had to fight Prussian imperialism and more recently the nazism of a mad painter. The free countries of the world have always presented a united front, which enables them to erase these awful nightmares which have haunted the world. On the morrow of the awful ordeal these very same free nations met at San Francisco to prepare a charter for the United Nations. Canada was co-signatory to the clauses of this charter where it was stated that, should a signatory country be attacked by another power, these countries pledged their help, and offered to come to the rescue.
On June 25, 1950, the United Nations commission in South Korea informed Trygve Lie, then secretary general of the United Nations, that the North Korean troops had crossed the 38th parallel, and were invading from east to west. Canada, as co-signatory to the charter of the United Nations, had commitments and, like other countries of the world, we were involved in military activities in that corner of Asia.
Our contributions through manpower and defence purposes have entailed a severe drain on our national budget. A discussion of the budget in its various provisions and implications might well be regarded as a general survey of the national economy, and an examination of the state of the country. Speeches delivered so far by some opposition members reveal the definite pattern taking the form of a concerted attack on taxation. Some criticism has been notable for its lack of constructive suggestions, and a dispassionate onlooker would gather the impression that the main purpose of the criticism is to tear down the budgetary structure, rather than consolidate its foundations.
Parliament, composed as it is of representatives of all parties, both government and opposition members, is presumed to be the mirror of the nation. Keeping this thought
The Address-Mr. Bruneau in mind, one may well inquire at this stage, what substantial segment of the country do the criticisms voiced so far represent. Some suggestions have been made as to high taxation, or some taxation measures that should be discarded, and the fiscal policies that should be made effective to provide the necessary revenue for the management of the country's affairs.
Canada's taxation structure is, at best, a delicate fabric. It must be designed to establish the proper balance between the national economy and the economy of the ten provinces constituting the dominion. No government, federal or provincial, relishes the task of increasing the burden of taxation; but there are times when a state of national or near-national emergency leaves no other course open to the government.
National necessity imposes sometimes on the government unprecedented duties such as the levying of taxes to provide revenues for the purchase of death-dealing armaments and the waging of war against the forces whose sole aim is the destruction of our civilization and all that it implies in the realm of human rights and fundamental liberties. The action which the government has taken on behalf of the people of Canada is actuated by but one desire, the determination to prevent occurrences such as the rape of Korea and the further enslavement of the free peoples of the world.
A nation is no stronger than the sum total of its individual strength. In this time of crisis, the people living in the 262 ridings that make up the dominion must integrate their efforts so as to give the fullest support to the government in the pursuit of its main policy, that of strengthening the country from within and helping friendly and still free nations to meet the threat of the common enemy.
True, anybody in this house would welcome a considerable reduction in taxation, but nobody would want to do so at the price of a democratic form of government.
A man of outstanding sagacity has set forth the axiom of the art of governing with a precision that has never erred. Junius, the great legislator, said, "Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty"; and, with Sir Wilfrid Laurier, I will add: "The cabinet form of government lends itself marvellously to this necessary vigilance: on one side of the house, those who govern and, on the other, those who watch." However, I am sure that our legislators, bearing in mind that their first care is the security of our land, the welfare of our fighting men, and the well-being of the nation at large, will, when possible, alleviate the burden of taxation. Millions of
662	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Bruneau dollars have gone into social security measures such as family allowances, unemployment insurance, old age security, veterans allowances, invalidity allowances in some provinces; and let us hope that before too long we shall be in a position to implement a program of health insurance assistance for our Canadian people. Such a plan, drawn in close co-operation with the provinces, would surely be a wonderful achievement on the part of this government.
Our defence program alone has drained our national budget of considerable sums of money. Nobody here will advocate drastic tax reductions at the sacrifice of defence preparedness. My constituency is in the happy position to make a not inconsequential contribution to this national effort. During the second world war, my riding, where topography of the land is admirably suited for aviation purposes, had the benefit of two airfields-one at Pendleton, and the other at St. Eugene. These two airfields, which played an important part in the expansion and full development of the eminently successful commonwealth air training plan, have been virtually unused since 1945 or 1946. A moderate outlay would be sufficient to ensure their rehabilitation and utilization. Hawkesbury has a flying club which has been in existence for several years now. The unflagging enthusiasm of its members has ensured its successful operation in spite of many handicaps, among others, the lack of finances. The preliminary training of fliers, under the direction of flying clubs like the one operated in the outskirts of Hawkesbury, is directly associated with the broad pattern of national defence. The theoretical and practical knowledge of flying acquired by these groups constitutes an important preliminary step in any national air training plan. Bearing in mind the overall cost of training each flier, the national budget is relieved of a portion of the financial burden which the complete air training course entails.
I should like to stress another factor that ties in closely with the national defence program. I have in mind the decentralization of industry. Economic and strategic reasons make such a decentralization increasingly imperative. Decentralization relieves transport congestion in heavily populated areas and facilitates the quick movement of traffic, in times both of peace and of war. New methods of warfare centred around the use of the atomic bomb and its more lethal companion, the hydrogen bomb, are undoubtedly the most compelling reasons for the decentralization of industry. Prescott county,
(Mr. Bruneau.]

situated as it is midway between Ottawa and Montreal, -can ideally meet the needs of decentralization. There is ample power for the operation of almost any type of industry, and the county is well endowed with rail and highway transportation facilities. The full development of Canada's agricultural possibilities is another paramount consideration. This constituency is most fortunate in that there is a fairly happy balance between its agriculture and its industry. We are all well aware of the outstanding part that Canada's agriculture played in the successful prosecution of two world wars.
On the basis of its farming population Prescott county ranks as the largest cheese-producing area in the British commonwealth with a yearly output of over 5,872,198 pounds of cheese from the 43 cheese factories in operation, which represents a value of no less than $2,024,521. My constituency relies upon the manufacture of this commodity for an income which is a very important factor in its economy and to that end I strongly urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to do his utmost to see that the support price is maintained at a level of not less than 30 cents to 32 cents for cheddar cheese. I hope that this spring we will not see a recurrence of a drop in the price of cheese with which the farming element in my constituency had to cope last spring. In the same way our agricultural class is at present also concerned over the prices of beef and pork.
Some amendments to the National Housing Act are to come before this house. Canadians throughout the country are in dire need of living accommodation at low cost as those with small incomes are unable to pay high rents for inadequate quarters. With our present world in turmoil and unrest one of the greatest stabilizing factors we could have would be homes owned by Canadian citizens and not have our people living in rented abodes where they are nothing but tourists under a two-year lease, where they live in tenements from which they can be evicted on the expiration of their contract.
We have just gone through a second world war after which many young couples have attempted to settle under circumstances of prosperity. Many of our young men are fortunate enough to be drawing large salaries and have decided to purchase homes, but after a while they may find this investment to be beyond their means. The strength of a nation depends a good deal upon the security of its inhabitants. Home owners are a great asset to any government because they enjoy a form of security for the preservation of

which they are willing to undergo great sacrifice. Furthermore, a national housing policy would be beneficial, not only to individuals but to the nation at large, because it would be one of the best weapons with which to combat communism.
We all want to see new homes sprouting throughout Canada and I hope methods will be devised by which prospective owners will find themselves in a position where they can build new homes. But we shall have to make sure that the initial payment, which becomes a condition of ownership, is not too high for the average income earner.
Canada is going ahead with the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. This project will considerably improve water communication between the head waters of the great lakes and the ocean, thus giving a tremendous impetus to shipping and improving industry and agriculture in both eastern and western Canada. Moreover, I believe it will prove in the not distant future to be of immense advantage from a military and strategic point of view.
I have the honour to represent in this house people of different nationalities and religious denominations who live together in harmony and bonne entente. There is never any friction or conflict between the different segments of our population. On the contrary, there exist the most cordial and sympathetic relations. We understand each other and in our courteous relations with each other we never stop to consider that one is Irish, Scotch, English or French. We think of ourselves only as Canadians having the same interests, the same aspirations and the same love for our country.
How much closer these ties and bonds of harmony and unity would be if we all lived under the same symbol, a truly Canadian flag to which we could look, a flag behind which we could all rally, could revere and love, a flag for which we could fight and die. Our country now ranks among the great nations of the world and I believe sincerely that we legislators owe it to our people to give them a true symbol of Canadianism. It is true that our boys are fighting and dying in Korea but they are doing so under the flag of the United Nations for the sake of humanity. This is idealistic enough, but would they not feel that they were fighting for a cause much dearer to them if they could only see their own Canadian flag streaming beside that of the United Nations. I hope sincerely that before not too long a measure will be brought into the house to give our people a Canadian flag which they can consider their own and love as their own.
As I have mentioned previously, Canada is now considered among the great nations
The Address-Mr. Nowlan of the world and I think it would be most beneficial if we had our representatives in the city of the seven hills, where most countries today have their ambassadors who are able to exchange views and bring back to their own governments information necessary in the management of their own affairs in regard to international relations.
With the presentation of the report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, we should now strive toward giving our young people a real opportunity to prove their ability and put their talents to good use. At the present time many of these people find it impossible to do this because of a lack of money. I suggest that there should be some form of youth department which certainly would not overlap provincial departments but which would rather constitute a vocational guidance school for our young people and which would, on a national scale, guide them in the liberal arts and sciences, in different fields of knowledge and agriculture and enable us to develop right here at home better trained citizens and not have to import skilled or specialized labour from abroad. This division, administered by a federal commission, would enable young men to attend schools, universities, industrial or experimental stations of their own choosing located in their own regions, where they could take their training in the language most familiar to them and in an environment most suitable to the development of their own talents.
In conclusion, sir, I will say that it is quite comforting for us legislators in this House of Commons to be able to stand up and debate, as free men, upon a legislative program prepared with a view to achieving security, prosperity and well-being for the people by whom we were entrusted with a mandate and, in this way, co-operate also towards bringing freedom and liberty of expression to other people living in countries where democracy no longer exists.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming into the debate after the weeks which have elapsed, it is perhaps more or less formal to commend the mover and seconder for the work which they did on that occasion. But any one of us who has had the responsibility or privilege of moving or seconding an address, in this chamber or in other chambers, realizes the responsibility and difficult nature of the task which confronts a new member on such an occasion. We certainly can congratulate both those gentlemen on the excellence of their efforts.
I do not, of course, propose to follow the remarks of the hon. member for Prescott
664	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nowlan (Mr. Bruneau) who has immediately preceded me, but there is one subject on which he touched indirectly that I will refer to in a few moments.
Before going on, I should like to congratulate, as have so many members, the two new ministers who have been sitting on the government benches since we last met. Whatever we may think of the political policies which they enunciate, we appreciate their personal qualities. We recognize the tribute which has been paid to them by their appointment and we wish them success personally, sir. We know that, with those peculiar qualities they possess, should they survive the next election they will undoubtedly adorn the benches of the opposition and develop still further there.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This is perhaps a unique occasion today as there is recorded in Hansard the proclamation read by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this morning- an historic document in which we find the new title of Her Majesty set forth as a preliminary to the coronation. I am sure his speech this day, and the records attached thereto, will be of historic significance for years to come-marking the evolution which takes place in this house and in this commonwealth as time goes on. It has been said by many others but I say, simply in passing, that we are all happy and all thrilled at the prospect of the coronation which will shortly take place. Those of us who are privileged to sit in this house are pleased that we should be here in the year immediately preceding the coronation.
The other night the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) gave a speech here which I thought was of some special significance. It was of particular significance to me, sir, because some of the matters on which I intended to speak at some length are adequately covered there; so I will speak but briefly on one or two of the points he mentioned.
One matter with which he dealt was the problem confronting the universities in Canada and university grants

particularly universities in Nova Scotia. Without repeating matters which he gave in some detail, I simply say that on page 635 of Hansard one finds recorded the average amounts of money paid to the various universities in the various provinces of Canada. One finds that the universities of Nova Scotia are at the bottom of the list receiving only $92.45 per student, while the figure ranges up to $483.16. Perhaps the latter is an unusual figure because it applies to the province of Newfoundland


where there are not so many universities, but there is a wide discrepancy in the amounts paid to the various universities within the various provinces. Nor is that all, sir; there is a marked discrepancy in the amounts paid to the different universities within the same province. I think the member for Halifax was right in urging that some special attention should be paid to the problem- not on a per capita basis of 50 cents per head for each province but on the basis of availability of students within each province.
In Nova Scotia we find a peculiar problem because of the fact that we have located in Halifax Dalhousie university with the professional schools-the medical school serving the maritimes and beyond, the pharmacy school, the school of dentistry and, sir, I am sure I will not be accused of undue modesty if I mention the school of law which is undoubtedly a very eminent school of law. Therefore, we have students from Ontario, the western provinces and the other provinces of Canada attending that law school. That influx of students coming to the professional schools at Dalhousie draws upon the per capita grant which is made to the province and, as a result, other universities serving that province draw far less. Those schools serving the humanities, undergraduate work, arts and sciences, receive as little as $50 per student. Those universities are serving a very useful purpose and, without boasting again, one might suggest that they are making a real contribution to Canada. One thing in which we have an advantage is that today instead of our graduates going to the United States to earn their living they are coming up here to Ontario, to Quebec, to Alberta and British Columbia, to develop the natural resources of those provinces. One only has to mention Borden of Brazilian Traction or Godsoe of British American, or Perry of Consolidated Mining and Smelting, to realize something of the contributions which those small universities are making to the development of the wealth of other provinces in Canada.
Without labouring the matter at length, sir, I can say that this is a matter which has caused the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) some concern. It is a matter which I have discussed with him and I do not think he is entirely satisfied with the arrangement that has been made. I do say, sir, that it is not a proper one; it is not a right one; and something should be done about it. The professors labouring in those colleges, teaching there, are performing a real national service but, because of economic circumstances, they are living on salaries which are not commensurate in any shape or form with those

paid in other parts of Canada or with the service which they are rendering. I do urge upon this government that steps be taken to reconsider this matter of university grants, and even a maritime unit might be feasible. After all, Dalhousie serves all of the maritime provinces and that way one would get more equitable distribution than one gets today when you have these watertight divisions or compartments between provinces.
One does not suggest that this government is responsible for education in Canada; but this government has accepted a responsibility towards the universities as recommended in the Massey report. This government did a remarkable job in assisting the universities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: What was the suggested remedy? Was it to take the population for the whole of the maritimes?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I said that would be an improvement. The same situation is true for Acadia, St. Francis Xavier and Mount Allison. They are serving the maritimes although perhaps not to the same extent as the professional schools. I do think it would be a help if the basis of the maritime unit were enlarged. I think we should go further and consider some direct assistance per student, on the same basis as was done during the war when this government did a remarkable job in connection with the rehabilitation of returned men. The government paid so much to each university for each student in attendance. I am not trying to give a concrete solution of the problem, Mr. Speaker. I quite appreciate the question my hon. friend put, but I do say that it is a problem with which we are confronted and a problem which must be solved if the eastern universities are going to function properly.
Another matter to which the hon. member for Halifax referred, and about which I
The Address-Mr. Nowlan intended to speak at some length, is the matter of the use of the ports in the maritime provinces, particularly Halifax. I shall not say much about it now. The other day I noticed in the newspaper that the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), the minister from Nova Scotia, spoke in Halifax-I have forgotten whether it was before a board of trade or some other organization-and dealt with the problem to some extent. On Friday night the member for Halifax put on the record some most alarming figures, showing that there had been a substantial decrease in the export of Canadian products through eastern Canadian ports, and a tremendous increase in the export of those products from United States ports. I shall not bother to put those figures on Hansard again, and I shall not weary the house by repeating them. Hon. members will find those figures in that speech, and they do indicate a trend. Unfortunately, a change has taken place during the last three years.
When the minister was speaking the other night, I believe he asked what one could do about it. I would suggest that there are two things which should be done. In the first place, we have in Canada these industrial fairs and exhibitions of various kinds which have been held in Toronto. We know that merchants, manufacturers and businessmen, not only from this country but all the countries of the world, come to these industrial exhibitions. I am informed by those who are close to the situation-I have not personal knowledge of these matters-that at all of these industrial fairs one finds public relations officers from the port authority of New York, the port of Boston, of Baltimore and all the eastern United States cities. Apparently these men occupy mammoth suites and have unlimited expense accounts. I am not suggesting for a moment that the mere fact the gentlemen are there with large suites and expense accounts necessarily influences the business to any extent; nevertheless the fact remains that these ports apparently find it a good investment to do that. I wonder how many public relations officers, how many representatives of our ports, are present at industrial fairs or exhibitions of that kind. I am told that there are none, although of course there are official representatives of the Department of Transport and of the port authorities.
However, there needs to be a more aggressive selling campaign put on, and to some extent much could be accomplished by seeing that our ports were properly represented at all fairs and meetings of businessmen. In a return tabled the other day I noticed that our army in western Europe, which I understand is substantially a brigade, has four
666	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nowlan public relations officers attached to it. If we have four public relations officers for that, then I suggest we should have at least one public relations officer doing a task for Canadian ports, and particularly the eastern Canadian ports.
Again, the member for Halifax said that there were many industries which were benefiting by national policy. He singled out the automobile industry and said that since they were benefiting from national policy it should be the duty of the government-at least this is the implication but it is not exactly what he said although I believe it is a fair inference from what he said-to see that those who benefit from national policy carry out their responsibilities toward the nation. Accordingly, the automobile industry should use Canadian ports for the shipment of products which they manufacture pursuant to that policy. I believe there is an argument in that connection.
In any event, sir, today business and government are so closely associated through matters of taxation, priorities, allocations and in dozens of other ways directly and indirectly, that it would be an easy thing for the government to at least urge, to advise and to encourage the export of Canadian goods through these Canadian ports. It is certainly a necessary thing, because they are a national need. They perform a national function in time of war. This nation cannot exist without them. There seems to be something radically wrong when we hear the boasting about the increase of our gross national product, and yet we find that the share of it which is going through these Canadian ports is getting less and less instead of more and more.
I recall once attending a film sponsored by the minister of finance. I am sure he regretted it because he came from Nova Scotia. I happened to be in the theatre one night when a new bond sale was being inaugurated under his auspices. Some firm had been retained to prepare the film and they showed Canada as stretching from the Pacific to the St. Lawrence, where it stopped. I am sure it was rather embarrassing to the minister. The other night I saw another powerful film prepared for "The March of Time". I saw a preview of it, and it was encouraging to Canadians. The only reference to Canadian ports and the only scene of them showed a group of immigrants going through the sheds at Halifax. It was stated that they were on their way to the possibilities which awaited them in Canada. This attitude is not too well appreciated in the east. I think the time is coming when something should be done about it.


Speaking about transportation, Mr. Speaker, I simply want to deal with a local matter. I want to say again what I have said in this house on other occasions, and that is that one of the transportation problems in the east which I think needs attention is the bringing into Nova Scotia of the Canadian Pacific Railway from Saint John to Digby and then up the valley to Halifax. In days gone by the principle underlying national policy dictated that our access to central Canadian markets should be by a long, tortuous route going up around the baie de Chaleur, up the Matapedia valley, and finally down the St. Lawrence. At that time policy dictated that we should be kept as far as possible away from the United States border, because it was assumed that at some time the United States would invade the provinces of Upper Canada and the Nova Scotians would have to come up here to protect them.
Now, policy dictates that we should be closely associated with the United States. We have markets there and we need accessibility to those markets. We, however, have to follow this long, tortuous route or else we have to ship l.c.l. across the bay of Fundy and then reload afterwards. Some construction work seems necessary both at Saint John and at Digby, and I hope that at some time in the not too distant future this matter can be rectified.	,
I am reminded of what the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bruneau) said a few moments ago about a national flag. I am not going to venture to discuss that matter at the moment. However, since the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is here, and since I believe this house and this building comes under the jurisdiction of his department, I want to refer to a matter which I think is of great importance. About the middle of last July, sir, I happened to come back to Ottawa. I came up to these parliament buildings here, the centre and capital of Canada. I found the place swarming, to use a slang expression, with tourists, both from the United States and Canada; there were thousands of them. I found that we had R.C.M.P. constables, wearing their red coats, patrolling up and down in front of this building. I even found an R.C.M.P. constable wearing a red coat and mounted on horseback patrolling in front of the building in order to give us a little national flavour. Then I found this graceful tower out here adorned with a flagpole reaching up to the heavens like a gnarled finger, without anything on it.
I think it is a disgrace to this country that in this capital of Canada, when tourists

come here-whether they are Americans, Canadians or whoever they are-to these parliament buildings the only flag they find visible from the parliament building is the flag of Norway flying over the Norwegian consulate down here on Sparks street. I realize the difficulty with respect to a national flag. I appreciate the fact that it should be settled and determined. I know there are difficulties which may delay that outcome. But, Mr. Speaker, what I say is this. A flag which is good enough to fly over this building now to advise the people of Ottawa-or alarm them-that their members happen to be sitting here, which flies here every day we sit, which flies at half-mast when any member of this house or of the other place dies, and which flies over our embassies abroad, is a flag that is good enough to be flying over this building every day of the year. In order to develop a national sentiment it would be much better to have a national flag upon which everyone can agree. But I suggest to the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bruneau) or to any other hon. member that certainly anything is better than this barren flagpole which sticks up here like a sore thumb every day during the time the house is not in session.
A moment ago I mentioned the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), but I notice that he has left the chamber. There were some things I wanted to say about his department. I am not going to speak at any great length now because, from the order paper and from references in the press to what is going on in another place, I learn that before too long we shall have legislation here dealing with the fisheries problems of Canada, and perhaps particularly those of the eastern seaboard. I think it is desirable, Mr. Speaker, that the new minister give special attention to those problems. His predecessor worked hard and undoubtedly made a contribution to the department which he administered. The new minister, with imagination and with drive, can perhaps accomplish even more.
One of those problems with which we shall be confronted before this house rises
is,	I believe, that concerning coastal waters. I believe that matter is now being debated elsewhere. I have heard there is an interdepartmental committee already appointed and dealing with that matter at the moment. I hope that committee deals with it seriously. I hope that the chairman stays here in Ottawa and gives some time to looking after
it.	I think Canada should take the lead in dealing with this matter of coastal waters. The whole conception of it is changing, as we know. European countries have altered their concept with respect to it. With its
The Address-Mr. Nowlan thousands and tens of thousands of miles of coast line, headlands, harbours and bays, I think Canada more than almost any other country in the world should be paying special attention to that problem; and when the time comes we shall discuss that matter at length. I want to impress upon the minister now, or when he reads Hansard, at any rate, that so far as the bay of Fundy is concerned there is a real problem which is interesting historically and which is open to solution today. If he goes back in history I think he will find that in the Rush-Bagot conversations of many years ago, or in the convention, the British who were then in charge of Canadian negotiations emphasized the fact that the bay of Fundy was a coastal water. The Americans said it was not a coastal water but that it was part of the high seas. No agreement was reached; they agreed to disagree, and the matter was left open. Now that this whole matter is to be reviewed, I think something concrete should be done in the near future.
Referring to the Minister of Fisheries, I should like to digress for a moment or two. I was intrigued by a statement he made here on Friday afternoon. The minister is always a most ebullient speaker, one who likes to rush in and charge at windmills and make political speeches which are sometimes scintillating and witty but perhaps not entirely authentic. I think he gave a brilliant example of that on Friday afternoon because, in referring to the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), my deskmate, or in replying to him, as reported at page 616 of Hansard, you will find that he was deploring the Tory trade principles of the Bennett depression days and said: "Look what we, the Liberals, have done with our magnificent trade policies as compared with those repressive, unfortunate and stupid Tory policies of Bennett."
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "hear, hear". Let him wait until I finish and see whether he says "hear, hear" then. He took the figures, as they are set out here; you will find them at page 616 of Hansard. He said that under the beneficent and brilliant leadership given by this government, the trade of Canada which under the policies of Tory Bennett was only $1 [DOT] 9 billion had now reached $8 billion, a little bit more than a 400 per cent increase. I was rather intrigued with these figures. I was impressed because it was one of the first things I had seen which had impressed me with the policy of this government, and I thought perhaps one should check on the figures a little bit. So I obtained the figures for the United States,
668	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nowlan and wondered what a dismal failure they had made and how they would compare with the scintillating leadership which had been given to Canada by this Liberal government. I found that in the same period trade had gone from $3-7 billion to $25-99 billion or in other words had increased seven times as compared with the increase in Canada. Whether that is a coincidence I do not know. I say I am not entirely impressed with the logic of the minister's argument; nevertheless that was his argument. If it was logical and sound, then I think this comparison should be put into effect, and one might deplore the fact that we did not have the Democrats or the Tories of Bennett or somebody else rather than these Liberals whose policies did not give us so much. I would also point out to the minister what happened to the government which increased the trade of its country by seven times while his government was increasing trade in this country by only four times. Three or four weeks ago the people, having become tired of it, kicked it out. That was not an entirely happy illustration for the minister to use.
Then he also rang the changes on the Tory gloomsters. I do not think I am divulging any secret when I say that the Tories are not the gloomy ones, but that there are others around here who are much gloomier than they are. If he wants to know who the gloomsters are in Canada, I can tell him who they are, or at least some of them; I could not take time to tell of them all because my time would run out. They are the fruit growers of British Columbia and of Nova Scotia, the fishermen and the lumbermen who have lost the British markets. They are some of the gloomsters. Then there are the cheese manufacturers who are prohibited from selling their cheese in the United States; and the tobacco growers who find that because of the crazy taxation policies of this government their industry is threatened with extinction. Then there is agriculture in general, because according to figures shown the other day in the columns of Chester Bloom, which were taken from the bureau of statistics, the various costs of agricultural production have increased at an alarming rate whereas the prices received by agriculture have decreased in a corresponding way.
One could go on and enumerate others in this country who are gloomsters. I would suggest that they have some cause for gloom. I do not think they are going to be particularly encouraged by the rather derisive laughter with which the Minister of Fisheries dealt with them. I would also remind the


Minister of Fisheries that there was a gentleman by the name of Stevenson who in embarking upon a campaign not long ago said he was not going to run his election campaign against Herbert Hoover; but before he got through he found he was running against Herbert Hoover. We know what happened. I suggest that when my hon. friends opposite start campaigning against R. B. Bennett in the days of the depression, and when they try to resurrect other speeches which men made in the past, then the political poverty of that party is certainly greater than we realize and its desperation is even greater than we had anticipated.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that this making of speeches seems to be a disease of the junior ministers from British Columbia. We have noticed in the press reports of speeches by ministers from that province. I am not sure what is the exact status of one of the ministers from British Columbia. He is something like Lucifer, suspended halfway between heaven and hell. Although he is still Solicitor General, he is taking over the Department of National Defence, or part of it, when the necessary legislation goes through. One of the functions of the Solicitor General is to recommend clemency and exercise mercy. That may be one of the reasons that incumbent is being brought into the Department of National Defence. I do want to tell him that the Department of National Defence is more suspect, under greater criticism and more discussed by the people of Canada generally than is any other department of this government, and that is saying quite a great deal. And if this minister expects to restore the confidence of the people of Canada in that department he should avoid going on political junkets and making cheap political speeches, because if there is any record that needs to be changed it is the record of the Department of National Defence.

That will keep him busy,
too.

I am not sure how much time I have left. I want to refer to a matter which came to my attention the other day. I found that a paper published in Toronto, which is generally considered to have some access to information from the government, and which is certainly not hostile to it, stated that tax reductions will come in July so the taxpayers in Canada will get the benefit of them before the election in October. The article states that this information is derived from an informed source, whatever that may be. It is one of the anonymous informed sources we hear of around here. I notice that it is datelined Ottawa, December 8.

I was rather intrigued by this suggestion of tax reductions, which have been asked for so often by the opposition, and I wondered if by any chance they would be brought in again on the eve of the election. I checked back to some other tax reductions and some records to see what took place during the last few elections. I find, for instance, that prior to the 1945 election the excise tax of 25 per cent on refrigerators was repealed by order in council 28 days before the election. It was reimposed afterward, and it was substantially reduced again before the 1949 election. I found that the tax of 25 per cent on electrical appliances was reduced by order in council 28 days before the election. After the 1945 election was won the tax went back on, and then it was reduced again before the 1949 election and reimposed at 15 per cent in the budget of 1951. One could go on. There was a tax on stoves, cameras and soft drinks. The 25 per cent was repealed in the 1949 budget and reimposed at 30 per cent in September, 1950. On candy and confectionery the 30 per cent tax was repealed in the 1949 budget and reimposed in 1950. The radio tax of 25 per cent was reduced to 10 per cent by order in council just before the 1945 election, and reimposed by radio again. Thus began radio ukase in Canada by the Liberal government in 1947. It was reduced to 10 per cent just before the 1949 election, and was increased again in the following budget after the 1949 election. One could go on, Mr. Speaker, giving example after example of those tax reductions; and the pattern has emerged of reducing before the 1945 election, increasing after the 1945 election, reducing before the 1949 election and increasing after the 1949 election, reducing now before the 1953 election and if this government by any misfortune happens to come back to power undoubtedly increasing again in the following budget.
We have heard a great deal of cyclical budgeting. That was the way it was described at one time, but we all know the term the press gallery coined for it and which is much more descriptive, namely cynical budgeting. And if we get a tax reduction on the eve of this election it would be the most barefaced, the most glaring example of cynical budgeting this country has ever known,
Beware the Greeks bearing gifts.

This morning the Prime Minister gave us a brief resume or review of what happened recently in London. I know of no matter of a positive nature which is of more importance to Canadians generally than is the problem of sterling and of accessibility to the British markets. Certainly, sir, there is no problem of such paramount
The Address-Mr. Mcllraith importance in eastern Canada; and when we have had a further report on it and have received greater details, we shall then discuss that matter on the budget or on some other occasion. We do hope and trust that as a result of the varied belated efforts which this government has put into the matter of dealing with the problem of sterling at the conference of commonwealth ministers some concrete good will emerge for the primary producers who are dependent upon that market.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is usual in taking part in these debates to say a word of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am very happy to do that, and since I am frequently accused of or being told that I am quite an ardent Liberal, I am particularly happy to do it because of the fact that these two hon. members confirm the belief I have always had in this House of Commons as the effective method of governing not only in this country but in the world today. I am a profound believer in the Canadian system of government and in the part the House of Commons plays in it. During my experience as a member of this house for some twelve years and the opportunities that are provided for contact with members of other government bodies in other countries I am only strengthened in my view on that subject. The whole history of each of these hon. members about whom I am speaking confirms me in that belief.
I should like to say a word about the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and particularly about one point he raised. He spoke about the difficulties certain of our universities in the area with which he is naturally most closely concerned have in financing their efforts. That undoubtedly is a very real problem, and I am glad to hear him raise it in this debate and say a word about it. It is an embarrassing and difficult problem, because the history of this country makes it impossible and undesirable for the federal government to interfere in the field of education. Yet while we recognize that fact, there is also no doubt that the universities and some of the other educational institutions are having some difficulty in carrying on their efforts, and need some further help.
I was glad to hear his acknowledgment of the good work done in the post-war period with veterans in the field of education, and to hear his reference to the federal grants to universities. There is one other phase of the subject he might have touched on that
670	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Mcllraith has been a very real help to some of the universities, namely national research council grants and scholarships. They are a very positive help to the science faculties, at least.
I am sorry the senior hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) is not in his seat. I propose to say something about his remarks of Friday last. Those remarks I found most upsetting and disturbing, and I am quite sure most hon. members feel that way about them. The hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) is naturally very proud of his constituency and his province, and I think quite justifiably. I have nothing but commendation for him for that. I have no doubt the constituency is a very fine one. Each of us, of course, thinks his constituency is the finest and his province the best. The province from which the hon. member comes is indeed a fine province, one that has come to be known not by its name but rather as "The Island". We know the affection with which other Canadians use that term when they are referring to Prince Edward Island.
However, the hon. member did say some things that I think must not be permitted to go unanswered. He was dealing with some unfortunate or bad publicity the province had received through an article appearing in a Canadian publication. In dealing with the article the hon. member made reference to a photographer from the constituency I have the honour to represent. In dealing with that photographer he quoted from a newspaper, the Summerside Journal and The Pioneer. Referring to this portrait photographer the newspaper article, in its first sentence, contains these words:
This big-feeling foreigner, now Canadian, who visited Charlottetown this summer on his tour for Maclean's magazine-
And so on. Apparently the hon. member quoted that with approval; and in his own comments, as they are reported at page 600 of Hansard, he said:
If Maclean's magazine wanted to get some information about Prince Edward Island, why did they not get in touch with some of the people who have been coming for years to Prince Edward Island, rather than go to a foreigner-who is now a doubtful Canadian-looking for a report they might publish later as, in this instance, they have done.
Well, it is the implication in those remarks with which I wish to concern myself, the reference to a fellow Canadian of long standing as a foreigner and, not only that, the implication that a foreigner is in some way a person to be held in less esteem, or despised. This fellow Canadian about whom the hon. member was speaking is a man who came to this country as a boy, about 1924, from a


country in which there were great political upsets and disturbances. I suppose had he come in more modern times the term "refugee" would have been used. He was then 16 years of age, and settled in the Sherbrooke area of the province of Quebec. In 1933, one of the years when things in this country were not very good from a business standpoint- and at a time when the then leader of the party to which the hon. member for Queens belongs was prime minister of this country- this young man, who had become a naturalized Canadian as soon as the necessary time elapsed after his entry into this country, started to carry on business here in Ottawa.
At first he was working for another man. In a very few months, when the older man went out of business, the person in question continued the business himself. He built up that business, and has become not only a portrait photographer of great reputation in the constituency I have the honour to represent, but a portrait photographer of great reputation throughout the whole of this country, of great reputation throughout the United States, the United Kingdom and indeed the whole world. Probably he is the best portrait photographer in the world; certainly he is one of the greatest.
I make nothing of the point as to his degree of greatness, but certainly it can be said that he is a very great portrait photographer. I do not know if other hon. members have shared my experience when visiting other countries, of being asked if I know this Canadian photographer, who took certain very famous pictures of persons known throughout the world. While this great Canadian photographer may be a small man physically, he is a man of very real stature, and I am sure the attack made against him and the references to him will not concern him personally to any great extent. Figuratively speaking his shoulders are very broad and he can bear attacks of this kind, and many more like them, without any damage whatever. But the implications of the attack are of real consequence, because this country is built up of persons coming from many different lands. Our racial origins are diversified. Some 48 per cent, by racial origin, came from the British Isles. The next largest racial group are of French origin, and the remaining racial groups come from some thirty or forty other countries, in varying percentages.
Great numbers of our population came here, by choice, as immigrants. In most cases they came because they felt there was a good opportunity here to develop their human personalities, earn their living, and provide opportunity for their children. Having come here they brought with them from their

homelands skills and cultural attributes. Those skills and cultural attributes have done much to develop this country. They have been a great factor in our present development. Not only are we fortunate in Canada in having been blessed with great natural resources, but also by the fact that our population comes from a diversity of origins, each contributing its own cultural background and acquired skills. These have been blended to make our Canadian nationality something of which each one of us can justly be proud.
This portrait photographer from Ottawa, this "foreigner", this "doubtful Canadian"- and I use the language of the hon. member for Queens-was chosen to be the representative of Ontario at a very impressive ceremony in this country when the new citizenship act came into force early in 1947. A most impressive ceremony was held in the Supreme Court of Canada on that occasion, when the Chief Justice of Canada presented citizenship certificates to representative Canadians. The man chosen from Ontario on that occasion was this portrait photographer who carries on business in the constituency of Ottawa West.
Surely if we are to continue to develop this country, we must continue to have immigration into it. That immigration must include people who come here feeling they can become full Canadians, if they meet the requirements, after the necessary lapse of time. They must never be made to feel that they will be second-class Canadians, third-class Canadians or fourth-class Canadians. They must have the right to feel that they and their children, provided they have met the conditions and have acted properly, are full Canadians the same as any others. The term "national unity" must in fact be something real, not just a phrase used in speeches. I do not want to say anything more personally about Mr. Yousuf Karsh, but I do want to say something in protest on behalf of those millions of Canadians who are in the same position, who have come here of choice, who have become full citizens and who want to carry on as full citizens, who want their children to carry on as full citizens.
Does not the hon. member agree that he is making a mountain out of a molehill?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, sir. I am glad that question has been raised. I consider that this goes to the very root of our national unity. Not only that, it involves a deep-rooted principle. When I started to practise my profession in Ottawa about the same time as this man was starting up in a little shop, I took a great interest in politics. I worked in some of the branches of the national young Liberal
The Address-Mr. Mcllraith organizations. There was one thing that impressed me, not so quickly at first but gradually, and that was this question of national unity. Our former prime minister used that phrase a great deal and was ridiculed for doing so. In that work I found that when we were considering current matters we were always coming up against the consideration of that principle. You began to realize that it applied not only geographically to this strip of country along-
I would consider this to be a matter between the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) and Mr. Karsh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: This matter was raised by an hon. member in this house, and judging by the calls I have had about it I consider it to be a most important matter of principle. If I may just finish my remarks, we had to consider national unity, not only from its broad aspect geographically and from the other variations by reason of great distances, but also as it affected persons because of different racial and language backgrounds. In the last number of years when I have dealt with representatives of governments of other countries, an opportunity for which I am most grateful, I have noticed that the one thing that seems to bear in on their minds is the fact that this country is one where there is more practical application of this idea of national unity and more hope for our people because of it than in any other country.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he consider that Mr. Karsh made a truthful statement in his reference to the food served in Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I consider that the hon. member for Queens was quite right in raising the question as to the food served in the hotel. There is no question that the hon. member was quite right in raising that matter and defending it to the limit. But that does not permit him to attack and cast aspersions upon a fellow Canadian citizen on the ground that he came originally from another country.
If the hon. member made such a statement in Armenia he would be kicked out of the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce

You should know.

speechtext: Yes, I did. Not only that, I am on record as speaking at a meeting not many blocks from this chamber during the election campaign. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce

That may be, but I just wanted to point out the technique that has been used. As I said, we talked about national unity and so on. So that I cannot be accused of drumming up something and making it into a question of principle I should like to go back to the record. You know, we Liberals are not ashamed to go back and read from the previous speeches of our leaders. We are not afraid to have them quoted. The hon. member for Eglinton is justifiably upset.
Just let me read to you thte remarks made by the former prime minister of Canada when he was retiring as leader of this party at the great Liberal convention held in August, 1948. There was a phonographic recording made of his words and I would commend it to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and to any other of his colleagues if they are interested. I will just put on record two or three sentences. Here is what he said:
It is a basic principle of Liberalism that all its policies should make for the maintenance and strengthening of national unity. If a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand. We should strive for that which will help to give to all our people a united faith in the future of this

great country. Our policies should be framed to serve the general interest and not the interests of any one section, class or group. Our outlook should not be local, or provincial. It should be a national outlook.
Our country is a federal state, occupying half a continent. We must seek our unity in diversity, not in unformity. Canada was created from diverse elements, each with proud and noble traditions and customs. It is composed of several provinces, each with its own history, and each with constitutional responsibilities which must be respected and safeguarded. Every one of us, if we are to be true Liberals, will endeavour to understand the background, the feelings and the outlook of other Canadians.
I notice that he waited until he retired to say that.

One cannot read that book and not be impressed by the recognition by the first Canadian prime minister of the problem of national unity, and the struggles to recognize the diverse backgrounds of the different parts of what became Canada. You cannot help but be impressed by his appreciation of his problem. I can only regret that his followers today have not the good judgment to read and study some of his views on that matter and apply them to themselves and to their policies. I make no apology whatever for making reference to that fact.

That is only your
judgment.

Perhaps it is not a good thing to isolate particular products like that; perhaps we would do better to take food purchases. Food purchases were 7i per cent higher in value and 7 per cent higher in volume in the first nine months of 1952 than in the first nine months of 1951. In another speech delivered by the Leader of the Opposition just last week end, which is reported in the Globe and Mail of Monday, December 8, he talks about the trading policy of this Liberal government. He went on to say that he would not be content to sit back in palsied impotence-that is the phrase he used. He referred to the government's trade policy as palsied impotence. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what is there to indicate palsied impotence in a policy that has resulted in our trade increasing to something over $8 billion last year? It will be slightly higher this year. The whole trade policy of the government has been anything but palsied impotence as indicated by the Leader of the Opposition. The whole policy has been to continue to expand and increase trade on a multilateral basis. The fact has been stated and restated here to the point where I am sure it must have aggravated many listeners.
This policy has been exemplified by these facts in the administration of the Department of Trade and Commerce. During the war years we had to close some 12 foreign trade offices. Since the war we have reopened 10 of those and in addition opened another 17 foreign trade offices. We have set up a commodities branch. We have set up an agriculture and fisheries branch. The United Kingdom and Canada have a continuing committee on trade and economic affairs which sits at irregular intervals during each year. The policy has been one of continuous and aggressive effort to seek to increase trade.
During a bit of crossfire the other night reference was made by one of the members of the opposition groups-I am sorry I have not the precise reference-to the period 1935-39. I just want to remind hon. members that with a very short bit of work I have been able to turn up some eleven or twelve trade treaties executed by this same Liberal party during those years. I ask hon. members if that is a policy of palsied impotence. I suggest that the palsied impotence is in the inability of the


opposition to develop its policy with respect to trade and expound it.

It will be noticed that the trade with Latin America is tremendously increased.
