In my opinion that is a substantial indication of the Liberal policy, and is a thoroughly good one.
I had intended to make some reference to industrial raw materials in relation to trade, but I fear my time is extremely short. I shall try to condense those remarks greatly. I just want to remind hon. members who are discussing this question of export of industrial raw materials of one or two basic facts. They are that last year our industry required to import something of the order of three times as much industrial raw materials as Canada exported. This is a hard fact. Now we are becoming less dependent on industrial raw material imports. I cannot perhaps elaborate, in the time I have at my disposal, on the development of Canadian industry in processing Canadian raw materials; but it is interesting that of industrial materials the main exports are pulpwood, nickel, asbestos, zinc, iron ore and copper. Our imports are crude petroleum, coal, raw cotton, crude rubber, raw wool, iron ore and vegetable fibres. In addition to that, we must import all the bauxite for the aluminum industry, all the cryolite for the aluminum industry and of course sulphur for the newsprint industry whose product is of tremendous export value.
On this question of iron ore, the situation today is that Canada must import more iron ore than she exports. We import iron ore to the extent of about $23 million in value, and we export iron ore to the extent of $19 million in value. Hence, when I read speeches by some hon. members and others decrying the fact that we export iron ore, I would just remind them that our steel mills could not carry on if we did not import more iron ore than we are at present exporting. There is a

reason for that, having to do with the quality of the ore and so on, and the need for mixing different ores.
The exports of industrial raw materials in 1939 were some $56 million and our imports in that year of industrial raw materials were $142 million. In 1951 the exports of industrial raw materials were $251-6 million and the imports were $724-1 million. In 1952, for the first eight months-those are the latest figures I was able to obtain-the exports of industrial raw materials were $184-2 million and the imports were $376-8 million.
The exports of foodstuffs-on the export of which our country is dependent to a great extent-in 1951 were some $905 million. I ask hon. members to consider well just what would happen to our exports of food materials if we stopped the export of industrial raw materials.

That gives total exports for 1951 of $3,914-5 million. In Canada today we are on the very threshold of our greatest national development. We who are assembled here are well aware of the great developments that have taken place during the past two decades. We are aware of the vast industrial progress that has been made, of the great improvements in our standard of living, and of the new spirit of Canadianism and Canadian unity that is creating here a country of unequalled opportunity.
We must also be aware, as we listen to the addresses by hon. members from the other side of the house, that we in Canada must always guard against those divisive influences, those sectional and regional appeals which in other countries have led only to confusion and despair. It believes in preserving all the rights and privileges of those in opposition so they may serve, and they are intended to serve, as constant, alert and vigilant critics of government measures.
All this is designed for the protection of the public. It is the very basis of our political system, but it should not degenerate into criticism for criticism's sake, nor should it become a long series of attacks and innuendoes bringing into disrepute the honourable actions of those who are responsible for administering the nation.

Certainly. We hear constantly from the members of the opposite side of the house what seems to be their theme song, "It is time for a change". Time


for a change, when our money is at a premium on the United States money market; time for a change, when we have almost full employment in Canada; time for a change, when our industries are busier and our payrolls higher than ever before in the history of Canada; time for a change, when the take-home pay of the average Canadian worker is higher than it has ever been; time for a change, when each and every Canadian citizen has more things than he ever had before, such as an automobile, an electric refrigerator, an electric stove, a radio, a home, and many other things he never owned before; time for a change, when every class and group of citizen is enjoying new prosperity; time for a change, when Canada holds the respect of most of the other countries of the world and when millions of people are clamoring to come here to make their homes; time for a change when Canada is at the threshold of its greatest era of prosperity, guided and helped by the able leader of this government and his ministers.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on the record what two leaders of finance in Canada had to say about the affairs of this country. I will not read the whole advertisement of the Dominion Bank but only the part that applies to my subject. Mr. Robert Rae, president of that bank, in an advertisement published in a Montreal newspaper on Thursday, December 11, 1952, had this to say:
Canada's population may be 30 million by 1975. Future depends on investment of savings, says Dominion Bank president.
Canada's national income has again achieved a new peak. The physical volume of production has also broken all records. The 1952 crop of wheat and coarse grains has surpassed that of any previous year. Export trade has been greater than ever before, both in dollar value and in physical volume. Capital investment in new plant and equipment has established a new record. Retail sales have been buoyant. The cost of living is much the same as it was a year ago. This means that the Canadian people are now living more comfortably than ever before.
The current rate of population growth is striking evidence of the faith which native-born Canadians and new Canadians coming from abroad have in this country's future. During the past twelve months the number of persons in Canada increased by no less than three per cent-a high rate of growth. If this rate of population increase is maintained Canada will have nearly 30 million people by 1975

twice as many as at present.
During the past four years, while Canadians were saving 8J cents out of every dollar of personal income, the people of Britain-faced with unprecedented need for the rebuilding and modernization of plant, equipment and housing-could only save one cent out of each dollar, due to the character and burden of taxation. Practically all of British investment during the post-war period has come from government funds and from corporate savings. In these fields also the rate of savings in the United Kingdom has been somewhat less than in Canada.

We Canadians may learn much from the present plight of Britain. The load of taxes which burdens us is less heavy than the load burdening the British people. The fiscal system here is less harmful toward enterprise than the fiscal system in Britain. Canada is rich in resources. The longterm prospects are bright. Developments now under way will increase greatly the range and volume of materials which the world needs and must have, and which Canada will be able to supply at fair and competitive prices. If risktaking and enterprise are encouraged, if Canadians are given an incentive to save and invest, Canada will continue to move forward to greater achievements.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to place on the record what Mr. Gordon R. Ball, president of the Bank of Montreal, had to say in an advertisement published in an Ottawa paper on Friday, December 12, 1952:
Canada today . . .
Who has
the lion's share?
It is not surprising that Canada should be viewed as a fertile field for the investment of money from abroad and still less surprising that, under existing circumstances, the lion's share of these funds should come from the United States. In the development of the resources of this continent, the international boundary line is becoming of less significance.
In point of fact, however, the relative role played by external capital in Canadian development has not been as large as is popularly supposed. For example, in the three years 1949-51 inclusive, the book value of non-resident investment in Canada increased by about $1,900 million, of which $1,700 million represented an increase in United States investment in this country.
While these figures in themselves appear large, they must be viewed in conjunction with the fact that in the corresponding period something like $12,000 million was spent in Canada for new capital development of all kinds.
In other words, then Canadians themselves provided, in this period, about $84 out of every $100 of new capital expenditures in this country, with foreign investors providing the remaining $16. It is also a fact that at the end of 1951 the proportion of Canadian industry controlled outside of Canada was somewhat smaller than in 1939.
If there are any Canadians who are inclined to view with alarm the extent of foreign participation in Canadian industry, the facts I have just recited should certainly tend to allay their fears.
I believe the citizens of Canada today are enjoying the most wonderful way of life it is possible to enjoy, and I feel sure that very few Canadians would want to go back to the days gone by. We hear complaints from many people, but is it not human for intelligent people to complain? We have not reached a Utopia; nobody ever will. No matter how high the standard of living there will always be those who will wish it were higher. Does the workingman want a full breadbasket with employment at high wages, with taxes at a high level, or does he want to go back to the uncertainty that existed in the days of the depression, when taxes were low and the breadline was long? Does the workingman
The Address-Mr. Bourque earning approximately $75 per week, and paying approximately $10 per week for income tax, want to go back to the days of not so long ago when he earned an average of $25 per week, if lucky enough to be employed, but paid no income tax. Personally I do not think so. He is better off today financially, socially and economically than he ever was before.
Does the workingman, want to go back to the days previous to the last war, when labour had almost reached the starvation point? Do the people want to go back to the days of not so long ago when our foreign trade was almost at a standstill? Do the people want to go back to the days when our farmers and our factories could find no market for their goods at home or abroad? Do the Canadian people want to go back to the days when our Canadian money was at a discount of 20 to 25 per cent on the United States market?
Nowhere else in the world outside of the United States can you find as high a standard of living as we now enjoy in Canada. The Liberal government provides the family allowances-a measure which was greatly derided by many members of the opposition, and christened by them the baby bonus-the old age pensions and pensions for the blind. These are some of the fruits of a taxation policy which is designed to create for Canadians a better and happier way of life. The Liberal government has given to all workers the protection of a sound unemployment insurance program which has eliminated for all time the need of a dole. The Canadian worker does not want charity, and the government recognizes and appreciates his position by providing a protection in which he can participate with dignity and with full respect for his position, as one who contributes to the development of our national wealth.
While each of us in this house represents a different constituency in Canada, a constituency with its own individual problems and its own individual claims for special attention and consideration, we realize that together we represent a great and growing nation. We do not seek uniformity of opinions or ideas, any more than we seek to destroy the individuality of each of our Canadian people. We welcome in Canada a diversity of races; we cherish the contributions to our Canadian civilization made by the English, the French, the Jews, the Italians, the Germans, the Scandinavian people and the people from many other lands who have come here to make their homes in our country. Each of these peoples has a vital contribution to

The Address-Mr. Bourque make to our way of life, and each of them should feel that he is represented in this free and democratic parliament. We want no repetition here of the hatreds which in Europe today are again producing the wave of anti-semitism which once characterized nazi Germany.
In this House of Commons we have a duty to perform to the people of Canada, a duty which goes far beyond the mere passage of bills and resolutions, a duty which involves providing leadership to the rest of Canada. No other deliberations in Canada receive the attention in the press and on the radio that is given to the deliberations in this house. Here, during the session, Canadians look for that inspiration and leadership which will symbolize their own faith in their country. The government of Canada, through the program it has carried out during the past 15 years, under the leadership of the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King and under the present able leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) through the program which was outlined in the speech from the throne, has endeavoured, and I believe has succeeded, in providing that leadership. Legislation has been introduced and enacted in the best interests of the country as a whole. Mistakes, when they have been made-and who is so perfect in this world that he never makes mistakes-have been recognized and rectified. It is entirely different from that type of criticism which sees nothing but evil in everything the government undertakes, which throws suspicion at each and


all of those who are responsible for the administration of the government, or which seeks to divide one section of our population against another. The constituency which I have the honour to represent is also literally a cross-section of Canada. Its population includes many races and several creeds. We have a variety of national backgrounds and a diversity of interests, but we are all united in believing first of all in our own constituency, and secondly in the nation of which we form a part. We would not welcome in Outremont-St. Jean any forces which sought to divide us one against the other, and we do not like that kind of force to be operating in our country. We believe that here in Canada there is room and opportunity for all, and we believe in seeing that all those who live and work among us are given an equal chance.
As a new member of this house I have much to learn, and I appreciate the many kindnesses and attentions which have already been shown to me, not only by the members of my own party but by the members of the parties in opposition. It gives me pleasure to think that I am received here not as an unreasoning partisan but as a loyal Canadian who is eager in this chamber to make some contribution to the welfare of his country. I believe in the government program which, over the past 17 years, has helped to produce such great prosperity in Canada. I believe in the many measures which have contributed so much to the welfare and happiness of all our people. I believe in the spirit which is evident throughout all the national legislation which over the years this government has introduced and implemented by efficient action. And I believe, too, in the right of all those opposed to the government to state their objections, and to have them seriously and thoughtfully considered by the hon. members in this chamber.
It is the privilege and the duty of the opposition to present counter-measures; it is their responsibility to offer at all times an alternative program to that of the government in power. I cannot believe, however, that the good of Canada is well served by criticism, real or implied, based not upon facts but purely upon political considerations. And I am sure my friends on the opposite side of the house will agree that our first obligation is to the people of Canada, and that only those things which add to the stature of parliament and contribute to the welfare of the country should be introduced into our proceedings.
No Canadians have ever had a greater opportunity than we to add to the glory and the prestige of Canada. Let us not throw

away that opportunity, but let us be united in purpose and love of country whatever our personal or political opinions may be. (Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I propose to vote in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). So as to avoid any possible misunderstanding about my position, I wish to give a few words of explanation.
I am not in favour of Social Credit and I am not associated with what is known in Quebec as the "Union des filecteurs".
I am voting in favour of the amendment not so much to show my approval of a principle of Social Credit, but rather because I hope, in doing so, to focus attention on a suggestion I want to put forward.
For the past few days, we have witnessed in this house rather acrimonious debates between members of the Social Credit party and members of other groups. I believe that the quality and tone of those debates will not serve to enhance the prestige of those groups among the public at large.
But that is not the matter I wish to raise. Since I came to this house in 1949, I have been astonished on several occasions to note the indifference with which the Social Credit doctrine has been received in this house, when it has not been ridiculed. For my part, this theory interests me, like any number of others, in so far as I can understand it. It seems to me that it might be interesting to know this theory, especially since its advocates boast of being able to cure the numerous evils which our present financial policies have not always managed to deal with successfully.
I have no intention of being a prophet of doom but, Mr. Speaker, what would happen here, in Canada, if the large international or supranational organizations, which influence our national policy to an ever-increasing degree, suddenly should decide to declare peace? That is bound to happen some day.
Our country, no more than any other, in fact, is quite unable to support, indefinitely, a war economy such as the one we have to cope with these days. Otherwise we should have to neglect that great principle which states that in order to defend itself a country must first of all ensure its own means of livelihood. Should we go on at this rate for too long, our very existence might be threatened whenever the time comes to 68108-44
The Address-Mr. Poulin transform a wartime economy into a peacetime one.
The apostles of the Social Credit faith claim that they are capable of lessening these economic catastrophes, even of preventing them. Would it not be worth-while to give these gentlemen a chance to express their theories freely, here or elsewhere, to serious-minded, unprejudiced people, who would listen to them attentively and intelligently?
There is no getting away from it; either this theory is absurd, unattainable and consequently dangerous; or else it is practical, attainable and consequently deserves consideration.
As regards the first alternative, we would be already far behind, for the harm would now be very much widespread and the old political parties-no disparaging sense being attached to the term "old"-know it by experience, because in at least two of the Canadian provinces, they are being soundly trounced by the apostles of the new creed.
As for the second alternative, there are some who would be only too happy to prove intelligently rather than by means of stupid denegations or inappropriate interruptions, the insanity and economic danger of this doctrine.
For my part, I refuse to believe that everything is basically wrong in the social credit doctrine, as long, at least, as the contrary has not been proved. I also refuse to believe that a considerable and ever-increasing part of the Canadian electorate is totally mistaken as to its value and that of its supporters.
There must be something to this, just as there must be something to the theories expounded by socialists, Liberals, Conservatives and, if I may be permitted to add this, independents. Otherwise our democratic system would be a complete failure.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat that in voting in favour of the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lethbridge, I mainly desire to stress the fact that more attention should be paid to the monetary theories of the Social Credit party. On the other hand, should they contain practical elements, capable of application, we would be able to make the most out of them.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal with the pressing and vital question of Canadian airports, the
682	HOUSE OF
The Address

Mr. Macnaughton place of airports in the life of this fastgrowing nation, the function of airports in our economic future, the importance of airports to the defence of the free world.
Most of us have a proud awareness of the present travel facilities provided by Trans-Canada, Canadian Pacific and other Canadian air lines. We agree with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) "that aviation is growing faster than Canada," but how many of us get the full significance of such a statement as Ronald Keith, editor of Canadian Aviation, made the other day. He said:
It is hard to realize that as recently as 1937- fifteen years ago-Canada was six days wide and relatively few Canadians had ever flown. Today, our country is only twenty hours from coast to coast, and last year nearly a million passengers flew on T.C.A. alone!
But those are only a few more facts and figures. If you want to get the full impact of what they mean may I suggest that the next time you have occasion to be at an airport anywhere in Canada, look at it closely, critically, watch the coming and going of planes, trucks, cars and people. Mostly watch the people. If you are in doubt about anything, ask the first twelve-year-old boy you come across. He can tell you better than I can ever hope to just what it means to live in a country only twenty hours wide, because you will find his main hope is that by the time he is a man, Canada will be only ten hours wide. And no doubt it will, if science has its way and provided we in this house see to it that Canadian airport facilities are adequate to meet the needs, not only of the growing travelling public but of this nation's booming commerce and industry as well.
I have suggested that you look critically at our airports, but I do not suggest that you seek only to find fault. In fact I am sure you will agree that, despite many obvious shortcomings, the picture of Canada's airport facilities is so good that we can afford to indulge in a little self-criticism. And that is not just my opinion, it is also the opinion of the world's top air travel technicians. We have come a long way from the cow pastures of not so many years ago to the 415 licensed airports of today. We have certainly progressed from the time, just after the first world war, when our investment in airport facilities was almost zero, to our present investment in airports of well over half a billion dollars.
You may say, and rightly, that much of this growth was forced upon us by circumstance. I say it is to the lasting credit of the ministry of transport that through the years it has known what it was doing, has fostered and nurtured Canadian aviation, and


channelled its development along the lines of undeniable common sense, so that today we have a solid foundation upon which to build for the future, as build we must if we are to keep pace with our natural growth and with the new demands which technical aviation advances impose upon us. Jet planes are almost here, remember.
How did we make the transition from cow pasture to modern airstrip, you will ask. The answer is that the real history of civil aviation in Canada started just after the first world war, when we found ourselves with a large supply of competent pilots and engineers, a few aircraft and airports, a little know-how, and a lot of enthusiasm. In June of 1919 the Air Board Act was passed in this house. This act, now known as the Aeronautics Act, together with the air regulations, which were first passed in 1920, are the basis for the air law of Canada. On New Year's day, 1923, control of civil aviation was placed in the newly created Department of National Defence. Progress, though steady, was unspectacular. A few ex-war pilots flew the north country airways. A few small companies were organized for photographic and charter flights. Then in 1936 we formed the Department of Transport, and under Right Hon. C. D. Howe civil aviation was moved from the Department of National Defence to this new department, to be combined with the meteorological division and the radio- now the telecommunications-division to form the air services branch.
Between the two wars a start was made on the development of an air mail service to the prairies. Small emergency fields and aids to navigation at intermediate fields were established by the federal government. Larger centres such as Winnipeg, Calgary and Edmonton provided their own airports, primitive affairs by present standards. In 1937 the coming of Trans-Canada Air Lines made it imperative that these fields be improved, and the federal government undertook to grant assistance in those cases where the municipalities would and could carry out the required improvements. Where the community was too small to make any major contribution, or where for other reasons it was felt the community could not be expected to take the initiative, the federal government built the necessary airports and services so as to ensure a continuous chain of ground facilities.
The demands of the second world war caused still further improvements to be made. Municipal airports were taken over on lease and developed as combined civil and military bases. A great number of entirely new airports were built to meet defence needs. Where

possible, these were so placed as to be usable for civilian needs when the R.C.A.F. was finished with them.
By 1946 the picture of our airports had changed beyond all recognition. The cow pastures had become large, expensive and complex plants requiring closely co-ordinated effort by many specialized services. It became increasingly evident that airport activities must be considered in two lights: one, the operation and maintenance of runways, hangars and workshops, administration buildings, and so on; and, two, the activities revolving around the aids to navigation such as radio ranges and beacons, communications, instrument landing system or ground controlled approach, air traffic control-both airport and airway control-and meteorological services which can only operate by virtue of a vast and complex system of communications covering the entire country and dependent on an even vaster system covering the whole continent. No municipality could hope to bear the cost of such a tremendous, complex system.
On the subject of costs, it takes anywhere from five to ten million dollars to build a major airport providing the services I have just described. It costs as much more if you include all the buildings and services constructed by and for the R.C.A.F. at such airports.
From the very beginning it was agreed that these aids to navigation are a federal government responsibility, partly because they are part of a larger co-ordinated system and partly because the costs were away beyond the ability of individual municipalities to pay. Where the municipalities felt unable to take on the maintenance of their airports, it has been necessary for the federal government to bear the entire cost of construction, operation and maintenance.
To get the full magnitude of the picture, you must remember that in 1939 Canada had 65 land airports. Our airways extended over about three thousand miles. Something like $5 million would cover the estimate of total airport and airway facilities of 1939. Today Canada has 143 hard-surfaced airports. Air routes and airways cover more than 14,000 miles. Four hundred and fifteen airport licences are in force. The total capital value of this tremendous airport and airway plant is something like $550 million, or 110 times more than 13 years ago.
So far as the financing of our major airports is concerned, you must keep in mind that all of them have some defence value, either immediate or potential. The question is, how can these airports be made to pay.

Airport activity should be divided into two parts, for accounting purposes. Part one is directly concerned with the landing, taking off and manoeuvring of aircraft. Revenue from airport landing fees at major airports, by the way, is said to be sufficiently high to cover maintenance and operating costs that can be directly assessed to aircraft activities. Part two covers the non-flying facilities such as hangars and workshops, administration buildings, equipment, garages, offices, restaurants and so on. To these a percentage of the cost of operating utilities must be charged. The problem is to increase revenue to cover the cost of facilities which cannot be assessed directly to aircraft activities.
With the exception of Ottawa and Montreal, every community of sufficient size to be expected to make any contribution toward an airport has made it. And for the record it is interesting to note that Montreal is said to derive a revenue benefit of no less than $3 million a year just because ICAO keeps its offices there. But apart from these two cities, most communities have bought the land on which their airport is now located. In western Canada, in some cases, the communities themselves have made considerable strides in airport development. So far as Ottawa is concerned, it is argued that Canada's capital city's airport should be a charge on Canada as a whole. Perhaps so, since because of its location, near defence headquarters and numerous scientific and research bodies, Ottawa airport runways are now being extended and facilities installed to make it one of the largest in the world, much larger than is necessary simply to serve the needs of a city the size of Ottawa, and at a cost far beyond the means of any one community.
Montreal's present airport, at Dorval, was developed largely to facilitate movement of aircraft to the United Kingdom during the war. Dorval, among other things, is one of the reasons why today Montreal is the aviation capital of the world, why the international civil aviation organization has its headquarters there, as has the equally important international air transport association, the agency which co-ordinates the activities of all the world's airline operators.
The picture I have painted so far has been rosy, so rosy that, as I said earlier, a little self-criticism cannot hurt us or detract from the splendid achievement of the Department of Transport through the years. But, for one thing, our very prosperity in aviation, the giant progress we have made, has flowed over us before we were really prepared for
684	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Macnaughton it. Although technically our airports are among the world's best, most up-to-date and safest, and although our engineers and technicians are well in the lead in keeping them abreast of latest developments, the impression the travelling public-you and I-get in going through our air terminals is inclined to be depressingly grey. It is not a bit unusual to find a large crowd of people jammed together, milling around in a waiting room far too small to accommodate them. If they go outside to get a breath of air-that is, if customs and immigration will let them outside-the prospect is anything but pleasing. In winter you face snowdrifts and icy blasts; in summer, a monotonous sun-baked landscape. Back inside, out of the cold or dusty heat, you can squeeze in for a just-adequate meal at some of the larger airports, or drop a coin in the coke-vending machine or automatic shoe-shiner at the small places. So far as the delayed passenger is concerned, he just sits and fumes. Sometimes he cannot even sit.
But let us leave for the moment the matter of the inadequacy of our airports in the way they try to cater to public needs. Although the deficiencies are annoying enough, they do nothing to detract from the progress made. Meantime let us consider seriously the importance of air travel and transport to this country. Just a month ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) pointed out that he expects total revenues from our commercial air carriers this year to exceed $80 million. That is five times as much as it was in 1946. In fact revenues have been increasing at a rate of between 17 and 20 per cent for the last few years, and show every indication of continuing to do so. Mr. J. R. Baldwin, chairman of the air transport board, has pointed out:
If rates of growth which have existed over the past three years in Canada and the United States continue-and this appears to be the case-then the faster rate of growth in Canada may mean that in virtually all fields of aviation, with the possible exception of cargo, Canada will not only be in an equal relative position but may pull ahead of the United States.
So far as future growth is concerned, it will be obvious that with our air lines and airports handling passengers at the annual rate of one for every fourteen Canadians-a million a year, that is-with half a billion dollars invested in airports, and hundreds of millions in planes and personnel and equipment in general, aviation is not just growing at the same tempo as the Canadian economy. It is, in Mr. Baldwin's words, "taking over new and additional fields of activity and has by no means reached the maximum degree of penetration of new markets."


In the air coach and air cargo markets there are tremendous new sources of traffic to be tapped. I hope you will not think it trite if I remind you that as our north country continues to pour forth its riches, so must our north-south feeder lines, and our east-west trunk lines, carry more and more air passengers and air cargo. In fact, without the planes you could not open up the country, and without the planes you certainly could not maintain contact once you had opened it up. So the future of a vast segment of the Canadian economy obviously depends on what can be carried through the air; where it can be set down, and in what quantities.
Consequently, traffic is increasing faster than facilities to handle it on the ground are being provided. The Toronto terminal at Malton is just managing to keep abreast of its traffic. The Vancouver terminal, also, can just barely keep up. The present Calgary terminal was converted to its present use at government expense. The federal government owns the building, which has tarpaper outside and a softwood floor inside. At the moment new terminals are being erected at Lakehead and Moncton which should be adequate for some years. At other points in the east and west, in smaller cities, the situation is not acute, even if the facilities are not completely modern and efficient and comfortable.
The main problem, of course, is how to make terminal facilities pay for themselves, especially since customs, immigration, health and the post office all take up a lot of space and do not pay for it. Also, a good deal of space must be allocated to public needs. The air services people themselves have to have space to accommodate the airport manager and his staff, air traffic control services, radio services and meteorological services. At Dorval, for example, the amount of space used by each of these government and air services adds up to 29-7 per cent. Another 25-7 iper cent is unrentable, and 31-9 per cent only can be rented. The remaining 11-7 per cent is basement, which is vacant and presumably unusable. Obviously the ratio of non-revenue space to revenue space is quite high, and it seems to the experts, so far as I can gather, that as long as this ratio remains the way it is no terminal building is likely to pay for itself. Air operations pay for themselves already, as I have pointed out. In order to make a terminal pay, then, it has got to be big enough and must include enough sound commercial enterprises of a nature sufficiently attractive to induce passengers and visitors alike to patronize them.

As a matter of fact it has been proved over and over again that airport terminals can be made to pay, aside from regular air traffic revenues. On this continent the most experienced voice is that of the port of New York authority, which over the years has had to solve the financing problems involved in the provision of what are known as "domestic" and "international" air services. As you are aware, New York airports must handle traffic not only American in origin but also between all parts of this continent and from Europe. If the port of New York authority were dealing with, say, the problem of Dorval in Montreal, which is in a measure comparable to New York airports so far as domestic and international traffic is concerned, you can be sure the first consideration would be to make a capital outlay sufficient to provide all the basic facilities essential to the operation of an efficient airport. This capital cost would then be supported by the general revenue of all the air lines using the airport, as well as by the development of concessions.
A comprehensive airport plan envisages construction of hangars, shops, offices, air freight terminals and other operating facilities. The construction budget for these amenities, according to the New Yorkers, would be supported by air line and other leases so that these amenities would immediately be placed on a self-supporting basis. So far, so good. But the New York port authority's fundamental concept does not stop there. It believes that airport development, to be successful, requires the judicial exploitation of all revenue and concession areas in each air terminal. This means the encouragement, by concession, of restaurants, shopping areas, facilities for recreation and amusement, spectators' promenade, and any other development which might contribute to the support of the project and to the obtaining of net revenues.
Many of the hon. members of this house have travelled, as I have done, extensively in the United States and Europe, so I am sure they will be disposed to agree that the port of New York authority's idea of how to make an air terminal pay is not too far-fetched for Canadians to grasp. In fact, those of you who have travelled in Europe will remember that the above-mentioned concessions were extended to include such items as a newsreel cinema, cafes, restaurants, cocktail bars, conference rooms for rushing businessmen, a nursery for harassed mothers, souvenir shops, dress shops, handicraft shops-all kinds of shops-exhibitions, tourist bureaux, observation decks, and even first-class hotels. I
The Address-Mr. Macnaughton might say that today there is room for a 200-bed hotel at the Dorval airport. The present hotel of 80 beds is totally inadequate to meet the situation.
In addition, really modem airports have such things as spur lines for the fast and efficient handling of rail freight; fully developed fringe areas owned or leased by the airport and containing busy warehouses and even factories; well landscaped surroundings, and whole communities which live by and with the coming and going of air passengers, air cargo and, almost as important, sightseeing throngs.
Yes, I said sightseers. I mean the kind of people who, a couple of generations ago, always met the afternoon train at the depot; the friendly Canadians whose instinct is to give silent welcome to the newcomer, and kind farewell to the voyageur. All they have done is transfer their affection from the railway station or the jetty to the world's modem equivalent. And then, of course, we have the youngsters. Most of them are stiff old-fashioned enough to be thrilled by the roar and throb of obsolescent airscrews, but lots of them have lost their hearts to the blowtorch swoosh and keening whine of the midcentury jet job and are already searching with their young minds the quiet chill spaces of the outer universe. Yes, these are the sightseers. That is one of the things I meant when, in my introduction, I suggested you look mostly at the people you will find around Canada's airports. If you think there are not enough of them to warrant attention from concessionaires consider that, during the summer months and well into the colder times, thousands of regular Sunday visitors throng Dorval, which is not easy to come by, being eleven miles from the heart of Montreal and situated in a pretty bleak setting. They come by bus, by car, by bicycle and on foot. If there were rapid transit they would come by that, too. Their object, as stated to me by my own constituents of Mount Royal, who live practically next door to Dorval, is to see the "biggest free show in town"; to see the more than one thousand passengers arrive daily, on 70 domestic flights and 14 or 15 transatlantic jumps. I can assure you, as will any of the oldtimers at Dorval, that just a little landscaping, just a little in the way of creature comfort and amusement, would bring many thousands more to this latter-day caravanserai, not only during the hours of sunshine but also during the spectacular airport night with its multi-coloured lighting effects and its thrilling rushing sounds.
Let us consider Dorval. It is an international airport in the true sense of the
686	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Macnaughton word. It is the European's and the American's first ground contact with Canada and Canadian ways. But instead of the voyageur peering into the showcase of this nation- which Dorval should be-his first encounter is with jammed waiting rooms, milling with crowds; cramped quarters for health, immigration and customs, making efficient handling almost impossible whilst waiting for transfer from international to domestic flights. Although Dorval is so close to Canada's first city-a bilingual city at that-and although frequently flying schedules allow transient visitors three or four hours between flights, you have to be a real adventurer to take a chance on a run into Montreal in search of the normal amenities of civilization which are somehow denied you at Dorval. Montreal is known for good shops, good hotels, good food and drink and entertainment. Why then should a traveller have to come so near to remain so far away?
Why cannot Dorval be so reconstructed and conducted that it will do a public relations job for the nation in the short time it takes the worldly-wise traveller from Antwerp or Abadan or Los Angeles to change planes? And just as much as we want to give the non-Canadian what he wants, we must be prepared to cater to the people of our own country; and airports, we must remember, have become in these times social and cultural rendezvous of the first magnitude, the meeting place for those who travel in the modern style as well as for those who think modern thoughts. There are millions such today. Just look at our air travel figures alone. These millions could turn your air terminal into the "coin box" of your airport. Let us start with Dorval, to design our air terminals so they will present the best shop window for Canada, not only to visitors from abroad but to our own people too.
All this foregoing is not just eyewash. It is good commercial horse sense, that is all. Other countries have made it pay off. So can we, once we, as Canadians, get used to the fact that you do not have to subject yourself to the discomfort of a log cabin at this stage in Canada's development, even though log cabins were good enough for grandpa and are even good enough for a whole lot of people who are currently engaged in pushing our mining frontiers northward to the Arctic. We are an air-minded country now. Let us realize it. As my good friend Leslie Roberts says in his splendid new book "Canada: The Golden Hinge", "there are too few Canadians and we tend to live in clumps, too widely separated for our own good. The growth of population and the development of rapid


internal communications is correcting this basic problem, but we still have a long way to go." But I might remind you, it is not so far for your constituents and mine to go to the local airport, and if we make it attractive enough for them they will soon make it the social and cultural bazaar it could and should be.
So much for the business of encouraging the public to support your airport. There are other sources of revenue, to be sure. There are air freight, air express, air coach service, to name a few. Most of you know that Canadian charter carriers have always carried substantial quantities of air freight into outlying areas and that air express and some air cargo has been carried in space available on main-line scheduled passenger flights. However, two recent developments are not so widely known.
First, new and larger types of aircraft, such as the Bristol freighter and Curtiss C-46 are now being employed on charter freight operations in northern Canada which, because of their greater load capacity and lower unit costs, are opening new aviation fields in these areas. Such aircraft make it possible to transport far greater volumes of traffic and provide a new flexibility to operations leading to the development of our northern regions.
Even more significant to the development of air cargo is the fact that we stand on the threshold of the introduction on a substantial basis of all-cargo scheduled main-line operations. A substantial volume of traffic has already been developed on such services in the United States. Canada, hampered by a shortage of suitable aircraft equipment up to this time, will soon be moving in the same direction. Several specific proposals for the introduction of all-cargo operations are now before the air transport board. Some idea of the general trend of development which may be expected can be obtained from the experience in the United States, where the growth of air cargo has been rapid following the expansion of all-cargo operations.
The principal advantage offered to the shipper by air freight is, of course, speed. There are, however, numerous ancillary advantages. Among the savings to the shipper are frequently reduced inventory requirements; savings on packaging; increase of sales of style merchandise which must be available for temporary spurts in sales; increase of sales of current interest merchandise such as newsreels, periodicals, etc.; savings through speedy shipment of parts which avoid production delays.
The increases in cargo traffic which undoubtedly lie ahead in the fairly near

future will necessitate substantial improvement in the cargo-handling facilities not only of the air lines but also of the airports where both materials-handling equipment and warehousing facilities will require expansion.
Another substantial development which lies in the future for Canadian aviation and will also lead to a marked expansion of traffic is provision of higher-density seating for air coach service. By the introduction of higher-density seating and possibly elimination of free meal services it may be possible to provide a reduction in passenger fares and as a consequence marked increases in traffic. Trans-Canada Air Lines and other transatlantic carriers introduced tourist fares on the Atlantic in May of this year and some similar trend may be expected in domestic services in due course. As a matter of fact, based on United States experience, a 25 per cent reduction in fares has been shown to produce as much as a 40 per cent increase in passenger volume. It is worth thinking about, and Canada's air line companies are doing lots of thinking in that direction these days.
It is these air coach and air cargo prospects and the steady growth of their present regular passenger, express and mail operations which have justified the orders for new Lockheed super Constellation and Vickers Viscount turbine aircraft which have been placed by T.C.A.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was dealing with the place and function of airports in our national and economic life. I had given a short resume of how the Department of Transport, with a long-range plan in mind, had carefully and wisely developed a chain of efficient airports across the country. I was attempting to point out the next necessary stage of development, namely the need for better terminal facilities, in particular at Dorval airport in Montreal. And it was not just a question of local pride. It is bigger than that. My purpose was to show that a heaven-sent opportunity exists to do a public relations job for Canada with the travelling public; furthermore, that it would pay for itself; and that even if it did not the government still has a social job to do in that regard. I was attempting to indicate new sources of revenue and I had pointed out that air cargo and air coach services were already knocking on the door.
The Address-Mr. Macnaughton
You are all familiar with the important work being done by the helicopter on military operations in Korea. It is also doing valuable work in Canada, performing such functions as depositing freight on mountain sides in British Columbia for the aluminum project, doing geophysical surveying in northern Canada, carrying mail in Newfoundland to outpost stations. However, the helicopter cannot come fully into its own until an economic passenger-carrying helicopter is available. The day when such a helicopter will become available in large numbers is not too far away, and there is every prospect that in less than ten years there will be regular helicopter services between some of our major cities. Such new services will present a host of new technical and economic problems ranging all the way from consideration of appropriate flight techniques over crowded cities to the building of helicopter alighting areas on the tops of railroad stations. There is no likelihood that the helicopter will replace the long-distance aircraft. It will be for transportation purposes, the short-haul adjunct to it, whose combination of slower speed and ability to land closer to the city centre will create new short-haul traffic.
The advent of the jet age will undoubtedly mean a revolution in landing strip design, for a variety of technical reasons; but the best authorities are of the opinion that it is no problem to plan and build advanced airport buildings right now. Just because a super-jet take-off strip may look like a toboggan slide does not affect the service in an airport restaurant or an airport hotel. And we had better start planning now, or the jet age will be upon us before we know it. I notice that the air line run by the C.P.R., that same company which, 64 years ago, saw the last spike-a gold one at that-driven into a railroad tie high in a Rocky mountain pass, the company which helped so much to give Canada confederation, are now saying to the world:
Across the Pacific, Comet jetliners, vibrationless, silent, smooth . . .
It shakes you a little. It makes you remember how, when you were younger, people used to say: "Canada has got responsible government, the world's finest bridgebuilding company, the world's greatest travel system and world's greatest future."
Yes, as an anonymous editor wrote on the dust-cover of Leslie Roberts' vital, significant "The Golden Hinge":
In the opening years of the second half of the twentieth century, Canada possesses a treasure trove of wealth which cannot be matched in the
688	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. D. F. Brown western world. That wealth lies in the seas off Nova Scotia; in the forests of the north; in the giant timber of the Pacific coast and its offshore islands. You'll find it in the mines of seven provinces; in the great Alberta oil pools; in the soil of the great plains. You'll find it in the orchards of Niagara and in the valleys of the Rockies; in the waters off the western coast; in the humming factories of the heartland, from Windsor eastward to Quebec. You'll find it, too, in the Canadian people and the qualities they possess.
Yes, the Canadian people; it is they whom you should watch when you pass through your next airport. Watch them, milling, patient, curious, interested in this modem wonder, trying to be a part of it. And as you watch them, agree with me that they deserve better than they have been given by us and agree, too, that if we give them better airports we will once again prove the truth of the adage that "it pays to be modern"; pays not only in extra revenues but in an extra line of defence against those who would destroy our freedom.

Mr. Speaker, may I add my congratulations to those of others who have spoken in this debate, to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have certainly served this house with distinction, and have brought credit upon their constituencies, and I might say also to the whole of Canada, in the attitude they have assumed in the conduct of the affairs of parliament.
I want to say a word about the licensing of radio-television sets. On another occasion I have spoken in this house with respect to radio licences, and I will not repeat what I had to say on that occasion. Suffice it to say that I am opposed to a radio licence because of the fact that such a licence is not collectable; and if it is not collectable and is paid by only a part of the population who are in possession of radio sets, I am opposed to it.
A report has appeared in the newspapers- and I do not vouch for its authenticity-that there is to be a radio-television licence fee of $15 imposed upon each radio television receiving set. In the constituency which I represent, Essex West, we have the United States on three sides of us. By reason of the geography of that part of the country we are south of the United States. Within a radius of a hundred miles there is a population of about three million people, which means that there are about three million people who would be in a position, as radio television set owners, to obtain broadcasts in the Windsor area. At the present time we have three channels of television, each emanating of course from Detroit. We have excellent reception; we have no complaints


whatsoever, television reception there is probably much better than in most places in the city of Detroit itself.
Anything that I have to say, Mr. Speaker, is not in condemnation of the C.B.C. or to be considered as such, because we are well served with radio broadcasting in that area. CKLW, which is a 50,000-watt broadcasting station, serves and has served that area very well for many years. We were opposed to the licensing of radio receiving sets until such time as the C.B.C. established what is now known as radio station CBE, and my praise for that station cannot be expressed in words. It is making friends not only for C.B.C. but for all Canada. Among the three million people who are potential listeners I know there are many thousands, and the record would so verify what I am saying, who listen to nothing but that particular radio station.
According to C.B.C. policy, as announced, I understand that in addition to the radiotelevision stations situated at Toronto and at Montreal, there are going to be other stations at Halifax, Winnipeg and Vancouver. This does not include a radio-television broadcasting station in the Windsor area, where we have three million potential listeners and viewers. For that reason we feel there should be no taxation without a corresponding benefit to the area.
I am not alone in that thought. I am supported by several resolutions I have received. I am not going to read those resolutions in full, but shall make reference only to that from the city of Windsor received on October 17, 1951, which indicates that it opposes any system of television licence fees that may affect local set owners until such time as those owners will get the direct benefit of Canadian-owned stations. This resolution is supported by resolutions from the town of Riverside, the town of Kingsville, the town of Sandwich East, the town of Harrow, the township of Mersea, the township of Gosfield North, the township of Sandwich West, and others.
So my first point is that I do not think there should be taxation unless we are to have the benefit of C.B.C. radio-television broadcasting.
Then the report states that the licence fee will be $15. Even in these modern days I believe such a fee is somewhat oppressive. It is too high. I would recommend that, if at some later time a fee is to be set, it should be nominal.
Finally I believe there should be no tax until some means is found whereby there will be full coverage; that is to say, a time

The Address-Mr. Rowe
when everyone in possession of a radio-television receiving set would be paying a licence fee. Until that time I do not think there should be any fee whatsoever.
In my view the government should be commended for adopting a careful attitude and for making a cautious approach to the subject, because I think much can be learned from mistakes made in other countries which will make it possible for us to develop this vital means of communication so that it may be used for the full benefit and advantage of the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is of interest to all to note such concern paid to the speech from the throne. The debate has proceeded for several days, and much has been said by hon. members on both sides of the house.
I should like to join those who have congratulated the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) on the splendid speeches they made in moving and seconding the address in reply. They are new members. I wish for them many years of happiness and satisfaction in the service of their respective districts. It was to be expected that, as new members, they would in faithful admiration compliment the government upon what it has done, and say little about what it has not done.
I believe this debate has brought to the attention of the house and the taxpayers the signs of the times. It has given an indication of what the government has been doing, whether it is smugly satisfied with what it has done or whether it has any ideas for the future. As hon. members will agree, the speech from the throne is in the nature of a pattern or a plan for the year's business. It is not given in as much detail as one might wish, or as we may expect to see later in the budget and in legislation to be brought down.
Some say that we will see a strange type of budget. This, of course, will depend upon what those who sit to the right of Mr. Speaker intend to do in the next twelve months. We must decide for ourselves, when we have heard what might be called boasting about our greatness, our great natural resources and the prosperity we have enjoyed, whether these conditions are basically sound, or whether they are the result of a post-war development, or the result of preparations for another war.
In any event there is no one in the house, and few in the country, who would view without a keen sense of pride the fact that Canada, a country offering the greatest opportunities of any country in the world, has made great progress. While the United States
of America may have increased its trade sevenfold in the last few years, Canada has increased hers fourfold. No similar number of people in the world enjoy the advantages of greater resources than we do.
However, I sometimes wonder if it is not important, either in one's private business transactions or in the transaction of public business, to stop, look and listen, even when things are going well. There never has been a time in the last several years when it was more necessary to stop and consider the basis of the prosperity we are now enjoying. In other words, I say this would be the proper time for stocktaking in this country. There is a feeling of uncertainty among business people. There is excitement among labour; there is unrest in agriculture; there is concern among military people. All across Canada people are asking themselves:	What
about tomorrow? I often wonder if we are not prone to become hypnotized with the type of prosperity brought about either by the war through which we have passed or in preparation against another war. I think of the millions and millions spent on the war that is past, and the millions being spent to prevent another one, and sometimes I wonder if we should not ask ourselves what will happen in the days ahead.
We have heard many rumours about state planning, but there seems to be very little preparation made for days of peace. I have always felt that we should put first things first. While I have been in the House of Commons a considerable number of years, I do not think I could be called a reactionary, because I have suffered reverses in politics for being too much the other way.
No one has greater sympathy than I have for the man who needs assistance. I could not have remained as long as I have in public life had I not recognized that need. But, in all sincerity, I say we should stop and be prepared to put first things first; because no matter how anxious we may be for social security, our first need is national security, and that national security depends upon financing, development and expansion. National security depends upon economic soundness in this country. I say again that it does not matter whether the Liberal party sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, is in power, or whether the reins of office are held by the party to your left; the fact remains that national security is of first importance.
I do urge that we work for a common purpose in this house. No matter how bitterly hon. members from the other side castigate the leader of our party, no matter how bitterly they castigate some of the things of years ago, we have many things in common. I say
690	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Rowe it is with common pride that we think of the great resources of Canada. It is with common interest that we speak about the great advances we have made. It is with a common thought that we talk about our magnificent future and our great resources. But I often think it is not always with common tactics that we try to approach these things.
After all, a popular political appeal is not always sound statesmanship, any more than popular learning is sound logic. There are all too many who seem afraid to face the future. There are all too few who seem brave enough to say what they think should be done. I sometimes become alarmed when I think that we are building up prosperity on war preparations. I see dangerous trends, and I know every hon. member of this house also sees them. Signals are being disregarded, storm warnings are ridiculed.
We must realize that this country is being overtaxed. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said it was only pretended overtaxation, pretended by the opposition. But I believe in the same speech he said that in one or two instances they might save only $3 million anyway, and he said that if it was all added together they would not save any more than $100 million. This indicates the trend of the times. It shows that a government in power is disregarding some of these fundamentals.
I ask hon. fhembers to realize that today we are paying in taxation $320 per person or $1,600 for every average fajmily of five. Realize what that means to the average home. We are paying in taxation today to this government twice as much as we pay to feed the whole population of Canada, and an amount almost equal to what we pay for food,* clothing and housing.
I know that progress knows no retreat. I know that we have made no more advance along certain lines than they have made in the United States of America. I know that following the first great war there was tremendous advance until 1929 and 1930. It was to be expected that following this last world war there would be a great improvement in our prosperity. We are blessed with rich resources in the form of gold, silver, nickel, copper, asbestos, every form of base metal you cam think of, plus iron ore and oil. In addition we have our great agricultural wealth, our forest wealth that exports more than all our base metals and wheat combined. These things are great blessings.. We could not help being prosperous in times like this, no matter what party was in power. When I hear hon. members tell of some panacea they have which has made this country


prosperous in the last few years I am absolutely amused at their nonsense. Even with the folly of our friends down in the far corner we would have had great prosperity in the last few years anyway. You could not have avoided it. The world was at our feet; great resources were at our hands. The Lord never gave so few people so much. You could not help but have prosperity.
What has the government done to bring about this prosperity? They have increased taxes and practised extravagance such as we have never known. I am not going to relate them now, but surely in the face of what we have heard in the last few months no one can say that the government are the great apostles of economy. You do not buy half a dozen raincoats for each girl in the service if you are trying to economize. You do not even buy them for your own girls.

The report goes on-and I am delighted as an old soldier to see that-in glowing terms to give credit to the rank and file of the army. Soldiers are not criminals. Soldiers do not thieve and pilfer naturally. Here and there there may be a case, as apparently there were a few limited cases at Petawawa. The door has been thrown wide open by this government by reducing the standard of education of the personnel who are enlisting so that it is below the standard which existed during world war II, a standard in which the educational requirements of officers are only those of junior matriculation. That is no standard to be required for an officer to hold the Queen's commission. It is a very definite lowering; and when you get that standard of education lowered, when you throw the doors wide open it is inevitable that


here and there you will find somebody not worthy of wearing the Queen's uniform will be enlisted. The general run of the men in the army today are just exactly the same as they have always been, good, honest, straightforward fellows; and you will find that in this report Mr. Currie emphasizes that. While he finds it necessary to call attention to lax controls, poor discipline and dishonest persons, he goes on to say that the opportunities existed in other places than at Petawawa, but they were not taken advantage of. These are his words, and I want to repeat them. I want to place them on Hansard because I think it pays a glowing tribute to the rank and file in the army.
It is mentioned in this context chiefly for the purpose of praising the personnel at other depots for not walking through the door which a fundamentally loose situation had opened before them.
There were the opportunities, owing to this fundamentally loose situation, owing to the lax system; owing to the faulty organization the door was wide open, but the soldiers in the majority of cases did not take advantage of that loose situation.
Then one is surprised to find that it was not at the request of the Department of National Defence that these investigations were carried out or, I should say, that these facts were first brought to the attention of the government. Although there was supposed to be an organization of supervision, of inspection and of general security in these camps, the first information, or the information which prompted action-and I correct that word because I will come to the matter in a moment-the information which prompted action was in an anonymous letter sent to the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Then it is very interesting to note on the next page that, after Mr. Currie has quoted that letter, he goes on to say that internal warnings have not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions. Surely the administration of the defence forces, surely the deputy minister, surely the minister himself must have seen the reports of the chief auditor, who reported that conditions were unsatisfactory.
Then he goes on to refer to appendix B, a truly frightening document which gives a list of the numerous headings, setting out points which the chief auditor of the department has had to call to the department's attention, and pointing out instances not only at Petawawa but all across the board, in all

the different camps where irregularities had occurred. Then Mr. Currie goes on with these words:
Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported, and in some cases worse. The process is then again repeated.
There has been no proper supervision- not supervision from the junior officers, because the junior officers do not see the chief auditor's report, but supervision from the government, supervision from the Department of National Defence, supervision from its headquarters right here in Ottawa.

There again is a most critical sentence. It may be that there has been great loss through theft and pilfering, but the loss which arises through waste and inefficiency is far greater than that caused by actual dishonesty. Yet we have been told over and over again by members on the other side of the house that there is no waste, that there is no extravagance, that there is no duplication. Here we have independent criticism. Here we have a report by a man who is recognized as having the highest possible character, which points out that the loss caused through inefficiency and waste may be far greater than the actual stealing which took place.
It is not entirely the fault of the regulations. On page 12 Mr. Currie says that the system, had it been enforced, was a satisfactory and good one. But it had not been enforced. Who is responsible for seeing that the regulations which are laid down are enforced? Surely it is the personnel who are at the top, at the head of this Department of National Defence. They are responsible for seeing that the orders they issue are properly enforced.
Then we come to a list of some 33 headings under which irregularities have been noted. I shall not read this long list, but I will make the observation that in the abridged edition of this report no mention is made of overexpenditure.
Then we find that there has been a failure in security. Certainly security is the duty of the general staff. The general staff are responsible for security. The report states that in addition to the serious collapse in security there was little to prevent or to detect organized plundering of military stores on a systematic scale, though apparently comparatively little of it took place. Then Mr. Currie goes on to say that he takes a serious view of this breakdown, that is the breakdown in security. Then these words are used by Mr. Currie:
If it is easy to pilfer military stores, then, by the same token, it is easy to sabotage military equipment.
What is the use of spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on civil defence if right in our own military organization there is a breakdown of security which would permit or allow the sabotage of military equipment?
Then Mr. Currie goes on to try to explain some of the reasons which may have led to this breakdown of administration, this breakdown of accounting, this breakdown of supervision, this breakdown of security.	He attributes it to the tremendous and sudden expansion of the Department of National Defence and the army works services, and its activities brought


about by the Korean war and by the large-scale defence program involved in carrying out our NATO activity.
Time and time again I stood up in this house during the years from 1946 to 1949 and warned this government that they were reducing their military organization far below any standard which offered a reasonable degree of security or a reasonable degree of protection against the possibility of another war breaking out. I warned over and over again that there was a too-hasty demobilization of government stores, a too-hasty demobilization of key personnel, a too-hasty handing over to a new generation of soldiers who had had no experience in administration.
We demobilized our stores, we demobilized our key men, we got rid of our equipment so that when the threat of Korea came and it was necessary for us to expand our forces to meet our NATO obligations we had this unseemly rush, this frantic organization to find new camps, to build up equipment which had been sold ior a song, to provide stockpiles of that sort of thing. What was the result? The inevitable result was the breakdown in the administration of our forces.
As one goes on through the following pages he notes that Mr. Currie refers to the sudden rearmament and the lack of an attempt to reorganize for the tremendous expansion. The need for the tremendous expansion was brought about because in those days we had so hastily got rid of our essential services, our essential personnel and our essential equipment. On page 17 of the report we find a criticism which strikes right at the root of our defence organization. These are the words that Mr. Currie used; they are not mine:
The situation was complicated by still another factor. The Department of National Defence including the army works services was largely staffed and manned by men whose military training had been received in wartime. Its establishment and administrative practices reflected more clearly the urgent needs and exigencies of war, when speed is everything and costs count not at all. The carryforward of this war psychology must be coupled with inadequate training and resultant ignorance on the part of personnel of their administrative duties and responsibilities. There was, in addition, indifference and reluctance on the part of military personnel to concentrate on administration to the degree required. It was not perhaps unnatural that these latter needs were largely forgotten or deliberately overlooked as soldiers gazed forward into the unknown consequences of the Korean outbreak, and foresaw still greater wars not very far away. But, if this spirit permeated the lower echelons of the army, it is more difficult to condone the same attitudes higher up.

There are many, many recommendations some of which, because of these interim reports, have no doubt already been put into effect or are being put into effect at the present time. But there are still lots and lots of recommendations in this report which should receive, and I imagine will now receive, the serious attention of the heads of the Department of National Defence.
However, I do not think that is enough. It has been clearly demonstrated in this report that the heads, the higher-ups, have not shown that essential grasp of the need for administration, the need for putting into effect a proper organization which is capable of working smoothly both in peace and in war. If there has been such laxity in administration here, then one cannot help but think that if a similar examination were made of the other branches of the army you might find that there is the same lack of proper appreciation of what is required here in peacetime for the defence of Canada at this time, for our obligations as far as NATO commitments are concerned, and for our obligations as far as our Korean activities are concerned.
If one studies military history you will find that all through the course of the history of the United Kingdom armies, the history of the United States armies, and even the history of the Canadian army, there have been crises arise which have shaken those countries to the core-and they have realized that there has been gross inefficiency in the administration of their armed services. To give an
The Address-Mr. Gagnon example, one recalls the terrible waste and dishonesty which existed at the time of the Crimean war, when supplies were sent out to the Crimea. The hay was rotten, the boots were all for right feet or all for left feet, and there was hopeless administrative inefficiency. The same sort of complaints were made after the South African war. It was realized shortly before the first great war that the armed forces of the United Kingdom were not ready and prepared to wage a European war. What happened then? Under those circumstances an independent commission was appointed to investigate all branches of the armed forces. As a result of those great investigations which were carried out by Lord Esher and by Lord Haldane, a complete reorganization of the armed forces took place.
A few years ago I suggested in this house that a commission somewhat similar to the Esher commission or the Haldane commission should be appointed to see whether our armed forces were organized in the right way to meet commitments which might be expected. I repeat that request now, and I say that this report underwrites everything I said at that time. This report demands, not in the words of the report but in the sense of the report, that a thorough investigation be carried out; that an independent commission be set up for a full investigation into the organization and the entire administration- both as to types of units and equipment that we have, and the whole organization and administration of our army-to see whether it is organized on lines which will enable it to defend this country and meet this country's obligations.

The year 1952 is coming to an end. Canadian taxpayers will have to inform Caesar of the income they have received during the past twelve months. Before proceeding with the main part of my speech, I would like to make a suggestion to the government in that connection. Although it is not a new one, it is of great interest to the electors of any constituency and to those of Canada at large, I am sure.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) might well consider, I think, granting a statutory exemption of 10 per cent in connection with charitable donations. At present, in order to benefit from the exemption granted under the act, the taxpayer
