The Address-Mr. Gagnon must file receipts obtained from religious authorities, charitable societies or other such organizations recognized by the minister. It is quite a tedious procedure for everyone concerned. As a result, our parish priests lose precious time and are sometimes placed in an embarrassing situation which is very easy to understand. On the other hand, an individual who, having made charitable donations without asking for receipts, is forced to ask his parish priest for a receipt covering charitable donations which, having been made elsewhere, have not profited his parish church in the least; that individual is thus quite embarrassed when the time comes to present himself at the rectory.
Why should one ask religious authorities in particular to act as benevolent agents for the government? Why ask them to work without pay for the income tax collectors and impose upon them irritating and unpleasant tasks?
Things have reached the point where sworn certificates are being asked from those who submit, for income tax purposes, vouchers signed by priests. I say that it is going too far and that the zeal of certain members on the staff of the Department of National Revenue could be tempered without prejudice to anyone. It is already painful enough to pay this annual tribute to the central power, without adding the injury of having the members of the clergy share our financial troubles.
I am, moreover, of the opinion that statutory exemption should also be granted in the case of medical expenses.
The government would be wise to show more confidence in the population and spare them, as far as possible, the necessity of going through all that red tape. The unreasonable demands of a burdensome bureaucracy are not readily satisfied and I would ask the Minister of National Revenue to think it over while preparing the next budget.
I wish now to be allowed to offer a few remarks with respect to a political event which has taken place since the last session.
The federal government, acting in that spirit of centralization which moves all its present leaders, has, after a great deal of effort, managed to sign taxation agreements with all provinces save one. The policy of the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and of his colleagues has finally achieved its end. The province of Quebec is now alone and French Canadians form, more than ever before, a separate section in our Canadian confederation.
The line of cleavage drawn between the two great races of this country now appears in all its depth. On the one hand we have the English-speaking provinces in coalition 

with the central authorities and, on the other, the old province of Lower Canada once more facing the advocates of union. But no one can blame the authorities of my home province for this unfortunate situation. The aggressor here is not Quebec, it is Ottawa. It is Ottawa which has violated the spirit of the confederative pact by resorting to overbidding and blackmail to lay its hands on those rights given the provinces by the constitution.

It merely asks for the return of those sources of revenue which were granted to it by the constitution.
Of course, one should not consider Ottawa as a hostile government; but as far as fiscal matters are concerned, one must admit that the aggressor is Ottawa and not the province of Quebec.

Only one province now remains out of this type of negotiation. I shall not repeat the arguments I stated previously in this house to defend provincial autonomy.
Let me say that the editor of La Terre de chez-nous gives me food for thought when he writes, in an article entitled: "An Invitation to Separatism'', that we might consider abandoning the policy that has brought us only disappointments, afflictions, injustice and ordeals in every province of Canada.
The latest example is what is currently happening at Maillardville in British Columbia. In his editorial Mr. Maurice Berube writes as follows:
"Ottawa's tactics, which consist in lowering the resistance of the provinces by picking at them one by one, are undoubtedly more successful than dealing with all of them at the same time on matters they must decide by common agreement. The government at Ottawa has deemed it more expedient to bargain and negotiate separately with each of them."
Some might say that it is a smart policy. It seems to us that this policy is much closer to the dictatorial ways which we have fought and are still fighting than to the ways of democracy, which we claim to defend as far as the China seas. It is, in short, the already very ancient policy of "dividing to rule". It was known in the days of the Romans.
Such procedure is highly unfair for those who refuse to be absorbed, just as it was at the time of the Romans or, not so long ago, at the time of the nazis and the soviets.
The chamber of commerce of the province of Quebec has submitted, in a remarkable brief to the provincial authorities, its views on federal-provincial relations in matters of taxation.
The chamber of commerce is not a political body. It cannot be accused of favouring one party to the detriment of another.
Representing the chambers of commerce of the various districts of the province of Quebec, its views are those of the best elements of the population, and its views are expressed in the best interests of the fatherland. Its denunciation of the centralizing procedure and the relentless efforts of the central power to take over provincial sources of revenue is a warning that must not go unheeded.

Mr. Speaker, I think the situation that has developed from the presentation of the Currie report has naturally aroused apprehension in all circles with regard to the general matter of the administration of the Department of National Defence. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) has rightly pointed out that if there has been faulty administration in one area, perhaps other matters should be investigated.
The Department of National Defence is, as we all realize, one of the most important departments of government, and has at its disposal a great deal of the money which is provided annually for general purposes. When we pay half of our collection of taxes into defence preparation, naturally we are interested in knowing whether we are getting value for our money. From time to time we have had instances where we have wondered whether we were getting full value, and this report which has come before us naturally makes one wonder whether the investigations should not be carried further.
How far does this extend? Is it restricted only to this one small works engineering department within the Department of National Defence, or are other things also worthy of investigation?
We had a suggestion made to the house some time ago that a joint committee of the two houses of parliament might very well be set up to conduct an objective and impartial investigation that would satisfy not only parliament itself but the people of Canada. We
704	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Churchill have perhaps reached the stage where that suggestion should be given very careful consideration.
I spoke in the house some time ago about matters of defence in relation to our men serving overseas; and it seems to me that the presentation of this report makes even more urgent some of the matters I dealt with on that occasion. After all, we are engaged in what we are pleased to call a cold war. We have troops across both oceans. Unfortunately, in some circles we have been calling the war in Korea a police action, and it may be that we are taking rather too complacently the world responsibilities that we have naturally assumed as a member of the United Nations.
I have been reading the accounts of the recent visit to Korea of the president-elect of the United States and the comments various military commentators have made with regard to the situation there; and I wondered whether we should not seriously be considering some of those points and investigating to see whether our efforts here in Canada are directed along the right lines with regard to that conflict in Korea. Presidentelect Eisenhower is quoted in the Gazette of December 15 as saying:
Finally, we must all recognize-in all our thinking and our planning-that the Korean war is but the most dramatic and most painful phase, for us at this moment, in our world-wide struggle against communist aggression.	'
I was endeavouring to find out, Mr. Speaker, whether reports from Korea were accurate concerning ammunition supplies for our forces there, whether we were not overlooking the serious situation that prevailed with regard to casualties. The Minister of National Defence made a statement on December 5 in reply to some of the remarks I had made. I might point out to the house that he shifted his position with respect to the question of casualties, and has made it appear that they are not as heavy or as serious as I was endeavouring to point out.
In commenting upon Dieppe, which caught the eye of those who were reporting the proceedings of the house, I had pointed out that the force engaged at Dieppe was stripped down of all non-fighting personnel, and had engaged in that struggle only those who were equipped and trained to enter into combat with the enemy. I pointed out that if we examined our forces in Korea and determined only those who were equipped to enter into combat with the enemy, we had, as far as infantry were concerned, only about 600 men per battalion or 1,800 per brigade; and drawing the parallel with Dieppe, I showed that TMr. Churchill,]

had there been no replacement or reinforcement for the forces in Korea the rate of casualties suffered was similar to that at Dieppe. Obviously if you at Dieppe had been able to rotate the battalions every two hours, why, in the course of the eight-hour conflict, totalling up all the numbers, the casualty rate would have been much less than it was. That was the whole purpose in that comparison, but I notice that the minister in his reply to me has suggested that the casualty rate in Korea was only 16 per cent. I quote from page 365 of Hansard, where the minister said:
In Korea the 25th Canadian infantry brigade have been there a total of 7,900 man years. The total number of casualties suffered numbers 1,248 or 16 per cent as opposed to the 68 per cent in eight hours at Dieppe.
This is a new way to estimate casualties in action. I was careful to suggest that the only reasonable way to estimate casualties was to take the fighting strength of a brigade and see what the casualties were in relation to that fighting strength. General Eisenhower, in his book "Crusade in Europe", mentions that 80 per cent of the casualties of an army in the field are borne by 20 per cent of the men, the 20 per cent who are actually in contact with the enemy. I think a mistake has been made in Canada in overlooking the fact that the casualties occur in that small percentage of the total force.
It is no reflection upon those who served elsewhere in an army that they are not called upon to engage actively with the enemy. You must have a certain percentage of men behind the fighting fringe in order to keep the fighting fringe operative. It is quite obvious that you must have lorry drivers; you must have mechanics to keep vehicles in repair; you must have men to supply food, ammunition, petrol and things of that nature. In actual practice it takes four or five men working behind the line to keep one man actively in the line with his rifle, mortar, machine gun or whatever it may be. The men who serve in the rear areas suffer from the long hours of hardship and endurance they must go through to keep in shape the vehicles, weapons and equipment used by the men actually in the line. In my experience I have seen men, in the second world war, working from daylight until midnight, unceasingly, day after day including Sundays, throughout an entire month. Their contribution was essential and effective.
Nevertheless, they suffered no casualties. If you axe going to consider casualties at all, then you must look at the portion of your troops in action, and estimate the casualties on that basis. With our brigade in Korea we maintain in the front line approximately 1,800 infantrymen. On them falls the brunt of the

action. They suffer the casualties. And when we have suffered, as the figures now indicate, something like 1,250 casualties, it is clear that those casualties have fallen mostly upon the 1,800 who occupy the positions against the enemy. Of course if you rotate the battalions several times in the course of two years, and then estimate the percentage on the basis of the total number engaged, it becomes very small. It would be just as reasonable-and just as useless for the purpose, in my estimation-to take the total number of men in uniform in Korea, in Europe and in Canada and say, "Well, our casualties are 1,250, and our total number in uniform is 100,000; therefore our casualty rate is only 1-25 per cent". That does not give the true picture at all.
Consequently I think it is time we in this country learned the lesson of estimating our casualties properly, having regard to the number of men actually engaged in action. That was my reason for drawing the parallel when I spoke the other day with regard to that particular situation, and mentioned not only Dieppe but also the first world war.
The minister replied, as reported at page 365 of Hansard:
It must be remembered and emphasized that the 25th Canadian infantry brigade is practically all in the active theatre of operations in front of brigade headquarters.
That may indicate to some people that the entire brigade is in constant danger. I think it is unwise to suggest to the relatives of people in the brigade that everybody in it is in constant danger. That is not normally the situation, and people's minds should be set at rest on that point. Not every man who serves overseas in an army is in constant danger. Often he is in no danger at all, and relatives should realize that fact. I think it is not advisable to make statements to the effect that the infantry brigade is practically all in the active theatre of operations in front of brigade headquarters. Normally, when in action, brigade headquarters is split into two parts, tactical headquarters being forward- well forward

and rear headquarters, which is well back. And it should be well back, because the people who are there are those who are concerned with the supply services of the brigade, and it is not wise to endanger their lives.
But I would say this, that the serving soldier in the line, if asked whether he would like to go back to tactical brigade headquarters, would welcome the opportunity. To him it would be about the same as returning to Canada; he would feel he was just about as safe. I have been in too many brigade 68108-45
The Address-Mr. Churchill headquarters not to realize that that is the situation, although they are in exposed positions.
So I do not think for one moment that the 25th brigade is all in front of brigade headquarters, unless the minister means the rear headquarters of the brigade. And of course the same is true of the smaller formations. Regimental headquarters, to a man who actually has to move right up to the enemy's lines, seems to be a relatively safe position. Those who have served overseas will realize that.
Perhaps I was more interested in the question of ammunition than in any other aspect of the situation in Korea. My question was: Is there a shortage of ammunition in Korea? Again, as reported at page 365 of Hansard, the minister gave this assurance:
So far as ammunition is concerned, the position in Korea is precisely as I outlined it the other day. Canadian troops have never been subjected to unnecessary casualties by any shortage of ammunition, nor are they in the least likely to be exposed in such a manner. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the amount of ammunition used in Korea far exceeds that ever used before in any campaign in the history of mankind for any force of a comparable size.
I had hoped that the minister would bring forward facts and figures as evidence upon which that statement was founded. I think the statement that more ammunition has been used in Korea than in any other campaign in the history of mankind, without any evidence as to the actual number of shells expended and small arms ammunition fired, is rather open to question. If it has been used in such great quantities there is surely no reason why we cannot be informed about it. However, my question concerned our own 25th Canadian infantry brigade, and not the total amount of ammunition expended by the United Nations forces in Korea, which perhaps would include the number of bombs dropped and rockets fired by our aircraft.
The situation as I see it is simply this, that we are suffering heavy casualties in Korea. We have had disturbing reports from other sections of the Korean front with regard to restrictions on the use of ammunition; and our own Canadian forces, through the press, have reported to us that there is a restriction on their use of ammunition. I wonder why there should be a restriction. One of my reasons for wondering is found in the report in the Gazette of December 15, which makes reference to General Eisenhower's visit to Korea. Quoting from that paper I find he said that he had three definite observations to

Second-In the strictly military sphere, certain problems of supply have reached serious proportions and require early correction.
To those who are familiar with military matters in the field, that is a very serious statement. It will be noted that he says certain problems of supply have reached serious proportions, and that they require early correction. He restricts it to the strictly military sphere. Does that mean that we are short of clothing for the troops, or food or gasoline? Are we short of lorries? Are we short of ammunition? When it comes down to the point of saying that it has reached serious proportions which require early correction, and you tie that in with these other reports about the restrictions on the use of ammunition, I cannot help but wonder whether it is not ammunition that is included in that particular statement.
Then a question that arises in my mind is this. Is the government of Canada as fully informed with regard to these matters as the president-elect of the United States? Is the government aware that the problem of supply in Korea has reached serious proportions and requires early correction? If the government is aware of that, what is being done about it? Are the lives of our troops in danger?
That is the type of information I think we should have in view of the situation there. That is the type of information I had hoped would be provided by the minister in his reply the other day. But that is not the type of information we received. We received some general statements reassuring us. But we want more than reassurance by way of general statements. We want reassurance with regard to our troops. We want reassurance with regard to the conduct of the entire war in Korea.
As I said earlier, all this seems to tie in with the reports that we are now receiving with regard to the situation in the Department of National Defence. Has an attempt been made to look into all these matters? Have the minister and his officials had the opportunity to keep in close touch with the situation in Korea?
Similarly one would like to ask questions about the 27th brigade over in Europe. What is the state of its supplies with regard to arms and ammunition? Are there ammunition dumps available? In case of sudden attack or the need of using that brigade in Europe have they the necessary means to carry on? Has there been anything lacking in the supply line or in the manufacture of munitions of war?
IMr. Churchill.]

These are all most serious problems, and they become more serious when you consider the mounting toll of casualties in Korea. A report in the papers today coming from United Nations sources indicates that in the last three months, that is September, October and November, Canadian casualties were 300, or at the rate of 100 per month. That is much higher than they were in the earlier part of this year and in 1951.
I have been looking into all the reports I could find in magazines and newspapers with regard to Korea, and I have become very much disturbed. We are assured that this is static warfare as in the first world war. For some reason it seems advisable to the higher command to send out active patrols all the time to patrol the enemy's lines. Casualties are suffered in these active patrols. I wonder about the usefulness of this patrolling action on the Korean front.
This was tried out in the first world war. It is supposed to maintain the morale of the troops, to make them fighting fit and to keep them alert and active. As some of these reports from Korea say, it is supposed also to keep the enemy constantly alarmed and disturbed and shifting from one position to another. I wonder whether it is worth while conducting that type of patrol action at the cost of precious lives.
What is accomplished? Is our intelligence service such that we have to obtain prisoners in order to find out what forces are fighting against us. I notice that the intelligence arrangements of the enemy were so good that when the first battalion of the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry arrived at the front they were greeted by a placard exhibited by the Chinese extending a welcome to them. They had that information without sending patrols into our lines to seize prisoners.
I believe that the proper procedure to adopt in Korea at this stage would be to remain on the defensive, which is the recommendation of General Van Fleet himself. When you are on the defensive surely you do not have to be sacrificing lives every day with these patrol actions. If you are going to launch an offensive these patrol actions might be necessary, but I do not think they are when you are on the defensive. Many men who served in both world wars were never in a patrol action. Many of them were most effective in destroying the enemy without leaving their positions. A comrade of mine in the first great war virtually annihilated a German battalion with one machine gun, and he was never on a patrol action in his life. The German defenders of Dieppe had no necessity to go on patrol action in order to fire effectively from their strongholds against our

forces on the beachhead. I question very-much that method of conducting war in Korea.
I was saying that I have been reading all the reports I could find in magazines and newspapers concerning this war. I wonder, as I wondered the other day, to what extent Canadian military experience is playing a part at the higher levels. What are we going to do? The suggestion is made that the war cannot be ended except by attempting to destroy the Chinese army and the North Koreans. That would cost the lives of a great many of our soldiers and of the United Nations forces. It would require reinforcements, because the Chinese army is much larger than the United Nations forces. If it were driven back or partially destroyed there are reinforcements across the Yalu river who could come forward.
Another suggestion is that there should be a withdrawal in Korea. That suggestion is rejected because the conflict is one of principle, trying to stem the attack of an aggressor against a peaceful and virtually, in 1950, defenceless country.
The suggestion is made by some commentators that the United Nations forces should be withdrawn gradually and replaced by South Koreans. That seems to make a great deal of sense. There are now five South Korean divisions actively engaged against the army, with five divisions in reserve. They are holding approximately 60 per cent of the front and in the course of time could take over a larger proportion. But to train and equip more South Koreans would take time. It would mean the provision of ammunition and arms from the North American continent. Are we prepared in this country to assist in that way? Are we producing munitions of war in sufficient quantities to assist in building up the South Korean army, thereby releasing Canadian forces?
Another proposal is that we simply go on the defensive-this is the one that makes the greatest appeal to me-and become strongly entrenched, holding the line for years if necessary. What difference does it make? We are engaged in a world-wide struggle against the imperialistic ambitions of Russia. It happens, as General Eisenhower pointed out, that the most dramatic phase is Korea, but the same type of thing is going on in Indo-China and Malaya; and we have had to build up defensive forces in Europe against any surprise attack. There is no immediate hope of release from that obligation.
I suggest that we must take the longdistance view and be prepared to remain on the defensive in Korea for a number of years if necessary. To end the war quickly and withdraw from Korea can only be done at a 68108-451

Mr. Churchill very great cost of life, and even if we did end the war there and withdrew from Korea we would not be at all sure that the same method might not be followed a year or two later and we would again find ourselves engaged in that country. In any case, if we do end the war in Korea, what about the situation in Indo-China and in Malaya, and in other parts where the communist powers might strike? The realistic approach seems to be to take the long-distance view; to decide that we are engaged in a cold war that is going to last for years; to make adequate preparation to meet any surprise attack, doing that by effectively providing the arms and munitions. That would be precisely the investigation that I for one would like to have conducted here in Canada, to see that we are providing arms and munitions against these possibilities. If we are not doing so, then surely we are failing to maintain our strength as a country. Are we right in simply laying the foundation for a general mobilization? Maybe that is not what is required. Perhaps a general war is not in the immediate future, and let us hope it is not.
If it is not necessary to provide for general mobilization in the course of a few weeks or months, is it not better then to take the longterm view of providing effective fighting forces and of providing munitions for our allies so that throughout the world we can make an effective stand against the communist aggressors? I think that could be done, and lives could be saved by providing the munitions of war and not sacrificing infantry forces as it seems to me we are sacrificing them unnecessarily in Korea now. I believe that expenditure of ammunition in unlimited quantities, rather than these probing attacks by infantry forces, is the answer to that situation. Therefore I hope we may be able to discover that in this country we are well prepared to provide the required munitions in unlimited quantities.
I mentioned General Eisenhower's report a little while ago and his statement that certain problems of supply have reached serious proportions and require correction. I hope that does not apply to munitions; and if it does apply to munitions, something should be done about them at least.
All this ties in with the world picture as we see it; a world struggle against Russian imperialism, or communism if you like to use the term. We have to resign ourselves to a rather long struggle, but it is better to spend money and effort on arms, armour and ammunition than to simply raise infantry forces and pit them against shells, mortar and machine gun bullets fired by the Chinese.

That is the situation as I see it, and I hope the investigation of our defence requirements in this country, and the general interest of parliament and the people in our defence matters, will bring to us before very long all the information we need with regard to the defence situation in our country and the contributions we are making with our allies elsewhere in the world to build up this bulwark against communism. Only by facing these facts and not glossing over them can we expect to get an effective contribution from our Canadian people. That is why I object to calling a war, which is resulting in heavy casualties to our troops in Korea, a police action. That is why I object to our failure to recognize the problem as it exists in Europe. Our failure there, as I have pointed out in this house on other occasions, is to provide armoured forces so that our men will be protected. It has been proven in both wars that armour, the use of tanks and armoured vehicles, saves lives. If we place emphasis on these matters then perhaps we will not only be doing our duty to our own country and performing our part in the affairs of the United Nations, but we will also be protecting the lives of those men who so willingly volunteered for service overseas. In this connection, I am inclined to believe that a cut in the income tax would be in order and welcomed by the taxpayer. It is true that national defence expenditures are considerable, but they may be measured, I think, with the economy of the country, since the intensive production which takes place will bring about in the course of this year, or of the next, a surplus of goods which we shall have to store away.
That is the reason which brings us to consider, together with this reduction in expenditures, a fairly noticeable reduction in the income tax.
In acting thus, the government will satisfy the taxpayer and will be thus encouraged to pursue its defence preparations and fulfil the nation's commitments as party to the North Atlantic treaty which will inevitably assure us peace remote though it may be.
Another question of interest which has given rise to a few speeches in this house last year is that of immigration.
Far be it from me to oppose the coming of immigrants to Canada for immigration lessens the burden of less fortunate countries while Canada profits by it in that she gets people qualified in various fields of activity who contribute to increase her revenues.
The government endeavours to accept only the immigrants that can increase the skilled labour force so necessary to our economy.
I congratulate the government for keeping to that policy which will gain us appreciable advantages. I feel however that the immigration department should keep on working closely with the Department of Labour in order to protect the interests of our working class so as not to deprive our own people of their daily livelihood.
I wanted to bring to the attention of this house these two questions about which the taxpayers are worried. If a little relief can be given as far as taxes are concerned-I agree that those taxes are necessary on account of our defence preparations and the assistance we have to provide to the weak 

it will be a wise administrative move which will be generally appreciated.
Tax reductions would not only give confidence to the public and free it from that terrible feeling of discouragement but would create, in the taxpayer, the will to pursue his effort to the utmost.
During the last war, the taxpayer realized that he had to do his utmost; that is why he was willing to make sacrifices. Today, how-

ever, while understanding what is expected of him, the taxpayer cannot submit as freely to the sacrifices he made during the war period of 1939 to 1944.
As far as health insurance is concerned, a matter which is very much discussed and highly controversial when it comes to the ways and means of applying it, there is no doubt that one group of society, the white-collar workers and small owners, find themselves in an unfortunate situation when visited by sickness; they have to do without required care or to run into debt to such an extent as to pledge their salary for a long period. In the near future, some means of assistance should be found to provide all the necessary and urgent care to that group.
The infirm, who are quite a burden for some families, also present quite a problem.
We will have to help them soon, but the time to do so will be when the taxpayer has been reasonably freed from the fiscal burden which has been thrust upon his shoulders in these confused and difficult days.
The last time I spoke in this house, in 1951, I dealt with the problem of inflation and controls. I gave my opinion on both subjects. I am now pleased to observe that the measures advocated, which were adopted by the government in order to curb inflation, have had the expected results and that we are recovering in an appreciable manner.
Now about controls. Many learned economists have recognized the fact that the government has been well advised not to resort to them and to rely instead on the law of supply and demand.
During the past few years, Canadian trade and the gigantic development which we have witnessed have made our economy the most solid in the world and brought about a commercial expansion previously unheard of in our country.
One has but to read an article published in the November 5 issue of the New York Times to realize this. Several American magazines have only praise for the wise and enlightened administration of the government of this country. Our hon. friends opposite would do likewise if they would only say the truth and forget their thirst for power. That would be asking too much of them. But the people, who are the judge, will soon make their decision and grant the government of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent a well-deserved renewal of its mandate.
For some time much has been said about taxation powers to give the impression that the government at Ottawa is taking over all taxation fields, to the detriment of the provinces and municipalities.
The Address-Mr. Leduc
Let us examine together the situation of the provinces as well as of the municipalities. In a speech he made in the house last week, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) dealt with this matter in a masterly [DOT] way. He stated that the government at Ottawa was not taking anything away from the provinces. Now, the province of Quebec, which ten years ago had a revenue of approximately $58 million, and, seven years ago, of $96 million, had last year a revenue of $275 million. Can we say that her taxing power has been curtailed? Is it not true that the province of Quebec has authorized certain municipalities, and even certain school boards, to levy sales taxes? Is it not true that the province of Quebec has, in certain cases, levied a sales tax of 5 per cent? Is it not true that the province of Quebec taxes fuel oil and coal used for heating houses? Is it not true that the province of Quebec levies a tax on the electricity used for lighting purposes? Is it not true that a meal tax is in force in the province of Quebec, a tax which does not exist in Ontario or elsewhere? Is it not true that there is a tax on cigarettes? Is not the cost of driving licences higher in Quebec than in Ontario? Is not gasoline taxed also?
Now, the revenue of the province of Quebec is five times what it was ten years ago and three times what it was seven years ago. Is the province of Quebec feeling guilty for these higher taxes? Contracts are awarded without tenders. Does that not indicate that there is money aplenty in the province of Quebec?
Now, as far as the federal government is concerned, it is one of the few governments who, in the past few years, have actually reduced taxes.
In 1945 the Canadian government collected, in revenue, $2,687 million; in 1946, $3,013 million; in 1947, $3,007 million; in 1948, $2,871 million; in 1949, $2,771 million and, in 1950, $2,580 million.
If the government was forced to increase taxes, it is because of the defence effort we have had to accept for the security of our country and for the repression of aggression. The government is always willing to decrease taxes when there is no necessity for the country to have as much money as is now the case.
Where do these amounts which we are now spending go to?-that is these $4 billion and more. For each dollar the breakdown is as follows: 3 cents to the provinces, 14-5 cents for social security, 5-5 cents for the various veterans allowances, 13-5 cents

The Address-Mr, Leduc for interest charges and 6 cents for debt reduction, that is the surplus that can be applied to tax reduction.
Have the municipalities lost their means of taxation? In my own community in 1944, revenues were $800,000 and we were enabled to reduce taxes. In 1952 this figure had gone up to $1,800,000, that is $1 million more in a period of some six years. Can it be inferred from that that the taxation powers of the municipalities have diminished? I could point out the case of several other municipalities of the province of Quebec which are in the same position.
When a municipality imposes a tax in order to meet the cost of certain municipal services, does it eliminate such tax, once the debt has been paid off? Quite the contrary; it keeps on using this means of taxation and even tries to find others in order to raise taxes even more. It is the sense of thrift that has vanished; our provincial and municipal leaders everywhere have lost all sense of thrift.
Is it possible that the increase in salaries and cost of materials might absorb these increases of revenue?

maintopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-REPORT BY MR. G. S. CURRIE. REPORT ON THE CANADIAN ARMY WORKS SERVICES WITH SPECIAL REFERENCE TO THE IRREGULARITIES UNCOVERED AT CAMP PETAWAWA

speechtext:
November 26, 1952
The Honourable Brooke Claxton, D.C.M., Q.C., M.P.,
Minister of National Defence,
Ottawa, Canada
Dear Sir,
In accordance with your request of April 21, 1952, I have conducted an investigation into the deficiencies and other irregularities of the engineering detachment of the army works services at Petawawa and elsewhere. My terms of reference were contained in your telegram of that date as follows:
Confirming telephone please undertake immediate investigation and report earliest possible date into deficiencies and other irregularities engineering detachment at Petawawa and related matters there, or elsewhere both to determine cause and make recommendations regarding security and accounting for stores equipment and services so as to prevent recurrence with any additional powers or terms of reference which are necessary to make complete and thorough investigation and report.
I accepted this task. May I express my thanks to you and to all departments of government, including of course the Department of National Defence, for the ready and full co-operation afforded me. I found the terms of reference suggested by you ample and complete for the purposes of the inquiry. It should be noted that interim suggestions made by me during my investigations have been already seized on, and important reforms are already being carried out.
My investigations have taken me not only to Petawawa, but also to Toronto, London, Borden, Barriefield, Vancouver, Regina, Quebec and Halifax. At all these points comprehensive general examinations were made of works companies and detachments.

maintopic: THE IRREGULARITIES AT PETAWAWA AND THEIR CAUSES

speechtext:
The conclusion I have come to is that, while there has been a general breakdown in the system of administration, supervision and accounting, it was only at Petawawa that extensive irregularities over a prolonged period of time took place. The contents of this chapter are chiefly based upon my studies there, because of the existence there of a combination of factors: lax control, poor
discipline and the presence of dishonest personnel. The combination proved disastrous.
It is mentioned in this context chiefly for the purpose of praising the personnel at other depots for not walking through the door which a fundamentally loose situation had opened before them. It does not fit the facts to indict or to smear the whole army works services personnel because of the sins of a handful of crooks.
The Discovery of the Irregularities and their Nature
At Petawawa, however, the crooks were present and took advantage of the situation, and it is an unhappy circumstance that the beginning of this investigation lies not inside the Department of National Defence and its full complement of regulations and supervising personnel, but with the receipt of an [DOT] anonymous letter couched in the following terms:
The Commissioner,
Royal Canadian Mounted Police,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,
There is reason to believe that an illegal transaction of army goods has taken place between army personnel of No. 3 works coy., R.C.E., and	company within the past few days.
This transaction involves the selling of several railway car loads of cook stoves and heaters without proper army authority. The C.P.R. station agent at Petawawa village could give you the destination of these cars.
No signature can be attached to this letter, but a good number of taxpayers have seen this deal and think that something should be done about it. If it is not an illegal deal, no harm will be done if enquiries are made, but yet if it is an illegal deal a number of other such transactions might be revealed.
Before reciting the irregularities and their circumstances uncovered by the R.C.M.P.- with the assistance later of the provincial police and the army provost corps-it must be said that internal warnings had not been lacking in the Department of National Defence. The chief auditor of the department had performed his functions conscientiously. Time and again he had reported unsatisfactory conditions. This is clear from Appendix "B" which summarizes his findings over a period of years. The deputy minister in each case had directed the quartermaster general to investigate and report. Lack of

adequate action at this point had, however, caused a progressive deterioration in the situation. Aside from reports being delayed for considerable periods of time, the record shows the next audit revealing conditions similar to those previously reported and, in some cases, worse. The process is then again repeated.
The actual irregularities uncovered at Peta-wawa are difficult to deal with in this report. The reasons for this, and for my dependence in large measure on police reports, are set forth later. The difficulties are enhanced by the fact that in various instances court proceedings have been instituted or are under contemplation. It is important, at this time, not to jeopardize these proceedings either from the point of view of the crown or of the accused. At the same time, it seems to me the public interest demands that this report should include a more or less detailed description of the nature of the irregularities which took place. I have therefore attempted to summarize them.
You will remember that, in each case, army personnel were involved; and that, in most cases, whether proceedings are taken or not, or whether these issue successfully for the crown, army goods have been recovered by the police which is fairly successful proof that army goods were widely spread in places where, under the regulations, they had no business to be. In a substantial number of cases, army personnel have signed statements admitting the correctness of the facts stated.
A series of transactions concerned the disposal of scrap metal. In one case, a proper contract was let for the disposal of 30 tons, in another, of 15 tons. It seems that some 550 tons were shipped out of the camp area, and that the proceeds from the bulk of the sale were pocketed by army personnel. Some of the metal thus shipped was not scrap at all. It consisted of serviceable material such as kitchen ranges, cannon heaters, shower-stalls, sinks and the like. Most of this material was recovered. In one striking instance, a large quantity of rails belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway was removed. When this loss was noted by the C.P.R. and questions raised, a spur line of the Canadian National running into the ordnance depot was taken up and the rails used to replace the missing C.P.R. track. Another case involved the collection of lead from rifle butts and its private sale.
A contract was awarded for the clearing of the camp "X" area. It covered the clearing of 206 acres, though only 166 acres were cleared and that not satisfactorily. In this, as in the scrap metal cases cited and, indeed, in others, 68108-46
National Defence-Currie Report army equipment was used although the contract called for the company to use its own equipment. During the clearing of this area horses were hired by army personnel and placed on the payroll under the names of non-existent labourers. In another instance, a civilian employee of the detachment got a contract for cutting and hauling cedar poles. Permission was given to use an army bulldozer and other equipment on the job. Lumber was apparently cut from the area to be trucked to Camp Petawawa. Its final destination cannot now be accurately traced.
An electric refrigerator was obtained from a local hardware store, and billed to the works department as other material. When electric refrigerators became available, the steel ice-boxes previously used were not returned to stores but turned into a hardware store and traded for other merchandise chosen by army personnel. A boat and several washing machines were obtained by putting through a false order for 1,000 bags of cement. The boat has been traced at Petawawa and one of the washing machines was located in the men's quarters. Rolls of linoleum were stolen, some of which was recovered later. Two freight carloads of pulpwood appear to have been stolen during the cutting of a power line.
In various instances it has been ascertained that army personnel were employed to construct such articles as boats, desks, beds, chests of drawers, coffee tables, chairs and, in one instance, a child's rocking horse, all for private use and not for government service. The material used was army material, and though some of it, the latter at least, was subsequently paid for by the personnel concerned, the wages of the workmen employed were not.
A dam was built on Tucker creek at a cost estimated at some $3,000 or $4,000. Its utility is not clear to me, and it was, in any event, not authorized by army headquarters.
In certain cases, persons buying army material were asked not to make cheques in payment (in whole or in part) to the receiver general but to individual army personnel. The amounts thus paid did not reach the public treasury.
In another case, a member of the detachment was hired by a private company and paid for 13 weeks at the rate of $100 a week. The company claimed its temporary employee told it that accumulated leave would permit him to fulfil his obligations which involved the setting out and detailing of houses in the camp townsite. The man in question denies this, stating he performed these private duties in his spare time. He also denies that there
714	HOUSE OF
National Defence-Currie Report was any secret and improper element in the transaction which was, nevertheless, clearly improper under the regulations.
Private and improper sales of gravel were made by responsible personnel in charge of a gravel pit leased under strict terms by the Department of National Defence.
It was the practice at Petawawa to lend cement and other materials from army stores to private contractors in the district. No record was kept of these loans, and the materials were usually not returned until the army asked for them. The explanation given was that the private work being done was of an urgent nature, that materials were scarce, and that only the government had the priorities with which to obtain them. It was also stated that personnel were not available to keep the proper records.
A contractor received payment in full on a $32,000 contract for laying sewer pipe and manholes, although some $4,000 of the work had been completed by the army before the private contractor began work. The explanation in this case was that a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation inspector erroneously accepted verbal progress reports from an assistant. The company also claims that the payment asked for was the result of an office employee being unfamiliar with procedures in such cases.
The Attempts to Estimate Losses
These, then, represent the ascertained cases of irregularity at Petawawa. How many more there may have been will never be known. It was apparent from the beginning of the investigation that the accounting records were in a chaotic condition and would be of little use in determining the nature and extent of irregularities. It is impractical, and perhaps impossible, regardless of the time which might be spent on examining records, to try and determine by this means the amount and value of the deficiencies.
This conclusion is based upon the results of a single, determined effort to ascertain by accounting methods the extent of the shortage existing in the case of a single item of stores. Cement was chosen as a test case, largely because the number of suppliers of that commodity were few in number and easy to find. Six weeks were spent in the effort. The suppliers produced their record of cement supplied to Petawawa. All army records were examined and audited. The contractors in the area to whom supplies of cement might have been given, sold or loaned, readily opened their books. As a result of the inquiry, it appeared that one loan of 3,400 bags of cement had not been returned. The

over-all shortage appeared to be some 18,000 bags, much of which may have gone into unauthorized projects of one kind or another, or wasted or pilfered in small quantities. It was impossible to ascertain exactly what had happened. But my test cement investigation convinced me that to attempt a similar study of all the 5,000 items of stores held would be endless and probably fruitless.
In such circumstances, when rigid accounting methods fail, police examination is the only available recourse left. This has been carried out with painstaking thoroughness, and leads me to the belief that most, if not all, the important irregularities have been uncovered. The police too, have been able to recover by far the greater quantity of the missing goods, and these have been returned to stores.
No reliable estimate of the total loss can be prepared. It does, however, appear probable that the total loss resulting from misappropriations and irregularities by military personnel at Petawawa was not large. The advantages gained by civilians dealing with corrupt military personnel are not clearly ascertainable. My view would be, however, that the generally lax administrative situation would give rise to waste and inefficiency far more costly in loss than that covered by actual dishonesty. The evidence examined does not disclose irregularities involving relatively large sums of money, but, rather, an impressive array of petty irregularities on an extensive scale.
Breakdown of the Accounting System
The fault did not lie in the accounting system, which was a good one had it been operated properly. It was a new system, based on American and British as well as Canadian experience, and embodied features which, theoretically, would have quickly checked irregularities as they appeared. Under the regulations, had they been enforced, it would have been possible to determine from the perpetual inventory records the quantities and values of engineers' stores which should have been on hand at any given time. Then, by means of a comparison with a physical count of stores, the shortages could have been ascertained. The regulations of the army works services require that a 10% inventory of stores be made every month. The accounting system, however, was not properly operated, nor were the regulation inventories methodically carried out.
My investigations show that at least 33 regulations have been in the past honoured more in the breach than in the observance with the result that many of the control features of

the accounting system were rendered ineffective. They had to do with:
(1)	Authorization of projects.
(2)	Approval of works orders.
(3)	Presentation of work orders as the only basis for issuance of stores.
(4)	Preparation of accounting cost estimates.
(5)	Follow-up by works company officers on efficient use of labour and material.
(6)	Return of excess materials issued to jobs.
(7)	Excess materials from one job being used on another.
(8)	Unauthorized projects and services.
(9)	Wasteful expenditures.
(10)	Segregation of stores and warehousing generally.
(11)	Physical inventory counts.
(12)	Disposal of stores.
(13)	Loans to individuals.
(14)	Splitting of projects to come within local authority.
(15)	Accounting for forms CAB's 83 and 83A by serial numbers.
(16)	Unauthorized forms.
(17)	Distribution of work orders.
(18)	Cross-charging practices.
(19)	Payments to military personnel rather than to the receiver general.
(20)	Padding payrolls.
(21)	Obtaining materials and commencing work prior to authorization of projects.
(22)	Unauthorized accumulation of materials from completed works and a failure to take on charge surplus materials.
(23)	Failure to record non-expendable stores issued to buildings.
(24)	Failure to record the change in location of installed equipment.
(25)	Errors in recording values on stock record cards.
(26)	Adjustment of discrepancies revealed at stock taking without reference to higher authority.
(27)	Irregular delegation of authority to sign work orders.
(28)	Estimated costs being exceeded by substantial amounts without reference to higher authority.
(29)	Labour and materials charged to approved works but delivered to other jobs.
(30)	Condition of real property records.
(31)	Inaccurate distribution in cost records.
(32)	Certain removable equipment was not listed accurately in property records and stores.
(33)	Improper loans of materials and rental of equipment to civilian contractors.

There was in addition a serious collapse in security. There was little to prevent or to detect the organized plundering of military stores on a systematic scale, though apparently comparatively little of it took place. If there is excuse for inefficient accounting, there is none for the failure of security which is, after all, a prime military consideration. I take a serious view of this breakdown. If it is easy to pilfer military stores, then, by the same token, it is easy to sabotage military equipment. My recommendations in this respect are fully outlined later.
Strains of the Korean War
My investigations of the problems, difficulties and shortcomings of the army works services outlined above suggest that they have been caused for the most part-but by no means altogether-by the tremendous and sudden expansion of its activities brought about by the Korean war and by the large-scale defence program involved in carrying out our NATO activities.
The establishment approved for the army works services after the second world war did not envisage the sudden expansion which was to take place in 1950. It was designed to carry out a purely peacetime role of planning, development and construction on an annual expenditure of approximately $20,000,000. This establishment became quickly burdened under the impact of the big-scale rearmament. In September, 1950, the program was increased to about $80,000,000. In the following April, it was increased to about $200,000,000. The program envisaged in the 1952-53 fiscal year aggregates about $250,000,000. The magnitude of this responsibility is reflected in an investment in plant and buildings which now amounts to $750,000,000 and is still rising.
During the 1952-53 period, the Petawawa detachment will expend something in excess of $1,000,000 on its own account, as well as having administrative responsibility for supervising some $20,000,000 of new construction performed by outside parties. It will readily be seen that the detachment's job is by no means a small one, but comparable perhaps to a medium-sized commercial construction company.
In the circumstances of sudden re-armament, the army works services of necessity was not permitted time to re-organize itself for this tremendous expansion, particularly since, it will be recalled, no one knew then whether the communist aggression in Korea was not the beginning of concerted Sino-Russian attacks in all available theatres of
716	HOUSE OF
National Defence-Currie Report war. Many sections of the services became completely overwhelmed with work.
The situation was complicated by still another factor. The Department of National Defence (including the army works services) was largely staffed and manned by men whose military training had been received in wartime. Its establishment and administrative practices reflected more clearly the urgent needs and exigencies of war, when speed is everything and costs count not at all. The carry-forward of this war psychology must be coupled with inadequate training and resultant ignorance on the part of personnel of their administrative duties and responsibilities. There was, in addition, indifference and reluctance on the part of military personnel to concentrate on administration to the degree required. It was not perhaps unnatural that these latter needs were largely forgotten or deliberately overlooked as soldiers gazed forward into the unknown consequences of the Korean outbreak, and foresaw still greater wars not very far away. But, if this spirit permeated the lower echelons of the army, it is more difficult to condone the same attitudes higher up. There, a higher degree both of intelligence and responsibility is essential. It was not always present in the degree required.

subtopic: PROPOSED REORGANIZATION OF THE ARMY WORKS SERVICES

speechtext:
Role of ihe Army Works Services
The army works services is not necessarily a distinct and separate unit within an army. It is, in Canada, an ad hoc organization, drawn from various units and groupings, chiefly the Royal Canadian Engineers, and including a number of civilians. Its function is to provide and care for accommodation of all kinds for the maintenance of the active and reserve forces of the Canadian army in Canada, and to provide land and structures, and care for them, in order to permit these forces to carry out their tasks. Thus it provides for defence and special works, provides and distributes engineer stores, creates Are fighting services and plans accommodation and other works requirements for mobilization and war.
It is included in the composition of the army for the sole purpose of providing necessary facilities for the rest of the army. It maintains the most direct contact with the civil engineering profession in Canada and its military components are thus kept abreast of current engineering practice in all phases of civil and related engineering.

Handling of Expenditures
Expenditures of the army works services are estimated each year in advance, screened carefully at all levels by the service, the staff and finally by the general officers commanding and the chief of the general staff. These are presented to the minister. The usual annual program of the army works services comprises the following main tasks:
(1)	The requisite maintenance program-a fixed commitment.
(2)	That proportion of the planned new
construction program approved by the government for the year.
(3)	The planning of further new construction and maintenance requirements.
The voting of funds in bulk allotments by parliament represents the direct control exercised by the people of Canada on the country's military activity. Funds so voted are controlled to varying degrees depending on the amount and nature of the expenditure. In all cases, the treasury officer, who is appointed by the Department of Finance to work within the Department of National Defence, must certify that the necessary money is available and that the expenditure is in fact in accordance with the purpose for which the funds were voted.
In addition, an "administrative" approval of the expenditure is necessary to ensure that the expenditure is in accordance with current government and National Defence policies, is economical, and is made in accordance with sound and fair business practices. With the department, such approvals can only be given by the minister and by the deputy and his staff, together with senior army officers who have been specifically delegated by the minister. The expenditure of public funds for construction purposes is further controlled by regulations requiring that large projects be screened by the Department of Defence Production and the treasury board to ascertain their effect on the current labour and material situation in the locality in Canada in which they are required. This special review is intended to prevent avoidable interference with the general economy of the country.
It is the policy at all levels to avoid using "direct to trade" purchasing powers, except where essential, to maintain the excellent relations which have been established with the Department of Defence Production and to use that agency as the normal purchasing channel. It is a further policy to use the contract method for construction and maintenance wherever possible and consistent with true economy and efficiency. In the normal course of events, all major new construction

projects are let by contract. Exceptions are made to the policy only in particular circumstances such as exist in northern Canada where it is desired to make use of the training value of large day-labour projects.
Limiting Factors
The capacity of the army works services to perform its tasks is hampered by-
(1)	Inability to obtain staff (civilian as well as military).
(2)	Delays in obtaining approval and in
the release of funds.
(3)	Effect of government restriction in the
use of day-labour and other restrictions in the method of purchasing and letting of contracts.
The administrative procedures involved in the above, to a varying degree, of necessity effect a reduction in the efficiency and the capacity of the army works services.
Objective
What is needed now is the creation of a system designed to fit the economic and efficient administration of a large and long-sustained preparedness program inside a national economy operating at full blast. This involves the abandonment, by all administrators of the program, of the war psychology with its emphasis on speed with resultant wastefulness and extravagance, and the substitution of an alert, economic and efficient operation, flexibly designed, to be sure, to meet emergencies, but designed also to become a more or less permanent part of Canadian life and government.
Need for Managerial Skills
The foregoing study and analysis of the situation at Petawawa have led me to certain general and specific conclusions regarding the future of the army works services, and the problems which confront it. These involve the recruitment and training of personnel on a basis quite different from that of the past. Changes in administrative methods and responsibilities are also needed. These involve organization and control.
Certain principles may be stated in this connection. The first of these is to have good men about. This is complicated in the army works services because:
1.	At army headquarters level it is basically a military organization and it is not free to pay the prices necessary to acquire top-flight administrators in key posts.
2.	Personnel in the R.C.E. and the army generally are sometimes promoted for reasons other than administrative
National Defence-Currie Report ability, e.g., in the army works services, engineering ability. Accordingly, an officer may find in his rise up the ladder that he is faced with successively greater administrative jobs for which he is ill-suited.
This situation has a parallel in civilian life in that the most important ablity of the head of a small business is technical ability. As the size of the business increases, the importance of managerial ability increases and that of technical ability declines. In medium-sized businesses, the two tend to be of equal importance. The most important quality in the heads of a large organization is managerial ability, and, the larger the concern, the more important this becomes.
Need for Reorganization
The emphasis in the army works services organization at one time was quite properly placed on technical skills, but, in its present size, emphasis should be shifted to managerial and administrative ability in key posts. The drive in civilian life is for efficiency and control, and these are major requrements of the army works services in its present state of expansion. Any deficiency in filling these posts will result in overloading the next in charge, and will throw the organization out of balance. Thus, a major problem confronts the army works services in filling its establishment at defence headquarters.
A problem of the army works services relates to organization since-
(1)	Its organization has been neither good nor adequate at all levels,
(2)	Organization changes which have been made are a result of some segment being overwhelmed.
(3)	Reorganizations approved by the civil service commission and establishment committees have not been realistic and reflect a lack of understanding of army works services problems.
To make an organization effective it is important to develop personnel. Plans in this respect normally include:
1.	Selection of candidates for training.
2.	Training to meet job requirements.
3.	Systematic and gradual development
through selected positions of responsibility.	[DOT]
4.	Control over appointments to key positions.
5.	Clear-cut assignment of responsibility for carrying out the program.
The army works services appear to have fallen down badly in this respect. Certain key positions have not been provided for. Key positions have not been adequately filled,

National Defence-Currie Report and training and control over promotion of personnel have not been conducive to maximum efficiency.
A well managed organization requires a fair wage structure properly administered. This requires a suitable agency sometimes referred to as a personnel manager. At present in the army works services this factor is not co-ordinated and well planned and has contributed in a serious degree to personnel problems in respect of civilians employed by the service. Changes usually occur on a piece-meal basis and normally involve fruitless disputes with the civil service commission and establishment committees. In many cases, unsatisfactory arrangements result. The functions of a personnel manager normally involve-
1.	Assisting in job analyses.
2.	Assessing relative job values.
3.	Comparisons with outside rates.
4.	Maintenance of records to show-
(a)	How wage rates compare with outside scales;
(b)	Recommended changes to maintain wage policies.
5.	Reviewing changes in job classifications and rates.
6.	In general to co-ordinate and initiate steps necessary to create and maintain a sound and fair wage structure.
Difficulties have arisen in the army works services organization arising from the employment of civilian personnel working alongside enlisted men in the same organization. It has been difficult to attract suitable and competent civilians to work for the army works services due to-lack of career possibilities-inadequate salaries-insecurity of employment.
In any reorganization, the establishment need not necessarily have the proposed military element, and, because of the relatively frequent changes in postings of military personnel, it might perhaps be better organized with more permanent civilians. This problem has, in all probability, appeared in other lands. In both the United Kingdom and the United States, civilians are used in the army works services in relatively larger numbers than in Canada. This has resulted in a marked saving in military manpower, and may also have the advantage of placing civilian-trained, rather than military-trained, men in many posts which are, after all, essentially civilian in character.
The Proposed Reorganization
I have drawn up four alternative plans for the needed reorganization.
Alternative No. 1
The first is to improve and further develop the existing organization by-
1.	Reorganizing the service at A.H.Q. and other levels so that it is more appropriate for its vast managerial responsibilities.
2.	Improving the calibre of civilian personnel (at least in key positions) by revising salary scales and more efficient selection methods.
3.	Creating suitable training courses in administration.
4.	Creating a suitable inspection and service division to keep top personnel fully informed on conditions and to act as an instrument to clear bottlenecks and train personnel on the job.
5.	Placing proper emphasis on administrative efficiency.
6.	Freeing top personnel from detailed administrative duties to enable them to make uninhibited inspections down the line so that they can initiate remedial action through the machinery created in 4 above.
7.	Generally implementing the various measures suggested by this report.
Alternative No. 2
The second alternative is to create a civilian organization running parallel to a military organization up through commands to army headquarters. This alternative would-
1.	Relieve military personnel of most of the administrative function and enable them to concentrate on planning and on executive direction of works.
2.	Open up career possibilities to civilians and thus attract high calibre permanent personnel and provide stability to administration now difficult to achieve.
The advantage of this course of action would appear to be the combining of greater administrative stability and efficiency with a valuable training element for R.C.E. personnel.
Alternative No. 3
The third alternative envisages the creation of a completely civilian army works services under the Q.M.G. but operating outside command channels and tied in directly to army headquarters. Such an organization as this would avoid considerable duplication in administrative work and delay in getting things done which are involved in the operation of the army works services through command channels. That is, something along the lines of a holding company with operating subsidiaries. Liaison at various levels whereby requests for work would flow into

the service would necessitate certain military-personnel attached to the organization. Also the broad planning function would continue under the chief of the general staff. Execution of such plans would then flow through the quartermaster general to the army works services.
The main advantages here would appear to be savings in administrative and technical manpower, and those generally applicable to, say, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The objections are that the army works services would, for the most part, cease to be a training ground for military engineers.
Alternative No. 4
The fourth alternative is that the Department of Public Works take over army works services. This might effect a certain saving in technical manpower not attained by the first and second alternatives but perhaps accomplished to a degree by the third alternative.
The objections are:
1.	A department which becomes too big tends to become unwieldy and inefficient.
2.	Non-utilization of R.C.E. engineers who do compensate to a degree for the shortage of civilian engineers.
3.	Too slow and cumbersome to meet army needs.
In assessing the possibilities of these various alternatives, short-term considerations and long-term considerations play a part. Precedent exists for alternative number 2 in the United Kingdom and the United States where army works services are largely civilian in structure. Alternatives 3 and 4 represent radically different structures and their introduction at this stage of expansion might create harmful confusion. It would, therefore, appear advisable to adopt alternative No. 1 at the moment and gradually develop *the organization along lines suggested under alternative No. 2. The introduction of civilian administrative and technical stores officers, *chief foremen of works and estimators would constitute a major step in this direction. Once this has been accomplished further development along the lines suggested by alternative No. 3 would be relatively easy. As long as the army works services exists in its present size, alternative No. 4 would appear to be unwise.
National Defence-Currie Report

The six major problems of the army works services appear to be:
1.	Organization
2.	Personnel
3.	Control
4.	Accounting
5.	Stores
6.	Security

During the fiscal periods following the Korean crisis the Department of National Defence has been physically unable to carry out its budgeted program of expenditures. In the case of the army works services the major obstacles have been poor organization, lack of control and of sufficient technical personnel.
Army Headquarters
For example, at army headquarters some fourteen different functions were the direct responsibility of one man. These functions were represented by the following:
1.	Finance
2.	Stores
3.	Real property
4.	Administration (H.Q.)

14.	Architect standards
The control of these functions involving expenditure of $20,000,000 was a big job. A program of $250,000,000 has made the task impossible. To correct this situation the department has recently developed a new organization for the army works services at army headquarters.
Under this new organization, the post of deputy quartermaster general (works) has been created. Directly responsible to him are two directors, namely, works and quartering, and responsibility is broken down under these two directors in a clear-cut manner.
Good organization in a large undertaking requires that not more than seven and preferably five functions report directly to
